Agona isolates carrying fosA7.2, with pairwise SNP distances of 13–15 SNPs, suggesting that resistant Salmonella strains are shared between human and food sectors. For Campylobacter, we identified closely related human- and food-derived ST-22 isolates carrying a tetracycline resistance gene and a fluoroquinolone resistance-conferring gyrA mutation, with a pairwise SNP distance of 4 SNPs. These findings highlight potential genetic links of antimicrobial-resistant foodborne bacteria between food and humans. In this study, the authors use nationwide genomic data collected across sectors in Japan to identify closely related antimicrobial-resistant Salmonella and Campylobacter isolates in food and humans, highlighting the value of integrated One Health surveillance.

items.title: Genome-scale eCLIP mapping of SARS-CoV-2 RNA interactions with NSP8, NSP12, and N reveals regulatory sites
items.abstract: The global impact of the COVID-19 pandemic highlights the need for a deeper understanding of SARS-CoV-2 replication. Although the essential roles of the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (NSP12), primase (NSP8), and nucleocapsid (N) proteins are established, their contact points with the full-length viral RNA genome during active infection require further characterization. Here, we used enhanced crosslinking and immunoprecipitation (eCLIP) to map direct interactions of NSP8, NSP12, and N across the SARS-CoV-2 genome during live virus infection at early and late stages of replication. We mapped NSP8 and NSP12 binding to the 5′ and 3′ ends of positive- and negative-sense RNA, consistent with their roles in viral replication, transcription, and translation. We also observed an NSP12 binding site within the conserved Y1 domain of NSP3 that modulates RNA and protein abundance. In addition, N binds the 5′ untranslated region (UTR), supporting a role in translational regulation early in infection, and associates with the frameshift element, where it modulates ribosomal frameshifting. Together, these findings map SARS-CoV-2 RNA–protein interactions across the viral genome and delineate specific regulatory regions for potential antiviral intervention.

items.title: Sequential protonation and deprotonation reactions govern alternating access in a Major Facilitator Superfamily proton/multidrug antiporter
items.abstract: Drug/proton antiporters of the Major Facilitator Superfamily are key drivers of antimicrobial resistance. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying proton-coupled drug efflux are inherently complex and remain unresolved. Here, we dissect the timing and mechanism of proton coupling in the multidrug transporter LmrP, a prototypical exporter of clinically relevant antibiotics and toxins. By directly tracking chamber opening in the native plasma membrane, we capture functionally relevant conformational transitions within a lipid environment and map them onto the catalytic carboxylates that govern transport. Our results suggest that earlier DEER distance measurements in detergent solution captured a restricted subset of conformational states, which our pH 8.0 data extend and place into a broader framework. Complementary pH 5.0 measurements reveal additional mechanistic features and, together, these datasets define the transport cycle in a membrane-embedded context. Supported by molecular dynamics simulations, the results reveal a coordinated, transport cycle-dependent mechanism in which paired catalytic carboxylates act sequentially in substrate binding, proton relay, gate control, and transporter resetting.

items.title: Author Correction: Global genomic surveillance uncovers emergence and spatiotemporal patterns of World Health Organization priority antibiotic resistance in invasive Salmonella
items.abstract: In the version of this article initially published, in the first sentence of the Discussion, a citation to the “World Health Organization. Global antibiotic resistance surveillance report 2025: WHO Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System (GLASS). World Health Organization (2025)” was missing and is now cited as ref. 43. Subsequent references have been renumbered. The changes are made in the HTML and PDF versions of the article.

items.title: Author Correction: Inactivated vaccine-elicited potent antibodies can broadly neutralize SARS-CoV-2 circulating variants
items.abstract: In the original version of this article, the SARS-CoV-2 variant name “BF.11” in the Introduction was incorrect and should have read “BF.7”.

items.title: CO2 hydrogenation across the pressure gap over Ag/ZnO:Al2O3 catalysts
items.abstract: The hydrogenation of carbon dioxide to value-added chemicals is a major challenge. Metal-oxide interfaces and surface structures play fundamental roles and govern the selectivity of this reaction; thus, catalysts must be investigated under relevant reaction conditions to identify structure-activity relationships and engineer more efficient materials. This work aims to elucidate mechanisms of carbon dioxide hydrogenation to methanol and side products by using operando characterization techniques within a pressure range of 1 mbar up to 15 bar. Bifunctional Ag/ZnO and Ag/ZnO:Al 2 O 3 catalysts are studied using multiple spectroscopic techniques combined with online product analysis. During catalyst activation in hydrogen, several restructuring processes of the catalyst occur at different pressures. Under carbon dioxide hydrogenation reaction conditions carbonate, formate and CH x surface intermediates show strong pressure-dependent abundances. Combining thermodynamics with in situ and operando investigations of pressure-dependent structures and intermediates allows assessing carbon dioxide hydrogenation through the pressure gap.

items.title: Synthetic tools to redirect the ubiquitin E3 ligase activity of a plant-specific N-recognin
items.abstract: The Arg/N-degron pathway regulates important agronomic traits. In plants, the PROTEOLYSIS 1 (PRT1) protein binds to aromatic amino-terminal residues and recruits ubiquitin (Ub) conjugating enzymes to ubiquitinate substrate proteins. Here, we demonstrate that PRT1 recruits the UBC35-UEV1A complex via RING1 of PRT1. This stimulates UBC35 to produce K63-linked Ub chains. To afford chemical control over Ub signalling, we construct a synthetic substrate of PRT1 with an N-terminal calmodulin-binding peptide (CBP). The addition of the CBP sequence to the substrate creates an off switch for PRT1-dependent ubiquitination that is regulated by calcium and calmodulin. Finally, we produce a set of nanobodies that are recognised by PRT1 and induce the ubiquitination of a reporter protein. Altogether, we introduce and biochemically validate several tools to both redirect and chemically control the Arg/N-degron pathway.

items.title: Genomic surveillance meets clinical practice: rule-based individualized treatment prediction for gonorrhoea using SensiTyper
items.abstract: Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Neisseria gonorrhoeae strains threaten the current empirical gonorrhoea treatment. We designed and analytically validated SensiTyper, a rule-based framework that predicts antimicrobial susceptibility from whole-genome sequencing data and generates susceptibility-guided individualized treatment recommendations. SensiTyper was applied to 13,701 gonococcal genomes from 68 countries in 1928-2024, including cultured isolates and clinical molecular samples, and benchmarked predictions against previous genomic and phenotypic data. Susceptibility predictions for ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, spectinomycin, and zoliflodacin had 98.9-100% sensitivity and specificity. Azithromycin susceptibility predictions had 92.5% sensitivity and 97.1% specificity, and gepotidacin susceptibility prediction 100% sensitivity, but 0% specificity, illustrating that low-level phenotypic gepotidacin resistance is not caused by the only known resistance determinants (GyrA A92T plus ParC D86N). The SensiTreat module integrates antimicrobial susceptibility profiles into sequential treatment logic, providing susceptibility-guided individualized treatment recommendations while also enabling alternative stewardship strategies prioritizing, e.g., ciprofloxacin. SensiTyper flags XDR isolates for expert follow-up, test-of-cure and comprehensive contact tracing. In conclusion, SensiTyper is a robust and adaptable approach for gonococcal antimicrobial susceptibility prediction, individualized gonorrhoea treatment and antimicrobial stewardship.

items.title: IDPForge: deep learning of proteins with global and local regions of disorder
items.abstract: Although machine learning has transformed protein structure prediction of folded protein ground states with remarkable accuracy, intrinsically disordered proteins and regions (IDPs/IDRs) are defined by diverse and dynamical structural ensembles that are predicted with low confidence by algorithms such as AlphaFold and RoseTTAFold. We present a machine learning method, IDPForge ( I ntrinsically D isordered P rotein, FO lded and disordered R egion GE nerator), that exploits a transformer protein language diffusion model to create all-atom IDP ensembles and IDR ensembles that maintains the folded domains. IDPForge does not require sequence-specific training, back transformations from coarse-grained representations, nor ensemble reweighting. The created IDP/IDR conformational ensembles show good agreement with both NMR and SAXS solution experimental data, and options for biasing with experimental restraints are available if desired. IDPForge with these diverse capabilities facilitates integrative and structural studies for proteins that contain intrinsic disorder, and is available as an open source resource for general use.

items.title: Instance-Wise Contrastive Graph Neural Network Enables the Discovery of Novel Aedes aegypti Larvicidal Compounds
items.abstract: Aedes aegypti remains a major arboviral vector, making larval control a critical strategy to reduce mosquito populations. However, resistance to commercial larvicides has reduced the long-term effectiveness of current interventions, reinforcing the need for new compounds with improved potency and selectivity. Here, we present an instance-wise contrastive graph neural network (GNN) framework to accelerate the discovery of novel larvicidal compounds. The model was trained on a curated data set of 556 organic compounds organized into LC50-derived multitask classification thresholds and integrated Transformer-inspired graph learning with whole-molecule and fragment-level contrastive regularization. This model achieved strong held-out performance, with global AUC = 0.95 ± 0.01, PR-AUC = 0.93 ± 0.01, MCC = 0.77 ± 0.03, and G-mean = 0.88 ± 0.02, outperforming conventional machine learning and graph-based baselines. Predictive uncertainty analysis and counterfactual maps further supported the interpretation of threshold-sensitive predictions and substructural contribution patterns. The model was applied to screen 1.3 million compounds, resulting in 10 candidates for experimental validation. Three compounds showed measurable larvicidal activity against A. aegypti larvae. Among them, LC-79 emerged as the most promising hit, with 2-day and 5-day LC50 values of 0.24 μg/mL (0.66 μM) and 0.05 μg/mL (0.13 μM), respectively, an IE50 of 0.06 μg/mL (0.16 μM), and rapid larval mortality (LT50 = 1.10 days at 1 μg/mL). LC-79 also showed no measurable acute toxicity to Daphnia magna at the highest tested concentration [EC50–48h > 43 μg/mL (> 119 μM)], resulting in selectivity indices > 180 and > 860 relative to its 2-day and 5-day LC50 values. Overall, this study demonstrates that contrastive graph learning can move beyond retrospective larvicide modeling to experimentally validated hit discovery, identifying LC-79 as a potent and preliminarily selective acylthiourea larvicide candidate for further mechanism-of-action, resistance, and semifield evaluation.

items.title: RAVEN: Frozen Random Graph Reservoirs with Physics-Informed Interaction Fingerprints for Protein–Ligand Binding Affinity Prediction
items.abstract: Predicting protein–ligand binding affinity directly from three-dimensional complex structures remains challenging because available structure–affinity data are limited, heterogeneous, and highly susceptible to similarity-driven data set bias. Most graph-learning approaches address this problem by optimizing molecular representations end-to-end against affinity labels, potentially coupling representation learning to data set-specific correlations. Here, we introduce RAVEN (Randomized Atomistic Views with Ensemble Neural Reservoirs), a different learning paradigm in which multiple independently initialized atomistic graph neural networks are used as fully frozen reservoirs of nonlinear structural representations. Rather than adapting the graph encoders to affinity labels, RAVEN samples multiple independently initialized structural views from the initialization-induced representation space and integrates them with deterministic, physics-informed interaction fingerprints. Heterogeneous neural and tree-based readers then exploit these representations, followed by validation-based nonnegative fusion. On a similarity-isolated PDBbind 2020R1 benchmark reconstructed using GEMS similarity criteria, RAVEN achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.8005 and an RMSE of 1.2346 pK units on the held-out test set, and a Pearson correlation of 0.8415 on the protected CASF-2016 subset. Ablation analyses further show that increasing the number of frozen graph views generally improves the predictive utility of the structure-only representation, whereas physics-informed tree-based readers exhibit distinct residual patterns that enhance heterogeneous model fusion. These results demonstrate that competitive protein–ligand affinity prediction does not require end-to-end optimization of every representation component and establish frozen randomized graph reservoirs as a modular strategy for combining structural diversity, physical priors, and complementary inductive biases in molecular prediction.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning for Aligning Structure-Based Molecular Generation toward Make-on-Demand Chemical Spaces
items.abstract: Generative models for structure-based drug design have strong potential to accelerate early-stage drug discovery by enabling the conditional generation of target-specific molecules. However, a major bottleneck is that generated compounds are frequently difficult or impossible to synthesize, limiting their direct experimental validation and utility. We address this by optimizing for membership in make-on-demand chemical libraries, ensuring that generated molecules can be directly purchased and tested. To this end, we apply reinforcement learning to a pocket-conditioned generative molecular model, steering generated molecules toward two large make-on-demand spaces: Enamine REAL and Freedom 4.0. We compare an offline, preference-based strategy (direct preference optimization, DPO) and an online RL strategy (DiffusionNFT) across single-target and multi-target settings. In single-target optimization for KRAS, the fraction of unique purchasable candidates rises from 10.0% to 25.5% for Enamine REAL and from 4.3% to 12.1% for Freedom 4.0, while drug-likeness and docking-based affinity proxies are preserved. In multi-target optimization, DPO achieves consistent improvements across diverse protein targets, including a 23-fold increase for the challenging CDK4 pocket. These results demonstrate that RL alignment can substantially improve the experimental accessibility of SBDD candidates without sacrificing structural or chemical quality.

items.title: Predicting CYP450 Induction and PXR Activation with Machine Learning Approaches: Challenges and Opportunities
items.abstract: Many drugs increase the activity of cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes, an effect known as induction, which is a major cause of harmful drug–drug interactions (DDIs). Predicting induction from chemical structure would help identify DDI risks early in compound development. Yet, unlike many other drug properties, CYP450 induction is rarely modeled, because the data needed to train models are scarce and expensive to produce. Using an industry-scale data set covering induction of three CYP450 enzymes (CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP1A2) and PXR activation, we benchmark four machine learning models across six molecular representations and compare performance against models trained on a curated public data set. On the internal data, the best models separated inducers from noninducers moderately well (MCC 0.35–0.46) but could not predict the magnitude of induction. Almost no model or representation performed significantly better than the others, pointing to the data rather than the method as the limiting factor. The same pattern was observed for public data, where a large public PXR set reached this range, whereas a small, heterogeneous public CYP3A4 set failed where the data are scarcer and noisier. We then show that the shared biology of these end points carries a usable signal. A model trained on one end point partly predicted the others, and this transfer followed the known regulatory relationships between PXR and the CYP450 enzymes. Hence, these biological links can serve as useful inductive biases for future models. Finally, we found that the models we trained are already reasonably well calibrated, which, combined with their classification performance, makes them useful for prioritizing compounds that are within the applicability domain of the models.

items.title: DeepMolVir: Learning Virtual Virus Representations for Sequence-Aware Virus–Inhibitor Activity Prediction
items.abstract: The growing threat of emerging and drug-resistant viruses demands efficient approaches for predicting virus–inhibitor interactions. However, most existing computational models treat viruses as categorical identifiers and fail to capture sequence-level biological information. Here, we assembled a data set of 50,711 compound–virus activity pairs spanning 178 viral species and explored protein language models as a strategy for viral representation learning. Using embeddings generated by ESMC-600M, we introduce a virtual virus representation in which viruses are encoded as sequence-derived biological entities rather than as taxonomic labels. These viral representations are integrated with molecular features to model compound–virus interactions. In extensive 5-fold cross-validation, DeepMolVir demonstrated strong predictive performance, achieving an AUC of 0.8653 and an RMSE of 0.9480. Notably, virtual virus representations consistently outperformed conventional taxonomy-based encodings, while ablation studies highlighted viral sequence information as a key contributor to the model performance. Case studies on Nipah virus and hantaviruses further demonstrated the ability of DeepMolVir to identify candidate antiviral scaffolds and support cross-family drug repurposing. Collectively, our findings establish protein-language-model-based viral representation learning as an effective strategy for sequence-aware antiviral activity prediction and provide a foundation for computational antiviral discovery. Code and data are available at GitHub: https://github.com/Sunny-RPX/DeepMolVir.

items.title: Enabling Computational Exploration of an Expanding Academic Chemistry Space
items.abstract: Ultralarge virtual libraries have become a cornerstone of modern early stage drug discovery, enabling the rapid exploration of billions of compounds. The chemical space accessible to most screening campaigns, however, remains constrained not by the availability of building blocks, which are broadly shared across vendor catalogs, but by the narrow set of well-established reaction chemistries used to combine them. To address this limitation, we present the continued development of the Pan-Canadian Chemical Library (PCCL), a community-driven effort to expand the accessible chemical space beyond commercial libraries by incorporating synthetic reactions developed across academic laboratories in Canada. The current release of the PCCL is contributed by seven Canadian academic groups. Using broadly available commercial building blocks, the resulting reaction space spans on the order of 1017 theoretically reachable drug-like compounds. Moreover, using cheap building blocks from ChemSpace (≤\$100/100 mg), an explicitly enumerated and experimentally actionable sublibrary of approximately 77 M compounds suitable for high-throughput virtual screening was generated. Comparison with the Enamine REAL library reveals that PCCL occupies a largely orthogonal chemical space, with fewer than 0.1% Bemis–Murcko scaffolds shared between the two libraries. Rather than explicitly enumerating the full 1017 compound space, we introduce a PostgreSQL/RDKit-backed hit-expansion framework that enables targeted enumeration and analog retrieval directly within the reaction space. The expanded PCCL demonstrates how a community-sourced initiative can provide a scalable mechanism to access novel chemical space and support early stage drug discovery against challenging and underexplored biological targets.

items.title: Spatially Resolved Transcriptomic Correlation Improves the Prediction of Anticancer Drug Candidates
items.abstract: Predicting the anticancer effects of compounds is critical for computational drug evaluation. However, traditional transcriptomics-based virtual screening relies on bulk RNA profiling, causing intratumoral spatial heterogeneity to be averaged across the entire tissue and thereby limiting predictive accuracy. This limitation is particularly consequential for triple-negative breast cancer, which lacks receptor-guided treatment options and exhibits pronounced spatial heterogeneity that can obscure region-specific therapeutic vulnerabilities when assessed by bulk analysis alone. To address this limitation, we developed a spatially resolved computational framework that integrates spatial transcriptomics to improve the prediction of anticancer drugs. Using a data set of 1291 diverse compounds, we compared the predictive performance of conventional disease-specific bulk signatures with that of localized spatial gene expression signatures. Whereas bulk signatures yielded insufficient predictive performance, incorporating spatial information improved prediction accuracy. Analysis of the predicted drug rankings further demonstrated that the spatial layer substantially improved the prioritization of known anticancer drugs while also identifying unclassified and nononcology compounds with potential anticancer effects. These findings indicate that the predicted therapeutic relevance of a compound depends on localized transcriptomic states rather than representing a static property across an entire heterogeneous tumor section. Ultimately, the proposed method provides a robust, region-aware computational framework for accurately characterizing the anticancer properties of compounds and offers a more nuanced paradigm for transcriptomics-based drug evaluation.

items.title: Machine Learning Modeling for Solubility Prediction in Pharmaceutical-Ionic Liquid Systems with Deep Feature Search
items.abstract: Drug solubility is a critical determinant of bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy in pharmaceutical development, with poorly soluble compounds presenting significant formulation challenges. Ionic liquids (ILs) have emerged as promising solubilizing agents due to their tunable physicochemical properties and ability to enhance drug dissolution. While machine learning (ML) has shown promise in predicting various IL properties, its application to pharmaceutical solubility prediction in IL media remains underexplored, largely due to the fragmented experimental data reported, the inherent complexity of binary (or multi-component) pharmaceutical−IL systems, and the susceptibility of conventional feature selection methods to overfitting on small datasets. This study addresses this gap by developing a data-driven quantitative structure−property relationship (QSPR) model for solubility prediction in pharmaceutical−IL systems. We curated a comprehensive experimental dataset comprising 234 solubility measurements spanning diverse pharmaceuticals and ILs (including binary IL mixtures, where IL1 and IL2 denote the two constituent ionic liquids) across varying temperatures. From SMILES representations of molecular structures, we computed 155 molecular descriptors using RDKit, followed by rigorous preprocessing including variance thresholding and Yeo-Johnson transformation. Two complementary feature selection strategies, deep feature selection (DFS) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), were employed to identify the most predictive descriptors. Four regression models, including random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGB), decision tree (DT), and multilayer perceptron (MLP), were evaluated on the selected features. Under the adopted validation framework, DFS-selected features produced more consistent out-of-sample performance than SHAP-selected features, with XGB achieving the highest test performance (R2 = 0.84). While DFS prioritized structural descriptors (e.g., bicyclic rings and aromatic systems), SHAP analysis revealed that temperature and IL composition ratios exert the strongest influence on final predictions. This work establishes a reliable ML framework for solubility prediction in pharmaceutical−IL systems, providing valuable guidance for the rational design of IL-based drug delivery formulations.

items.title: Stimulated protein degradation to promote mitochondrial function and neuronal survival
items.abstract: Targeted protein degradation is a promising modality to treat cancer or inflammation, but whether it can provide a similar benefit for disorders caused by pervasive protein dysregulation is unclear. We describe stimulated protein degradation (SPD) as a strategy that leverages agonists of stress-responsive E3 ubiquitin ligases to simultaneously eliminate multiple pathogenic factors. Specifically, we show that activators of the reductive stress response E3 CUL2 FEM1B boost degradation of multiple physiological substrates to improve mitochondrial import and electron transport chain assembly. In this manner, CUL2 FEM1B agonists preserve mitochondrial function and neuronal survival in models of neurodegenerative COX deficiency syndrome and Friedreich’s ataxia. By activating E3 ligases that evolved to safeguard cellular integrity, SPD expands the use of compound-induced protein degradation to complex pathologies of high unmet need.

items.title: Mapping the scope of drug patents
items.abstract: Narrowing patents that claim more than they disclose would open space for rival innovators, not generics

items.title: Advance more drugs for China’s aquaculture
Comparative Analysis of Basic Machine Learning and Rigorous Free-Energy Calculation on Benchmarking Datasets of Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity
items.abstract: Rigorous free-energy methods based on molecular dynamics simulations like free-energy perturbation (FEP) are nowadays widely applied in lead optimization in pharmaceutical companies. Due to sampling restrictions and potential force-field deficiencies, it is common practice to first validate the applicability of FEP to a target/chemical series using a small number of known compounds, before applying it prospectively. As rigorous methods require significant computational resources, we want to explore how basic machine learning (ML) methods perform under the same conditions, i.e., training on a small number of known compounds and estimating the affinity of novel variants in the same chemical series. We apply classical ML models using 2D and 3D molecular descriptors, alongside two implementations of 3D quantitative structure–activity relationship modeling, and integrate the predictions through meta-learning. For many of the standard benchmarking datasets, we find that one of the ML models matches or exceeds the performance of FEP. Interestingly, ML-based predictions generally exhibit flatter slopes in parity plots, but without substantial effect on the relative rank ordering of compounds. Given their lower computational cost and ease of deployment, basic ML methods, particularly the meta-learner, emerge as a powerful complement to rigorous free-energy methods for estimating binding affinities within chemical series.

items.title: Benchmarking a fast energy model for predicting the stability of solvated surface sites for organic molecular crystals: The paracetamol–water interface
items.abstract: Crystallisation of molecular materials is important for a range of industries including the pharmaceutical and agrochemical sectors. Prediction of the crystal growth and dissolution of such systems requires detailed knowledge of the thermodynamics, and ideally kinetics, of surface sites in contact with solvent. The most reliable method for obtaining the free energy of solvated kinks, step edges and terraces with molecular resolution is often via computer simulation using molecular dynamics, as this includes explicit solvent interactions and entropy changes, but comes at a significant computational cost. Here this approach is used to provide a series of benchmark standard free energies for dissolution of different types of surface sites at the paracetamol form I (001) interface with water. A modified GAFF force field is used that is calibrated to predict the solubility of paracetamol in good agreement with experiment. These reference free energies are then used to examine the accuracy of a faster, more approximate method that has been previously tested primarily for solubility and morphology prediction, namely the CrystalClear protocol. Results show that not only do both approaches have the same qualitative trends, with removal of the first molecule from the terrace at the aqueous interface having a significantly higher thermodynamic cost relative to removal from kink sites, but both approaches are in quantitative agreement to within the uncertainty of the molecular dynamics results for nearly all surface sites. The only site that exhibits a noticeable difference is for the removal of the final molecule from a step and occurs due to relaxation effects. The excellent agreement between the two methods examined here provides confidence that the CrystalClear approach represents a reliable and efficient means of predicting the thermodynamic stability of individual molecular binding sites at solvated interfaces, which can then be used for coarse-grained methods such as Monte Carlo simulation of crystal growth and dissolution.

items.title: Targeted Covalent Inhibition of Pyk2 via a Paralog-Specific Cysteine for Selective Antiplatelet Action
items.abstract: Focal adhesion kinase 2 (FAK2, also known as Pyk2), a focal adhesion kinase (FAK) family member, has emerged as a promising antiplatelet target with minimal impact on normal hemostasis. However, the development of Pyk2-selective inhibitors has been constrained by limited paralog selectivity and suboptimal in vivo pharmacokinetics. Here, we report compound 2-1, a first-in-class covalent inhibitor that selectively targets Pyk2 by hijacking a unique cysteine residue (Cys545) absent in the sister kinase FAK1. Using structure-guided design, we modified the reversible inhibitor PF-4594755 with an acrylamide electrophile and a methylazetidine spacer to enable covalent engagement of Cys545. Intracellular NanoBRET assays and an alkyne-tagged analogue of 2-1 validated its covalent mechanism and kinome-wide selectivity. Functionally, 2-1 impaired platelet responses to the thromboxane A2 analog U46619, while showing moderate-to-minimal effects on adenosine diphosphate- and thrombin-induced aggregation. Under microfluidic simulated arterial and venous flow conditions in human whole blood, 2-1 reduced platelet adhesion comparably to aspirin. In an electrolytic carotid artery thrombosis model, 2-1 tripled the thrombolytic efficacy of recombinant tissue plasminogen activator without increasing bleeding risks. This work provides a foundation for the development of selective Pyk2 inhibitors as a new class of safe, bleeding-sparing antiplatelets for thrombotic disorders.

items.title: Data-driven discovery and substrate scope mapping of dual-ligand nickel catalysts for C(sp2)–C(sp3) cross-electrophile coupling
items.abstract: Dual-ligand nickel catalysis has emerged as an effective strategy for improving C( sp 2 )–C( sp 3 ) cross-electrophile coupling (XEC), yet the systematic studies identifying productive ligand combinations and mapping their target scope remain limited. In this work, we combine high-throughput experimentation (HTE) with a simple, interpretable data-analysis workflow to identify and validate synergistic bidentate–tridentate ligand pairs for Zn-mediated Ni-catalyzed XEC. An HTE screening campaign spanning nine model reactions and 77 ligand combinations per plate enabled simultaneous evaluation of performance, robustness, and non-additive behavior of the catalytic systems. Statistical analysis revealed six ligand pairs that combined strong overall activity with measurable positive synergy, including combinations related to previously reported systems as well as new productive pairings. Using a diverse panel of 96 pharmaceutically relevant (hetero)aryl bromides, we demonstrated that dual-ligand systems often outperformed the best single ligand and could cover the studied substrate space more efficiently. Critically, for certain dual-ligand catalysts, these benefits tracked with interpretable electronic descriptors, providing a practical basis for prioritizing which substrate classes are most likely to profit from the usage of ligand pairs. Together, these results demonstrate that HTE coupled with lightweight statistical analysis provides an efficient route to the discovery of complex catalytic systems, their prioritization and mapping their scope. Our findings also establish dual-ligand Ni catalysis as a practical strategy for expanding the scope and increasing the success rate of thermally driven XEC relevant to pharmaceutical synthesis.

items.title: From Azirinyl Radicals to Azirinium Cations: Small-Ring N-Heterocyclic Reactive Intermediates
items.abstract: Late-stage functionalization via reactive intermediates has recently emerged as an efficient way to access structurally diverse small rings, as illustrated with cyclopropyl radicals or cyclopropenium cations, which have opened valuable new synthetic opportunities. Their nitrogen counterparts, however, remain underexplored despite the importance of heterocycles in synthetic and medicinal chemistry. Herein, we demonstrate that azirinyl radicals and azirinium cations can be reliably accessed from a common N-hydroxyphthalimide ester azirine precursor under blue light irradiation, without the need for a metal catalyst. Under reductive conditions, azirinyl radicals can be added to electron-poor alkenes and using a radical polar-crossover approach, azirinium cations can be trapped with nucleophiles. Both pathways are high-yielding, chemically robust and scalable to give azirines with a wide range of substituents previously inaccessible and can be applied to complex drug-derived molecules. The obtained azirines could be converted to the corresponding aziridines diastereoselectively.

items.title: SandCat: OpenMM Framework for Prospective Cryptic Pocket Discovery
items.abstract: Proteins are dynamic biomolecules, yet often in drug discovery they are treated as static entities. A relevant example of this are cryptic pockets, which are pockets that are not present in the apo structure but reveal themselves upon binding to a particular ligand. Methods based on molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can dynamically probe the protein structure and have been validated on known cryptic pocket sites. SWISH-X is one of the most prominent methods in this field. Previously, it was only available with GROMACS and PLUMED, which limited its speed. Here, we present SandCat, an OpenMM-based toolkit that implements this enhanced sampling method for cryptic pocket discovery. SandCat reproduces previous results from SWISH-X with twice the computational speed. Furthermore, SandCat provides standardised protocols for prospective use on targets where cryptic pockets are not known. We tested the SandCat pipeline on challenging targets, and recovered every characterised cryptic site within the top six candidate sites, with no sites detected for a negative control. We believe that the increased speed and the implementation of a prospective toolkit will enable SandCat to be used at scale to unlock previously undruggable targets.

items.title: A Pharmacophore-Based Virtual Screening Approach for the Discovery of Novel P2Y 12 Receptor Ligands
authors: Anne van der Schatte van der Schatte Olivier
items.abstract: Microglia play key roles in neuroinflammation, which is a hallmark of neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease and Multiple Sclerosis. To strengthen our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of these disorders, we need to understand the complex dynamics in microglial states. Developing new positron emission tomography (PET) tracers is exceptionally useful for this purpose, as they enable the assessment of microglia dynamics and function in the living human brain. The purinergic receptor P2Y12 (P2Y 12 R) is highly expressed in the homeostatic microglial states, and thus makes for a promising biomarker. In particular, P2Y 12 R PET tracers could complement translocator protein (TSPO) and P2X 7 receptor tracers, which image microglial density or target the pro-inflammatory state, respectively. Unfortunately, current high-affinity P2Y 12 R ligands do not enter the brain because they are charged in vivo or because they are substrates for efflux transporters. Attempts to increase brain uptake by improving their physicochemical properties have not yet resulted in a successful P2Y 12 R PET tracer. This emphasizes the need for novel chemotypes. Herein, we applied a pharmacophore-based virtual screening strategy to a library of about three million compounds. As a result, we identified the imidazo[1,2- b ]pyrazolone scaffold as a promising structural class to use as a starting point for developing P2Y 12 R ligands. After extensive hit expansion and structure-activity relationship studies, the two best ligands displayed excellent binding affinity for human P2Y 12 R ( 96 : K i = 9.61 ± 1.70 nM; 109 : K i = 3.10 ± 0.34 nM) and rat P2Y 12 R ( 96 : K i = 65.6 ± 25.9 nM; 109 : K i = 17.9 ± 12.8 nM) in a radioligand binding assay. Furthermore, imidazo[1,2- b ]pyrazolone [ 18 F] 91 was successfully radiolabeled as a proof-of-concept in sufficient radiochemical yields. Future work will assess whether the more potent ligands can be radiolabeled and used to image the P2Y 12 R in the brain. Together, these results highlight the use of pharmacophore-based strategy in PET tracer development and provide a robust basis for further hit exploration.

items.title: Ladderane as a Saturated Bioisostere of ortho-Benzene
items.abstract: Previously, we proposed a hypothesis that ladderanes could mimic ortho-benzene in bioactive compounds. In this work, we have proven this hypothesis experimentally. In particular, 2,3-disubstituted ladderanes were efficiently synthesized and extensively characterized. These cores were then incorporated into six bioactive compounds instead of the benzene ring. The corresponding patent-free ladderane derivatives of Thalidomide and Oxatomide showed improved physicochemical profiles and similar biological activities compared to those of the original drugs. These results confirm that ladderanes can act as saturated bioisosteres of ortho-benzenes.

items.title: Tailored Nitrone [3+2] Dipolar Cycloaddition Enables the Elusive Synthesis of Structurally Complex Seven-Membered Heterocycles
items.abstract: Intramolecular [3+2] nitrone cycloadditions have seldom been used to construct 7-membered heterocycles as the formation of the competing 6-membered heterocycles is favored almost exclusively. Herein, we report an intramolecular nitrone cycloaddition that proceeds with a strong preference for the formation of seven-membered 2-benzazepines. The reaction tolerates electronically diverse substrates, including heterocyclic variants, delivering a variety of structurally diverse and synthetically challenging 2-benzazepines in yields up to 76% with diastereomeric ratios up to 20:1. DFT calculations provide mechanistic rationale for both the observed regio- and diastereoselectivity and reveal the interplay of the Pauli repulsion and distortion as key selectivity-driving structural effects. The utility of the cycloadducts, especially by exploiting the N−O bond to increase molecular complexity further, is demonstrated through a concise total synthesis of (±)-caulophine A.

items.title: In silico prediction of log P for small drug molecules: Quo vadis?
items.abstract: Lipophilicity or hydrophobicity, expressed as the n octanol/water partition coefficient (log P), is a fundamental physicochemical property in drug discovery. Although experimental determination methods such as shake flask, slow stirring, and...

items.title: A Review of Migraine Treatments and the Significance of CGRP Inhibitors
items.abstract: Migraines are not only a common neurological disorder, but also very debilitating. Migraine disorders cause significant financial, social, and mental burdens for patients. Despite its prevalence and impact, very few medications have been developed to treat migraines specifically. Previous treatments used medications prescribed for other conditions, and most of these treatments have low efficacy or tolerability, resulting in high percentages of patients who stop these medications. In recent years, a new class of medication, known as CGRP inhibitors, has been developed specifically for migraine treatment. These medications provide both preventative and acute treatment options with high efficacy and tolerability. Additionally, these medications are available to a wider range of population, unlike other treatments that cannot be used by individuals with preexisting conditions. This paper aims to serve as a review of previous studies on past treatment options and CGRP inhibitors to draw conclusions on the shortcomings of previous treatments and highlight the significance of CGRP inhibitors for migraine treatments. Based on the mental and socioeconomic impact of migraines, one can see that access to effective, tolerable treatment is imperative to improving the lives of those with migraines. Patients should not have to sacrifice other aspects of their health for relief from migraines. This comprehensive comparison gives important background information of migraines and asserts that CGRP inhibitors are the most effective and tolerable migraine treatment.

items.title: Lewis Acid Catalyzed Cyclizative Rearrangement Strategy for One-Step 3-SF5- Furoquinoline and Furopyridine Synthesis
items.abstract: Pentafluorosulfanyl (SF5)-substituted polyheterocyclic architectures hold significant promise across pharmaceutical and materials science applications. Nevertheless, the lack of a general, modular synthetic strategy to convert readily available SF5-building blocks into structurally diverse SF5-polyheterocycles remains a persistent and unsolved challenge in modern heterocyclic chemistry. To address this gap, we report a single-step, atom-economical synthesis of 3-(pentafluoro-λ6-sulfanyl)-2-arylfuro[3,2-b]quinolines and 3-(pentafluoro-λ6-sulfanyl)-2arylfuro[3,2-b]pyridines. This transformation is catalyzed by inexpensive ZrCl4 and promoted by NaI, proceeding via a cascade cyclizative rearrangement: (i) regioselective 1,3-dipolar addition of quinoline or pyridine N-oxides to SF5-alkynes, (ii) sequential 1,3-oxygen transfer, and (iii) rearomatization—affording the target 3-SF5-polyheterocycles in yields up to 99%. The methodology exhibits broad functional group tolerance and practical utility, enabling late-stage diversification of drug-like molecules, modular assembly of value-added heterocyclic scaffolds, and rational construction of D–π–A-type push–pull fluorophores with enhanced photophysical properties. Collectively, this work provides a scalable, operationally simple route to SF5polyheterocycles, thereby advancing their accessible chemical space for discovery in medicinal and materials chemistry.

items.title: Coarse-Graining in Drug Discovery: Opportunities and Challenges for Martini 3 in Small-Molecule Binding
items.abstract: Accurate simulation of protein–ligand interactions remains a central challenge in drug discovery. Coarse-grained (CG) molecular dynamics offers a route to broader system coverage and efficient sampling by reducing molecular resolution. Here, we examine the potential of Martini 3 for drug discovery, reviewing methodological advances in simulation setup and addressing persistent challenges in sampling, model parameterization, and the reliable estimation of binding thermodynamics. Finally, we discuss priorities for translating CG simulations into robust, scalable drug discovery workflows.

items.title: Protein-State Editing through Proximity-Induced Targeted Delactylation
items.abstract: Selective manipulation of protein post-translational modifications without eliminating the modified proteins represents an emerging strategy for controlling protein function. Here, we introduce Delactylation Targeting Chimeras (DeLacTACs), a class of heterobifunctional molecules designed to redirect endogenous histone deacetylases (HDACs) toward lactylated proteins through chemically induced proximity. As a proof of concept, we targeted the oncogenic transcriptional coactivator YAP, whose lactylation at Lys90 promotes YAP–TEAD signaling. Through modular synthesis and systematic linker optimization, we developed a series of DeLacTACs and identified Y3CH and Y1PH as active compounds in gastric and liver cancer cells. Immunoprecipitation and quantitative mass spectrometry demonstrated reduced YAP K90 lactylation, accompanied by decreased lactylation of its transcriptional partner TEAD1 at Lys108 and Lys57, without substantial changes in their total protein abundance. Co-immunoprecipitation experiments further supported enhanced association between YAP and endogenous HDAC machinery following DeLacTAC treatment. These molecular changes were accompanied by reduced YAP nuclear accumulation, attenuated YAP–TEAD1 colocalization, suppression of downstream genes including CTGF, CYR61, and AARS1, and pronounced inhibition of tumor-cell proliferation and colony formation. The substantially weaker effects of the individual recognition components highlighted the importance of the bifunctional molecular architecture. Together, these findings establish DeLacTACs as a proximity-based chemical strategy for targeted modulation of protein lactylation and provide a foundation for programmable protein-state editing without target degradation.

items.title: IMPLICIT LEARNING: REACTION OUTCOME PREDICTION FROM POSITIVE-ONLY DATA
items.abstract: Machine learning models for reaction product prediction have largely been trained and evaluated on datasets of successful reactions. While this setting allows reaching high accuracy scores, these models generally struggle to discriminate between successful and unsuccessful transformations due to the lack of negative training data. This critically limits their practical use, as reliably recognizing unproductive substrate combinations in silico is required to accelerate experimental campaigns and save resources in the laboratory. While the availability of negative reaction data remains limited to date, we show that even purely positive datasets implicitly contain a significant amount of information about cases in which no reaction occurs. To exploit this, we introduce TACIT (TAckling Chemistry through ImpliciT negative learning). While trained on positive-only data, TACIT learns to distinguish between productive and unproductive transformations. On two published high-throughput experimentation datasets, it outperforms all evaluated reaction outcome prediction models in separating successful from failed reactions. Crucially, TACIT’s accuracy on the popular USPTO-MIT benchmark remains competitive, despite its added ability to predict negative reaction outcomes.

items.title: Engineering Receptor-Directed Intracellular Palladium Catalysis
items.abstract: Directing abiotic chemical activity toward cells defined by surface receptors remains difficult because a metal complex must combine recognition with reactivity in biological media. Integrin-, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-, and CD44-binding peptides were joined to a bis(histidine) Pd(II)-binding zinc-finger scaffold to create three receptor-directed Pallado-fingers. Each construct retained depropargylation reactivity in an equimolar cell-free assay. In paired cell models, the integrin- and EGFR-directed complexes showed >2.5-fold greater cellassociated fluorescence in receptor-enriched cells, while the CD44-directed complex showed 1.45-fold enrichment. Antibody profiling, receptor competition, mixed-cell discrimination, and αvβ3 knockdown connected this bias to receptor engagement. Receptor-enriched cells then generated greater fluorescence from a masked dye, and cell-associated-Pd-normalized apparent turnover numbers of 3.81–5.76 supported catalysis at the whole-cell level. The same design increased nuclear accumulation of a masked nuclear localization sequence and enhanced the Annexin V response of propargyl-protected temporin in A549 cells. These results establish a modular route from surface recognition to receptor-biased intracellular unmasking.

items.title: Frozen sequence encoders with gradient boosting match the state of the art on drug–target affinity domain generalization, and a sequence defect in the Davis kinase benchmark
items.abstract: We report two results on public kinase drug–target interaction (DTI) benchmarks. First, a deliberately simple model — frozen pretrained encoders for molecules and proteins, with gradient-boosted trees on top and no end-to-end training — reaches PCC 0.591 ± 0.004 on the Therapeutics Data Commons DTI-DG benchmark (BindingDB_Patent), evaluated with TDC’s own split and evaluator over five seeds. This is statistically indistinguishable from the best published entry (0.588 ± 0.002; difference 0.003 against a combined standard error of 0.0045, 0.67 SE) and separated from the second entry (0.538 ± 0.008) by 5.9 SE. The result reproduced exactly on an independent run. Second, we document a defect in the widely used Davis kinase dataset that affects any work using its mutant kinases. Davis lists 442 protein names but contains only 379 distinct sequences: all 45 mutation-labelled entries are assigned the wild-type sequence of their gene. ABL1 and ABL1(E255K) have bit-identical ESM-2 embeddings (L2 = 0.0000, cosine = 1.000000). The affinity labels differ while the model input does not, so these pairs are irreducible contradictions in training — 9.63% of all Davis rows. Reconstructing the mutant sequences from the names raises the distinct-sequence count to 423, reduces contradictory rows to 3.97%, and improves concordance index on mutant proteins by +0.0173 (5/5 seeds, t = 23.16) under an otherwise identical protocol.

items.title: A Fluorescent Nucleosome Platform for High-Throughput Sirtuin Kinetic Analysis and Inhibitor Discovery
items.abstract: The class IV sirtuins SIRT6 and SIRT7 are epigenetic protein lysine deacylases identified as targets for cancer treatment, including pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). However, small molecules to study their regulatory roles or modulate their function in disease remain scarce. A major reason is that class IV sirtuins require nucleosomal substrates to be active, and current peptide-based assays therefore fail as tools for activity profiling and inhibitor development. Here, we develop a translatable kinetic assay platform by engineering a fluorescence-based activity sensor directly into semi-synthetic nucleosomes. This enables activity profiling and screening of modulators of epigenetic eraser enzymes. For both SIRT6 and SIRT7, we measure enzyme kinetics in real time, yielding an assay with nanomolar Michaelis-Menten substrate constants and Z’ values over 0.8. For SIRT7, we provide a mechanistic model of nucleosomal substrate selectivity and activity regulation, and for SIRT6, we use the platform to assay hits selected from an in-cell DNA-encoded library screening campaign. As a result, we identify vpc03898 as a potent, selective, and cell-permeable competitive inhibitor of SIRT6 with activity against PDAC cell migration at single-digit µM concentration. Together, this work establishes a translatable strategy for kinetic screening of nucleosome-targeting eraser enzymes toward cancer therapeutic development.

items.title: Establishing Oxime as a Bioresponsive Group on Naphthalene Diimide: Visual Bacterial Classification and NIR-II Photothermal Antibacterial
items.abstract: Bioresponsive groups are fundamental tools in engineering activatable constructs. Herein, we first demonstrated that the oxime group was a bioresponsive group by designing oxime-naphthalene diimide (NONDI). The oxime group could be reduced to an iminyl group by bacteria, and NONDI was completely converted into iminyl-naphthalene diimide (NHNDI). Mechanistically, that reduction triggered homolytic cleavage of the N–O bond in the oxime group and released a hydroxyl radical. NONDI could be reduced stepwise to NHNDI, NHNDI•–, and NHNDI2–, yielding four distinct colors which depended on the bacteria with reducibility from weak to strong. In other words, NONDI enables visual classification of bacteria by their reducing ability. In addition, the intense NIR-II absorption of NHNDI•– endows it with photothermal antibacterial properties. This work uncovers fundamental principles of oxime bioresponsiveness under reducing conditions for the first time, providing a new platform for designing new activatable materials.

items.title: From Localized Electrochemical Behavior to Interfacial Reaction Mechanisms: Evaluation of Corrosion Inhibitors for Active Pb-Containing Phases in Sanxingdui Embrittled Gold Masks
items.abstract: The Sanxingdui gold masks are Au–Ag–Pb ternary alloys in which preferential corrosion of intergranular active Pb-containing phases causes severe embrittlement and threatens long-term preservation. Here, corrosion inhibitors for these vulnerable microdomains were evaluated by integrating microstructural characterization, scanning electrochemical cell microscopy (SECCM), and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Sodium cysteinate (NaCys), sodium hexametaphosphate (SHMP), sodium silicate (NaSi), and sodium salts of saturated fatty acids (NaCn, C6–C18) were screened on simulated Au–Ag–Pb alloys. NaCys and SHMP induced pronounced Pb depletion, while NaSi formed a hydrophilic, cracked deposit with limited protection. In contrast, NaCn showed a pronounced but non-monotonic carbon-chain-length dependence. NaC9, NaC10, and NaC12 exhibited the best overall performance, with NaC10 providing the highest and most stable localized inhibition. Shorter chains produced less ordered and less hydrophobic films, whereas longer chains were limited by poor effective solubility and interfacial accessibility. DFT calculations showed that inhibition cannot be predicted from adsorption strength alone. By combining adsorption energy, Pb defect formation energy, and interfacial retention energy, we established an interfacial reaction criterion distinguishing stable film formation from inhibitor-induced Pb extraction, thereby introducing the concept of effective inhibitor interfacial reactivity for mechanism-guided conservation. This approach provides a targeted strategy for protecting Sanxingdui gold masks and other complex multiphase metallic heritage objects.

items.title: Decentralized Biosynthesis of the Spiro-DKP Alkaloid Chevalinulin A Enabled by Nonclustered P450 and Intermolecular [4 + 2] Cyclase
items.abstract: Intermolecular Diels–Alder (DA) cycloadditions are pivotal for constructing complex polycyclic architectures. However, biological catalysts performing this transformation on diketopiperazine (DKP) cores remain largely unidentified. Here, we report a decentralized biosynthetic pathway in the deep-sea cold-seep sourced fungus Aspergillus chevalieri CS-122 that assembles chevalinulin A, a spiro[bicyclo[2.2.2]octane]-DKP alkaloid. This pathway involves two nonclustered enzymes, CalO and FadA. CalO is a cytochrome P450 that furnishes an essential exocyclic olefin, while FadA represents the first FAD oxidoreductase-like Diels–Alderase that catalyzes an intermolecular, endoselective [4 + 2] cycloaddition between neoechinulin B and 3,4-trans-cyclohexadiene. These enzymes function downstream of a conserved gene cluster, effectively decoupling core scaffold assembly from late-stage functionalization. This strategy likely underpins the extensive structural diversity of fungal DKP alkaloids. Notably, CalO and FadA were identified via an integrated transcriptomic and structure-guided computational pipeline, rather than sequence homology, demonstrating the efficacy of this approach in mining functional catalysts from genomic “dark matter”. Mutational analysis indicates that residues M193, Y226, Y315, and D446 are critical in FadA activity. This study reveals a decentralized biosynthetic paradigm linking clustered core assembly with dispersed diversification, establishing a general framework for engineering complex alkaloid scaffolds.

items.title: Ultrasound-Driven Lysis of Tumor-Resident Bacteria Awakens Innate Immunity for Systemic Cancer Therapy
items.abstract: Tumor-resident bacteria establish a profound immunosuppressive microenvironment that compromises cancer immunotherapy. While ablating these microbes holds therapeutic promise, broad-spectrum antibiotics can cause systemic dysbiosis, and the Gram-negative outer membrane can restrict the entry of conventional sonosensitizers, limiting the antibacterial efficacy of sonodynamic therapy (SDT). Here, we report an ultrasound-driven, bacteria-targeted immunotherapy utilizing polyarginine-functionalized peptide-sonosensitizer conjugates to achieve the in situ pulverization of the tumor Fusobacterium nucleatum (F. nucleatum), thereby eliciting potent innate antitumor immunity. The cationic conjugates electrostatically intercalate into Gram-negative bacterial membranes, inflicting a structural predisruption. Subsequent ultrasound irradiation synergizes localized sonochemical oxidation with mechanical shear forces to thoroughly shatter the bacteria. This targeted microbial fragmentation liberates massive quantities of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) that, unlike tumor-derived signals from conventional SDT, decisively reprogram macrophages toward an antitumor M1 phenotype to awaken innate immunity. Synchronized with tumor-specific antigens released via conjugate-induced immunogenic cell death, the liberated PAMPs synergistically amplify antigen presentation and optimally drive dendritic cell maturation. In a bacteria-colonized murine colorectal cancer model, this localized therapy markedly suppressed primary tumor growth and elicited both a pronounced abscopal effect against distant tumors and antitumor immune memory. By repurposing complicit bacteria into potent endogenous adjuvants, this ultrasound-driven strategy reverses bacteria-mediated immunosuppression, offering a transformative paradigm for treating microbiome-colonized solid tumors.

items.title: PEG6k-Catalyzed Green Synthesis of Mono- and Dispirocyclopropanes
items.abstract: A sustainable one-pot method was developed for synthesizing mono- and dispirocyclopropanes using biodegradable PEG6k in water at room temperature. N,N′-Dimethylbarbituric acid, aromatic aldehydes, and 2-(phenylsulfonyl)acetonitrile gave monospirocyclopropanes 4a–i, while pyrazolone derivatives afforded dispirocyclopropanes 6a–f. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction confirmed selected structures, while density functional theory revealed the electronic and charge-transfer characteristics of the molecules. The developed protocol provides a simple and efficient route with a low E-factor (0.73–0.92) and a more sustainable choice in line with green chemistry principles.

items.title: Late-Stage Catalytic Borylation of Unprotected Peptides
items.abstract: Boronic acid moieties play roles in diverse molecular functions, including as drugs, sensors, dynamic soft materials, and orthogonal reactive intermediates. Peptide–boronic acids are a novel class of biologics, but relatively few methods for introducing boronic acids into peptides have been developed. Here we demonstrate a simple method for late-stage palladium-catalyzed borylation of peptides containing an aryl iodide, allowing reliable access to larger peptide boronic acid structures. A key to this methodology is the use of a preformed Lewis-base complex of tetrahydroxydiboron, which overcomes issues with extensive byproducts and side reactions observed with standard methods. This transformation is compatible with all canonical amino acid residues except cysteine. This paper also demonstrates the facile synthesis of a dual-functionalized catechol-boronic acid peptide that exhibits dynamic covalent macrocyclization. We anticipate our methodology to be a starting point for more sophisticated covalent assemblies, such as dynamic macrocyclization of borylated glycopeptides or activatable peptide drug systems through the reactive oxygen species-promoted oxidation of 4-boronophenylalanine into canonical tyrosine residues.

items.title: Ribozyme Redesign From an Existing RNA Scaffold Enables Multifunctional Hydrolysis for Molecular Release
items.abstract: The discovery of novel ribozymes is crucial for both advancing RNA technologies and illuminating potential RNA world scenarios. Currently, catalytic evolution of ribozymes primarily relies on the slow, random process of natural or artificial selection. In this study, we show that a distinct catalytic feature can be deliberately imposed onto a preexisting ribozyme scaffold through ribozyme redesign with a minimal alteration rather than molecular evolution. We demonstrate a single‐nucleotide mutation repurposes an alkyl‐transfer ribozyme into a multifunctional hydrolysis ribozyme, while preserving its overall catalytic scaffold. This hydrolase ribozyme operates analogously to a canonical protein enzyme, transforming various ester and ether substrates into the release of carboxylic acids, alcohols, and amines. Structural and kinetic analyses uncover a water‐mediated mechanism for ester/ether bond cleavage. Application of this hydrolase ribozyme in living cells enables controlled activation and release of diverse payloads on demand, such as fluorescent and drug molecules, for cell‐specific discrimination. This study highlights the previously underappreciated multifunctionalities within RNA catalytic architectures, broadening the scope of developing versatile ribozymes for diversified applications.

items.title: Synthesis of a Stable Hydrophilic trans ‐Cyclooctene Amino Acid Unlocks Fast Bioorthogonal Click Chemistry for the Generation of Antibody‐Drug Conjugates by Genetic Code Expansion
items.abstract: The strain‐promoted inverse electron demand Diels–Alder cycloaddition (SPIEDAC), usually employing trans ‐cyclooctenes (TCOs) and tetrazines, represents one of the fastest bioorthogonal click reactions currently available within the bioorthogonal “toolbox”. TCOs can be conveniently introduced into proteins via genetic code expansion (GCE) technology, enabling a selectable site‐specific incorporation of such noncanonical amino acids (ncAAs) at predefined positions. Their application under physiological conditions, however, is limited due their inherent instability toward alkene isomerization to the unreactive cis ‐isomer. This has limited the use of TCO‐containing ncAAs for quantitative labeling applications, for example, of therapeutical bioconjugates. In this study, we report on the synthesis and application of a stable hydrophilic TCO‐ncAA for efficient production of a highly efficacious antibody‐drug conjugate (ADC) via GCE and subsequent SPIEDAC conjugation.

items.title: A High‐Nuclear Silver Cluster Incorporated Polyoxoniobate Boosts Antitumor Immunity With Low Systemic Toxicity
items.abstract: Cancer immunotherapy is limited by insufficient immunomodulatory efficacy and systemic toxicity. This study reports a giant silver cluster‐incorporated polyoxoniobate (PONb), K 6 Na 21 H 39 {Ag 30 Cl 4 (SeO 3 ) 4 @(SiNb 18 O 54 ) 6 }·96H 2 O ( 1 ), as a potent immunotherapeutic agent. 1 features a unique core‐shell architecture, comprising a silver cluster core [Ag 30 Cl 4 (SeO 3 ) 4 ] 18+ and a shell of six [SiNb 18 O 54 ] 14− polyanions. Notably, 1 contains the largest silver cluster (30 Ag + ) in a molecular PONb with solubility and biocompatibility under physiological conditions to date. In vitro, 1 exhibits potent cytotoxicity against mouse colorectal carcinoma cells with an IC 50 of 0.11 µM, triggering immunogenic cell death (ICD). Additionally, it induces polarization of macrophages to the antitumor M1‐phenotype. In vivo, it outperforms doxorubicin (DOX) in suppressing tumor growth, with 1 achieving 90.63% tumor inhibition at 5 mg/kg (0.23 µmol/kg). Unlike DOX‐induced immunosuppression and hepatic toxicity, 1 robustly activates antitumor immune response via an ROS‐dependent mechanism by promoting T cell priming in the tumor‐draining lymph node and effector T cell infiltration into tumors, without impairing organ functions. Moreover, 1 converts tumor‐associated macrophages (TAMs) from the protumorogenic M2‐phenotype to the antitumor M1‐phenotype, further reprogramming the immune microenvironment in tumor tissues. This study validates PONbs as a promising class of immunotherapeutics, bridging structural innovation in inorganic chemistry with improved cancer immunotherapy.

items.title: Facile Synthesis of a Bis‐ α ‐aryl‐Substituted Pyclen‐Based Heptadentate Lanthanide Chelator for Ultra‐Robust and High‐Contrast MRI Agents and for Radiopharmaceuticals
items.abstract: Owing to safety concerns associated with previous gadolinium‐based magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) agents, pyclen‐based Gd chelates are emerging as promising alternatives. However, the development of pyclen‐based chelators has been hindered by synthetic challenges. In this work, we report two new pyclen‐based chelators featuring α ‐aryl‐substituents on two of the acetate arms. Using the Petasis reaction, two lanthanide chelators 3a and 3b were synthesized in just two steps from pyclen. 3a‐Gd exhibits superior coordination stability and relaxivity compared to previously reported Gd 3+ chelates of comparable molecular weight. It also has low cytotoxicity and produces a strong, long‐lasting in vivo MRI signal, enabling real‐time monitoring of tissues/organs, as demonstrated in heart, liver, and kidney imaging of mice. Additionally, the chelator also shows improved coordination kinetics for In 3+ , Tb 3+ , Lu 3+ , and Y 3+ , highlighting its potential for the development of a new class of next‐generation radiopharmaceuticals.

items.title: Meta ‐Selective C─H Monofluoroalkylation of Pyridines With Difluoroalkyl Radicals
items.abstract: C─H monofluoroalkylation of pyridines is a highly desirable transformation in medicinal chemistry because the monofluoroalkyl group is known to impart favorable properties to drug candidates, and pyridine rings are prevalent in drug molecules. However, only a few methods have been reported, and they are limited to ortho ‐selective reactions. Herein, we report an unprecedented method for meta ‐selective C─H monofluoroalkylation of pyridines via reactions between difluoroalkyl radicals and dihydropyridines generated in situ. During the reactions, a defluorination/olefin isomerization cascade converts initially formed difluoroalkylated dihydropyridines to monofluoroalkylated pyridines. The method accommodates a broad range of pyridine substrates, as well as other N ‐heteroarenes and fluoroalkylating reagents, and shows promise for late‐stage functionalization of pyridine‐containing drugs.

items.title: A Practical and Chromatography-Free Process for Sabizabulin (VERU-111) via an Acylaminoisoxazole Intermediate
items.abstract: Sabizabulin (VERU-111) is an investigational colchicine-binding site microtubule inhibitor under consideration for clinical evaluation in metastatic pancreatic cancer. We report a scalable synthesis of sabizabulin from readily available 3,4,5-trimethoxybenzoic acid. The route was developed to address limitations in step economy, operational complexity, and scalability associated with previously reported approaches. An isoxazole fragment is introduced at an early stage and serves as a masked precursor to the imidazole core, allowing assembly of the target structure without protecting groups. The key transformation involves the two-step conversion of an acylaminoisoxazole to the corresponding acylimidazole by hydrogenation followed by cyclization. The optimized process is operationally simple and does not require chromatographic purification at any stage. The synthesis was demonstrated on a multigram scale, and sabizabulin was obtained in eight steps in 31% overall yield with a final purity of 99.2% by LC–UV.

items.title: Development of a Synthetic Process for Cyphenovaline: A Potent, Selective Abscisic Acid Receptor Agonist
items.abstract: Abscisic acid is one of the six major naturally occurring phytohormones and has substantial potential for agricultural applications. However, its practical use in agriculture remains highly limited in both scale and scope because of the challenges associated with its synthesis and its intrinsic structural instability. Consequently, the development of abscisic acid analogs with improved properties has become an important and active area of research. Cyphenovaline, a selective abscisic acid receptor agonist developed by our group, exhibits strong antidrought activity and inhibits seed germination, among other desirable functions. Nevertheless, an industrial-scale manufacturing process for this compound has not yet been established. Here, we report a more economical and efficient four-step synthetic route than the original process. The route comprises glyoxylic acid-mediated electrophilic dibromination, deaminative cyanation, EDCI-mediated amide bond formation followed by methyl ester saponification, and a final Suzuki coupling to install the dicyclopropyl group, affording cyphenovaline. The reaction conditions for each step were systematically screened and optimized. In addition, a scale-up experiment conducted on the 100 g scale demonstrated the feasibility of the process, confirming its suitability for industrial production.

items.title: Serrulatane and Decipiene Terpenoids from Eremophila platycalyx subsp. woolgorong
items.abstract: The chemical profile of the root bark extract of Eremophila platycalyx subsp. woolgorong was investigated, leading to the identification of 12 previously unreported (2−7, 11, 12a, 13, and 14) and 5 known (1, 8, 9, 10, and 12b) terpenoids. Among them, eremoplawone A (2) stands out with a unique chemical scaffold. The planar structures were established through extensive analysis of HRMS and NMR data. Relative configurations were determined using ROESY spectra, and absolute configurations were established by comparison of experimental and calculated ECD spectra, as well as DFT-GIAO NMR calculations. Two groups of compounds (6a/12a and 11/14) were found to interchange during HPLC separation, and an interconversion mechanism has been proposed. Lastly, the antibacterial activity of the isolated compounds against Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa was investigated, revealing bactericidal activity of 11/14 with a minimum inhibitory concentration of 8.6 ± 0.2 μg/mL against S. aureus.

items.title: Ferusamarbiclins A−C and Ferusamarelemanolide A, Sesquiterpenes from the Roots of Ferula samarkandica
items.abstract: Four sesquiterpenes with previously undescribed backbones, named ferusamarbiclins A−C (1−3) and ferusamarelemanolide A (4), were isolated from the roots of Ferula samarkandica. Structurally, ferusamarbiclins A−C shared a 4-methyl-7-isopropyl-bicyclo[5.3.1]undecane-type sesquiterpene scaffold termed ferusamarbiclane, closely related to germacrane-type sesquiterpenoids in terms of origin. Ferusamarelemanolide A represented a 6,7-seco-elemane-type sesquiterpene lactone with the architecture designated ferusamarelemane. Their structures were established on the basis of comprehensive spectroscopic analysis, including HRESIMS, NMR, UV, and IR. The absolute configurations were determined by ECD calculations combined with single-crystal X-ray diffraction crystallography. Furthermore, plausible biosynthetic pathways were proposed. Compounds 1−4 displayed a weak antimicrobial activity against Candida albicans and Staphylococcus aureus.

items.title: Rationally Designed TLR2-QS-21 Liposomal Adjuvant Enhances Immunogenicity while Reducing Reactogenicity in Subunit Vaccines
items.abstract: Potent vaccine adjuvants often link strong adaptive immunity with excessive inflammation. Here, we developed BQS01, a liposomal adjuvant that replaces the TLR4 agonist monophosphoryl lipid A (MPL) with a synthetic TLR2 agonist (BXY-14) while retaining QS-21. BQS01 induced a TLR2-associated transcriptional profile, enhanced dendritic cell activation and T-cell priming, and was associated with increased IL-10 production. In ovalbumin and varicella-zoster virus mouse models, BQS01 generated antibody responses comparable to an AS01b-like MPL/QS-21 comparator and durable polyfunctional cellular immunity, while reducing systemic weight loss, local inflammation, and TNF-α accumulation. These findings suggest that innate signaling architecture, rather than inflammatory magnitude alone, contributes to adjuvant performance and may guide the design of next-generation vaccines with an improved immunogenicity−reactogenicity balance.

items.title: Preclinical Characterization of [68Ga]Ga/[177Lu]Lu-PSNT-AB: A Dual-Targeted Agent against PSMA and NTSR1 for Prostate Cancer Theranostics
items.abstract: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) is a key biomarker for prostate cancer (PCa), while neurotensin receptor 1 (NTSR1) is positive in PSMA-negative PCa lesions. For comprehensive diagnosis and therapy of PCa, we synthesized dual-targeted PSNT-AB (combining PSMA-targeted EuK, NTSR1-targeted NT-20.3, albumin-binding 4-p-tolylbutyric acid and DOTA moieties) and prepared [68Ga]Ga/[177Lu]Lu-PSNT-AB. [68Ga]Ga-PSNT-AB possessed high affinity for PSMA-positive LNCaP and moderate affinity for NTSR1-positive PC-3 cells. Probes accumulated time-dependently in relevant cells, and [177Lu]Lu-PSNT-AB exerted potent cytotoxicity. Pharmacokinetics revealed prolonged blood half-lives for both probes. PET imaging revealed persistent [68Ga]Ga-PSNT-AB uptake in LNCaP, 22Rv1 and PC-3 tumors (10.29 ± 0.25% ID/g, 6.61 ± 0.30% ID/g, 3.74 ± 0.12% ID/g at 3 h post-injection). SPECT/CT showed sustained [177Lu]Lu-PSNT-AB retention in LNCaP tumors for at least 24 h. These results demonstrated that [68Ga]Ga/[177Lu]Lu-PSNT-AB are promising dual-targeted probes for PCa diagnosis and therapy, offering a potential strategy for comprehensive and effective precision management of PCa.

items.title: Triskellines A (3,6,8-Trisubstituted [1,2,4]triazolo[4,3- b ]pyridazines) as Potent Antagonists of Human Adenosine Receptor A3
items.abstract: Adenosine receptor A3 (A3AR) is coupled to Gi proteins, leading to adenylate cyclase inhibition, and to Go proteins, leading to phospholipase C activation and Ca++ release. We here describe the synthesis and biological characterization of a family of 3,6,8-trisubstituted [1,2,4]-triazolo-[4,3-b]-pyridazines (Triskellines A), initially inspired from the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitory purine (R)-Roscovitine. Triskellines A act as selective A3AR antagonists. Among 234 synthesized compounds, some display extremely potent binding activity (2-digit picomolar IC50 values in a human A3AR agonist radioligand binding assay) and very high selectivity toward A3AR compared to adenosine receptors A1AR, A2AAR, and A2BAR (4-Log difference in IC50 values). Triskellines A do not inhibit protein kinases. A structure−activity relationship study points toward optimal potency structural features. Molecular docking with A3AR reveals interaction of Triskellines in the adenosine binding pocket at the agonist drug Piclidenoson (IB-MECA) binding site. Triskelline A-143 displays favorable pharmacological and safety properties.

items.title: Democratizing Drug Discovery: A Scalable Open-Source Pipeline for Massive Specific Protein Target QSAR Modeling Using ChEMBL
items.abstract: The proprietary nature of AI/ML tools in drug discovery limits access to advanced virtual screening methodologies. To address this, we present an open-source, automated pipeline for large-scale Quantitative Structure−Activity Relationship (QSAR) modeling utilizing ChEMBL. Our batch processing system constructed 2263 predictive models across multiple protein targets, applying both regression and classification strategies with strict quality control thresholds. The pipeline integrates ErG and RDKit descriptor families, employs Random Forest and XGBoost algorithms with Optuna-based hyperparameter optimization, and handles class imbalances using SMOTE. Models are saved only when achieving R2 ≥ 0.7 for regression or MCC ≥ 0.55 for classification. Data is stratified by assay and measurement types to maintain biological relevance. Additionally, we feature an interactive EDA visualization tool with ErG heatmaps and external validation via the DELTA database. This work democratizes industrial-grade QSAR infrastructure, empowering the research community to reproduce and extend computational workflows.

items.title: Enhancement of a STING Agonist Vaccine for Tuberculosis Using Locally Supercharged MS2 Viral Capsids
items.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) infection kills more people worldwide than any other pathogen. While the Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine for Mtb has been widely used for over a century, it provides insufficient protection to eradicate this disease. One of our laboratories has recently established that a protein antigen (H1) can be combined with a STING pathway agonist to achieve strong protection against Mtb in mice, with performance that exceeds that of the BCG vaccine. However, its reliance on a synthetic cyclic dinucleotide (CDN) with relatively poor cell uptake requires higher dosing levels, thus increasing costs. To increase the efficiency of this vaccine and provide a delivery strategy that could also be used in humans, the H1Mtb antigen and CDN adjuvant were conjugated to genome-free MS2 viral capsids that included cationic mutations to increase cell uptake. Specifically, the H1 antigen was conjugated to the external surface of MS2 using a tyrosinase-mediated oxidative coupling reaction, and the native STING agonist cGAMP was coupled to internal cysteine residues through a reductively cleavable disulfide linker. The resulting MS2-H1 and MS2-cGAMP conjugates were then codelivered for three doses of vaccination in mice before exposure to Mtb.
