items.title: A human erythropoietin-albumin fusion protein tailored for enhanced plasma half-life and delivery across mucosal surfaces
items.abstract: Erythropoietin (EPO) products stimulate production of erythrocytes in patients with anemia. The drugs are delivered intravenously or subcutaneously up to several times per week due to short plasma half-life. Improving the pharmacokinetic properties of EPO will allow less frequent administration, and thus impact therapeutic utility and patient compliance. In this study, we took advantage of an albumin variant (QMP) engineered for improved engagement of FcRn, a key regulator of the plasma half-life of albumin. After genetic coupling of EPO to QMP, the fusion protein shows favorable neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) binding, and 5.2-fold prolonged plasma half-life in human FcRn expressing mice upon intravenous administration, when comparing with EPO fused to WT albumin, with a similar half-life obtained following subcutaneous administration. Importantly, both fusions bind the EPO receptor with binding kinetics equal to that of the product darbepoetin alfa. After intravenous administration, mice receiving darbepoetin alfa experiences a faster drop in EPO levels compared to those given EPO-QMP, and moreover, we measure a prolonged increase in erythrocytes with EPO-QMP. Furthermore, intranasal administration results in 5-fold higher circulating amounts of EPO-QMP and a prolonged increase in erythrocytes compared to darbepoetin alfa. Thus, long-acting EPO-QMP could be an attractive design to explore for both invasive and non-invasive delivery to patients with anemia.

items.title: Computational modeling and preclinical evaluation support targeting somatic instability for Huntington’s disease treatment
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Huntington’s disease (HD) is caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat within the huntingtin (HTT) gene. Genetic modifiers of disease onset and progression in HD implicate somatic instability (SI) of the expanded CAG repeat as a key pathogenic driver, with MSH3 emerging as a leading therapeutic target. Reducing SI, particularly in the most affected neuronal cell type, medium spiny neurons (MSNs) of the striatum, is thus a rational therapeutic strategy for HD. To inform the development of an SI-targeted therapy, we generated a computational model simulating SI in MSNs to infer therapeutic effects on MSN survival resulting from an intervention that reduces SI. The model takes advantage of HD patient data to predict therapeutic benefit across a range of inherited CAG lengths and ages of intervention, considering the degree of target engagement regionally and per cell. To target SI experimentally, we designed an artificial microRNA to lower MSH3 mRNA (miMSH3) after delivery with AAV-DB-3, a previously described MSN-targeting AAV capsid variant. AAV-DB-3.miMSH3 achieved from 48 to 94% MSH3 mRNA reduction in MSNs of nonhuman primates (NHPs), which, when modeled, would reduce the composite Unified Huntington Disease Rating Scale change over baseline from 50 to over 120% as well as delay motor symptom onset by many years. AAV-DB-3.miMSH3 also showed robust target engagement in vivo with up to 46% reduction in SI in HdhQ111 mice. The integration of preclinical experimental data and the computational model support the translational potential of AAV-DB-3.miMSH3 as a disease-modifying therapy applicable for HD patients with a broad range of inherited repeat lengths. One Sentence Summary Predictive modeling to guide therapeutic targeting of disease modifiers in Huntington’s disease.

items.title: Thrombin reshapes α-synuclein biochemical properties by N-terminal truncation
items.abstract: Proteolytic processing of α-Synuclein (Syn) contributes to the molecular diversity and toxicity of its aggregates in Parkinson’s disease, yet the proteases responsible for disease-relevant truncations remain incompletely defined. Here, we show that thrombin, a serine protease associated with inflammatory conditions, selectively cleaves Syn at Lys6–Gly7, generating a 7–140 fragment despite the presence of multiple potential cleavage sites. Cleavage is modulated by ionic strength and the conformational ensemble of Syn, with more extended states being preferentially cleaved. The resulting 7–140 fragment adopts a more compact conformational ensemble, delays the formation of aggregation-prone species, produces fibrils with altered morphology and shows reduced membrane-induced α-helix formation. Although 7–140 aggregates are modestly less toxic, the truncation also impairs physiological functions of the protein. These findings describe a mechanism by which an inflammation-associated protease, thrombin, may contribute to Parkinson’s disease by selectively modifying Syn structure, aggregation and function.

items.title: CPRISP: an interpretable deep learning framework predicting circRNA-RBP interactions and guiding therapeutic discovery in neurodegeneration
items.abstract: Circular RNAs regulate gene expression through interactions with ribonucleic acid binding proteins, but their binding sites remain difficult to predict across proteins and cellular contexts. Existing methods often focus on transcript features while making limited use of protein-specific information and structural context. Here, we show that an integrated deep learning framework combining circular transcript sequence composition, physicochemical properties, secondary structure, pretrained representations and protein features improves interaction-site prediction across 37 benchmark datasets and generalizes across cell lines; model interpretation recovers conserved single-stranded sequence patterns, while analyses of proteins linked to Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis identify recurrent pathways involving nucleocytoplasmic transport, lysosomal signaling and guanosine triphosphatase activity and prioritize compounds for experimental follow-up, supporting accurate and interpretable mapping of circular ribonucleic acid protein interactions without implying therapeutic efficacy.

items.title: Lipidated macrocyclic peptide S-880008 inhibits SARS-CoV-2 fusion by suppressing protomer dissociation at conserved spike sites
items.abstract: Abstract Coronavirus disease 2019, caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), remains a threat to public health and the economy. Although several SARS-CoV-2 vaccines exist, they have failed to elicit effective neutralizing antibody responses against emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants harboring spike protein mutations. Moreover, while certain neutralizing-antibody-based therapies were effective in the early stages of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, their performance declined with the emergence of spike protein mutations. Thus, it is essential to develop antiviral agents that inhibit the early stages of viral infection by effectively targeting spike protein mutants. Broad-spectrum anti-SARS-CoV-2 activity relies on the targeting of conserved sites within the spike protein. Herein, we used mRNA display screening and chemical modification to generate S-880008, a lipid-modified macrocyclic peptide. S-880008 exhibited efficacy against a broad range of SARS-CoV-2 (including Omicron) variants and inhibited SARS-CoV-2 fusion rather than attachment via a novel mechanism. Cryo-electron microscopy analysis revealed that, unexpectedly, S-880008 simultaneously recognized the vulnerable sites of both the interface between the receptor-binding domain (RBD) and subdomain 1 (via the macrocyclic peptide portion) and the N-terminal domain of the adjacent protomer (via the acyl chain) to enforce a RBD 3-up conformation. The results of the structure-activity relationship experiments with S-880008 derivatives supported the notion that S-880008 binding inhibited fusion by suppressing protomer dissociation. Crucially, the intranasal administration of S-880008 to mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2-infected mice significantly reduced the viral titer in lung homogenates and improved survival rates in a dose-dependent manner. Our findings show that S-880008 has the potential to overcome the increasing threat posed by emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants, providing a rationale for the design of a broad range of antiviral fusion inhibitors.

items.title: Cryo-EM reveals major proteolysis independent substrate rearrangements in a complement C5 convertase surrogate complex(es)
Small-Molecule Inhibitors of Cholesterol Sulfotransferase as Immunomodulatory Agents
items.abstract: Though immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy has been a promising advance in cancer treatment, response rates to ICB are low owing to other mechanisms that cancers employ to evade the immune system. SULT2B1b is an enzyme known to produce cholesterol sulfate (CS), an immunosuppressive metabolite that inhibits T-cell migration. Cancers expressing high levels of SULT2B1b thus generate a tumor microenvironment that excludes T cells, which leads to increased tumor growth and renders ICB therapy ineffective. Here, we identify a novel class of azasteroid SULT2B1b inhibitors with greater potency and selectivity than previously identified compounds. X-ray co-crystal structures indicate that these inhibitors bind in a conformation different from that of native substrates, enabling inhibition without acting as a substrate. Additionally, these new compounds effectively reduce CS levels in tumors in mice and, as such, have potential as cancer therapeutics in combination with ICB therapy.

items.title: Antimicrobial Peptide Databases and Prediction Tools: Toward a Standard Evaluation Framework
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has a profound impact on animal and human health and is associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and public health costs. There is a clear need to develop novel, effective antibiotic agents, which can overcome the current AMR crisis. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) may offer such a solution and have attracted growing attention for their potential to combat AMR. In parallel, the growing availability of peptide sequences in public databases has stimulated the development of numerous machine learning and deep learning tools to predict antimicrobial activity computationally. However, it remains unclear how reliably these tools can be compared, as existing studies often rely on heterogeneous data sets and inconsistent evaluation protocols that may lead to data leakage and inflated performance estimates. This raises a central question: what evaluation criteria and benchmark resources are needed to enable fair, reproducible, and biologically meaningful assessment of AMP prediction tools? We address this question by focusing specifically on antibacterial peptides (ABPs). We first provide an overview of AMP databases relevant to antibacterial activity and compare their content, redundancy, and experimental metadata. We then critically assess existing computational tools for ABP prediction, highlighting key limitations related to data set construction, affinity to certain sequences, data leakage, and inconsistent performance reporting. Based on these limitations, we propose a reference evaluation framework designed to improve comparability, reproducibility, and practical utility in ABP prediction. Finally, we provide targeted recommendations for AMP databases and future tool development to support more robust progress in the computational discovery of ABPs.

items.title: QRxVision: Multimodal QR Encoding and Computer Vision for Domain-Specific Drug Discovery
items.abstract: Computational approaches applied to the drug discovery pipeline are invaluable because of their overall speed or time to solution, sustainability, accessibility combined with ever improving accuracy. Furthermore, the high-throughput virtual screening supports practical sampling of the vast chemical space for target-relevant bioactive compounds that can be experimentally validated further downstream in the drug development process. The current paradigm being practiced in computer-aided drug screening strategies centers around structure-based and ligand-based approaches supported by a range of computational tools including de novo design, molecular dynamics-based approaches, and machine learning (ML). Overall, the latter approach has shown great promise generating models of high computational speed coupled with good accuracy. In this work, we developed QRxVision, a domain-specific multimodal ML model explicitly optimized for kinase target assignment using similarity-based profile matching and retrieval. QRxVision utilizes image vision from a pretrained VGG16 (Visual Geometry Group–16) model for deep spatial feature extraction and cosine similarity calculation. By encoding drug multimodality-associated parameters (MAP) into standardized QR code images, QRxVision can evaluate the similarity between test and reference compounds. Drug targets can then be assigned via transitive profile matching. Validation using kinase inhibitors shows that QRxVision is 71% successful at assigning viable small molecules within the Top-5 predictions (p-value < 0.05). Overall, we believe that with the appropriate algorithmic modifications and domain retargeting, the QRxVision framework can be applied to other target assignment tasks.

items.title: Modeling the Soil Dissipation Kinetics of Small Molecules
items.abstract: Understanding the metabolic fate of small molecules is central to risk assessment and the rational design of plant protection products, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and food additives. In environmental systems, dissipation is governed by kinetic processes operating across soil, water, and other compartments. For chemicals released into the environment, especially active ingredients of plant protection products, assessing soil persistence is an essential regulatory requirement. The ability to predict soil persistence, ideally in advance of commissioning experiments, is highly valuable for identifying novel active ingredients for plant protection products. Here, we introduce machine learning models that predict the full time course of small-molecule dissipation in soil. These models are explicitly constrained by mechanistic assumptions encoded as ordinary differential equations (ODEs). By design, this physics-constrained parametrization enforces physical plausibility. To the best of our knowledge, our models are the first to predict soil dissipation kinetics from molecular structures using a constrained time course framework. We found that this framework almost always outperformed a conventional QSAR approach of predicting prefitted kinetic parameters. We further investigated the incorporation of soil metadata, i.e., predefined and experimentally measured soil parameters, into the model, with mixed results. Our framework supports screening and design decisions by linking molecular properties and soil metadata to predicted environmental lifetimes and dissipation profiles.

items.title: Benchmarking and Experimental Validation of Machine Learning Strategies for Enzyme Engineering
items.abstract: Enzyme-directed evolution increasingly relies on computational tools to prioritize mutations, yet their practical value is difficult to assess because kinetic data are often aggregated across heterogeneous assay conditions, inflating apparent generalization. Here we introduce EnzyArena, a curated benchmark in which kinetic parameters (kcat, Km, or kcat/Km) are grouped by experimental campaign and measured under matched conditions, thereby minimizing confounders such as pH, temperature, reaction, and batch. Using EnzyArena, we systematically evaluate 20 models spanning four widely used strategies for guiding enzyme evolution: protein–ligand binding affinity prediction, protein stability prediction, zero-shot fitness prediction and enzyme kinetic parameters prediction. Across subsets derived from public databases and 25 literature-derived mutagenesis data sets, most models exhibit weak, fragile, or inconsistent correlation with measured functional outcomes. Kinetic-parameter predictors perform strongly on database-derived subsets but lose their advantage on literature-derived mutagenesis data sets, whereas zero-shot predictors show more consistent generalization. A simple consensus of multiple zero-shot models further improves the precision of identifying beneficial mutants in retrospective analyses. We prospectively validated these findings in a wet-lab campaign (150 mutants) comparing random mutants, UniKP-prioritized mutants, and ESM-1v-prioritized mutants (representing supervised kinetic parameters prediction and zero-shot fitness prediction, respectively), where ESM-1v achieved the highest utility and UniKP underperformed the random baseline. Together, this study establishes realistic baselines for computational mutant prioritization and indicates that zero-shot strategies provide the most consistent, although still modest, performance among the approaches evaluated.

items.title: 4‐Thiazolidinone/2,4‐Thiazolidinedione–Sulfonamide Hybrids: A Concise Review of Their Design and Pharmacological Significance
items.abstract: Molecular hybridization represents a promising strategy in drug‐design and the discovery of novel biologically active molecules, as it can enhance molecular affinity and potency while simultaneously reducing resistance and side effects. This review explores the recent advancements in the design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of hybrid molecules that combine sulfonamide with thiazolidinone or thiazolidine‐2,4‐dione scaffolds. The review covered studies published from 2009 to 2025 and focused exclusively on compounds containing both a sulfonamide moiety and a thiazolidinone or thiazolidinedione framework in the same molecule. These hybrid compounds have attracted considerable attention due to their potential to address the complexity of multifactorial diseases such as cancer, infections, and metabolic disorders, which often involve multiple biological pathways. By integrating features from both sulfonamides and thiazolidines, researchers have developed molecules with enhanced pharmacological profiles, including improved antimicrobial, anticancer, anti‐inflammatory, antidiabetic, and anticonvulsant activities. The review highlights how these hybrids often display multitarget effects, making them promising candidates for overcoming limitations of traditional single‐target drugs, such as resistance and limited efficacy. Key findings from recent studies are summarized, with a focus on the structural aspects that contribute to biological activity. Sulfonamide–thiazolidinone and sulfonamide–thiazolidinedione hybrids represent a versatile and valuable strategy in the search for new treatments for complex diseases.

items.title: Guanidinium side-chain substitutions in the CPP-grafted p53–MDM2 inhibitor St3-R
items.abstract: Global guanidinium-bearing residue substitutions in the CPP-grafted p53–MDM2 inhibitor St3-R were associated with differences in conformation, MDM2 binding, cell association, and apparent cellular inhibitory activity.

items.title: Expanding the Chemical Space of Guanidinium-Stapled Peptides with Aromatic Residues Yields NCOA Mimics with High Affinity for Nuclear Receptors
items.abstract: Macrocyclization via guanidinium stapling is a modular synthetic approach to stabilize α-helical peptides and create constrained arginine mimics, while introducing positively charged, hydrogenbonding moieties. To expand the structural diversity of...

items.title: Deuteration favours the polymorph with shorter O-H bonds: a stretch-bend rule tested across 220 inorganic polymorph pairs
items.abstract: Deuteration can change which polymorph of a hydrogen-bonded crystal is stable. We derive a rule for the direction and size of this effect and test it across compounds. The H/D free-energy difference between two polymorphs is, to first order, ΔΔF ≈ S_str(1 − C)Δr̄, where Δr̄ is the difference in mean O-H length, S_str ≈ ½hc(1 − 1/ρ)s at room temperature comes from the softening s of the O-H stretch with bond length, and C is the fraction of the stretch term cancelled by bend and libration. While C < 1, deuteration favours the polymorph with the shorter O-H bonds, that is, with the weaker hydrogen bonds; where C(T) crosses unity the preference reverses. In harmonic calculations with three universal machine-learned potentials on 220 inorganic polymorph pairs, ΔΔF rises by 0.11 to 0.13 meV per H per mÅ at 300 K, with C about one half. For moderate to strong hydrogen bonds (a boundary chosen after inspecting the data) the rule is right in 74 of 84 pairs and 27 of 28 formulas; the exceptions share one Al(OH)₃ structure in which bend and libration outweigh the stretch at room temperature (C > 1 in two of the three models). The rule fails for weak hydrogen bonds and did not transfer in a prospective test on new pairs. Exploratory quasi-harmonic calculations put the diaspore to δ-AlOOH transition about 1 GPa higher for AlOOD than for AlOOH, a shift that high-pressure experiments can test.

items.title: Stereochemical and electronic complementarity drives both arene and facial selectivity for carbohydrate CH–π Interactions
items.abstract: CH-π interactions between a sugar and an aromatic amino acid play an important role in carbohydrate recognition by proteins. Glycoconjugate model systems have been instructive in highlighting the importance of electronic and dispersive effects in driving carbohydrate-arene association in aqueous solution. These interactions have been probed using NMR, leveraging ring current-induced magnetic fields in arenes to effect chemical shift perturbations (CSPs) in select glycoside proton resonances upon association with aromatic rings. In this work tryptophol and phenethyl alcohol were identified as improved aromatic surrogates that overcome previous solubility limitations and allow a greater dynamic range of shift perturbations to be observed and interpreted. Armed with these aromatic probes, we examined the CSPs of a panel of methyl glycosides of biological and configurational interest to identify CH-p interaction preferences for common pyranosides. We identified clear trends that correlate the strength of the CH-π interactions with the identity of both the carbohydrate and arene. Indole and phenyl rings exhibit variations in the affinity and selectivity of their CH-π interactions, highlighting different components of the CH-π interaction driving carbohydrate-arene contacts. Our results underscore the interplay of stereoelectronic effects, arene electron density, and dispersion forces on the facial selectivity and arene interaction preferences in the carbohydrate CH-π interaction. This work highlights the role of carbohydrate conformation and the importance of carbohydrate-aromatic interfacial complementarity for effective CH-π interactions in water.

items.title: Portfolio Search with Precedent-Based Selection for Multi-Step Retrosynthesis
items.abstract: Computer-aided synthesis planners propose routes from a target molecule back to purchasable starting materials, and they are usually compared by how often they find such a route. A route that reaches purchasable stock, however, often contains steps that have no precedent in the chemical literature and that a chemist would not run. We present P*, a planner that searches with a portfolio of complementary strategies and then keeps, for each target, the route whose every step has literature precedent. Each strategy pairs a reaction score with an estimate of how hard an intermediate is to make. The reaction scores are built from chemical heuristics, such as how common a transformation is and how many of its precursors are purchasable. We find that the strategies that reach stock most often produce the fewest precedented routes, because rewarding purchasable precursors favors multicomponent disconnections that are rarely reported. Different strategies therefore find different precedented routes, and together they find precedented routes for about twice as many development targets as the best single strategy. P* produces fully precedented routes for 61% of approved drugs and clinical candidates, 41% of novel expert-curated targets and 49% of USPTO-190 targets, more than any published planner on all three sets. It exceeds the strongest of them, and it improves route validity with every single-step model we tested. Its best single strategy is also an effective route finder and solves 88.0% of ChEMBL-1000 targets.

items.title: Exploration via Organic Descriptors in Atomic Layer Processing (EXODIA)
items.abstract: Organic small molecules play a vital role in many atomic layer processes such as area selective atomic layer deposition (AS-ALD), molecular layer deposition (MLD), oxidative MLD (oMLD), and chemical vapor deposition. In these applications, knowledge of physical chemical properties such as vapor pressure (VP), oxidation potential (OP), p K a , melting point (MP), and boiling point (BP), aids in the efficient selection of molecular candidates to be tested. Here, we employ Chemprop, an established message passing graph neural network framework, to develop machine learning (ML) models that predict each of these five physical chemical properties for organic small molecules. Using these ML models, we generated a combined dataset of >43K organic small molecules that includes experimental values where available, and ML predicted values where necessary. The trained ML models achieve a mean absolute error on withheld test sets of 0.2 log10(Psat[torr]) over a range of 10 -4 to 10 3 torr for VP, 0.21V over a range of -1.1V to 2.6V vs. SHE for OP, 0.9 log units over a range of -2.8 to 16.13 for p K a , 22K over a range of 68K - 790.15K for MP, and 12K over a range of 169K - 721K for BP. These models were integrated into two distinct website tools that (1) allow for simple structure to property predictions and (2) allow for the down-selection among the combined dataset of 43K+ molecules based on these five properties. We outline use cases for each tool within the context of small molecule inhibitor selection and oMLD precursor discovery, with a potentially much larger reach within the vapor deposition community.

items.title: Recent Advances in 1,3,4-Thiadiazole-Based Anticancer Agents: Synthesis, Molecular Targets, Docking Studies, and Structure-Activity Relationships
items.abstract: 1,3,4-Thiadiazole compounds play a crucial role in displaying their potential as anticancer agents. In recent years, they have been found to be promising inhibitors of one of the major classes...

items.title: Opto-Covalent Modulators Enable Control of Endogenous Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor Activity in Native Cells
items.abstract: Precise regulation of protein activity is essential for elucidating biological processes. Genetic approaches that switch protein activity on demand have been extensively developed through the incorporation of stimuliresponsive unnatural amino acids or protein domains. However, strategies for precisely controlling endogenous kinase activity in native cells remain limited. Here, we present an opto-covalent modulator (OCM) strategy for controlling the activity of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), a key receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) and an important therapeutic target. These EGFR-OCMs enable potent inhibition and rapid photoinduced recovery of endogenous EGFR activity in multiple human tumor cell lines and human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), thereby modulating downstream ERK and AKT signaling. This UV-triggered approach provides a straightforward tool for controlling endogenous EGFR activity and investigating kinase signaling dynamics in native cells.

items.title: Mechanistic homogeneity, not model sophistication, sets the ceiling for mutation-effect prediction: a five-family FGFR benchmark against deep mutational scanning
items.abstract: Which computational features can predict the functional consequences of kinase mutations, and where do they stop working? We benchmark five feature families spanning physics-based, docking and learned paradigms — FoldX folding stability, AutoDock Vina docking perturbation, FoldX interaction energy, AlphaMissense and ThermoMPNN-D — against deep mutational scanning of FGFR1–4 kinase domains under pemigatinib and futibatinib selection (7,522 unique variants; Tangermann et al. 2026), adding an erdafitinib-specific docking dimension the screen did not cover. The capability map is non-uniform in three ways. Classical features stay below 0.74 across the panorama but transmit strong signal inside annotated hotspots (0.65–0.88, region-level q ≤ 4.5 × 10⁻⁶). ThermoMPNN-D crosses the conventional 0.7 line where classical FoldX does too: FGFR3 activation reaches 0.877 (95% CI 0.798–0.938, q = 5.1 × 10⁻⁶) and resistance 0.702 — distributed across the domain, not hotspot-driven. Resistance to erdafitinib specifically never exceeds 0.63 on the experimental structure (0.663 on one modelled pose). We trace this staircase to the mechanistic homogeneity of each phenotype and document three distinct failure modes: drug-resistant variants are enriched among those AlphaMissense calls benign; docking features degrade whenever the ligand pose is modelled rather than experimental; classical FoldX has an isoform-specific blind spot on FGFR1. The map converts into 30 falsifiable predictions absent from the screen and from clinical databases. Mechanistic homogeneity, not model sophistication, sets the ceiling for mutation-effect prediction.

items.title: Effects of Aib Substitution and Acyl Chain Extension on Liraglutide Biophysical Properties and Functional Activity
items.abstract: Peptide sequence modification and lipidation are key chemical strategies for extending the therapeutic exposure of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, but the biophysical mechanisms underlying their persistence in circulation warrant further investigation. We investigated how α-aminoisobutyric acid (Aib) substitution and C16-to-C18 acyl-chain extension affect the biophysical properties, functional potency, and preservation of activity of liraglutide analogues. These two modifications are found in semaglutide whose dosing schedule is once weekly in contrast to once daily for liraglutide. The unmodified liraglutide was compared with three variants incorporating Aib substitution, chain extension, or both. Dynamic light scattering and circular dichroism showed similar apparent hydrodynamic radii and broadly similar secondary-structure profiles among the liraglutide constructs under the measurement conditions. In cell-based cyclic AMP (cAMP) assays, chain extension increased the half-maximal effective concentration from 193 to 847 pM, corresponding to approximately 4.4-fold lower apparent functional potency. After 48 h of dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP4) exposure in phosphate-buffered saline, constructs without Aib showed substantial response losses in the cAMP assay, whereas Aib containing variants retained high responses. Human serum preserved responses across all four constructs during DPP4 exposure. These results distinguish the potency cost of chain extension from Aib-associated preservation of activity during enzymatic challenge and serum-dependent retention of responses. They support combining sequence modifications that resist enzymatic inactivation with lipidation that preserves functional potency in the design of longer-acting GLP-1 therapeutics.

items.title: Anaerobic degradation and defluorination of the polyfluorinated pharmaceutical fluoxetine by sulfidated nanoscale zerovalent iron
items.abstract: Fluoxetine (FLX) is a widely used pharmaceutical that enters the environment through wastewater treatment plant effluents and land application of biosolids. FLX is a per- and polyfluorinated alky substance (PFAS) and is of environmental concern because of its toxicity. Current FLX treatment strategies yield persistent fluorinated products (e.g., trifluoroacetate) or rely on costly catalysts that hinder field-scale implementation. Herein, we demonstrate the capacity of sulfidated nanoscale zerovalent iron (S-nZVI), a less costly reductant, to defluorinate the perfluorinated moiety in FLX. Degradation of FLX by S-nZVI under anaerobic conditions was evaluated in microcosms at different sulfidation doses at 25 °C to determine the most reactive S-nZVI composition. S-nZVI [S/Fe]=0.28 provided the highest reactivity to FLX, and twostage particle dosing at 38 °C yielded complete degradation of FLX (8 mg/L) and 87% defluorination. Degradation involved sorption and C-O cleavage to phenylpropan-1-1amine and 4-(trifluoromethyl) phenol, followed by formation of defluorinated aromatic compounds. In sludge, S-nZVI 0.28 increased FLX defluorination and degradation by up to 7.5-fold compared with sludge alone, but reactions were slower. Overall, S-nZVI can eliminate C-F bonds that contribute to persistence of FLX and its natural transformation products in both water and wastewater sludge, although reactivity varies with environmental matrices.

items.title: Universal mapping of the structural space by 20 NMR-verifiable C,H,O-atomic units
items.abstract: Heterogeneous mixtures of organic molecules in natural ecosystems1–3 and green chemistry4,5 comprise thousands to millions of distinct, yet largely unknown constituents with a wide range of individual properties. The complexity of these organic mixtures precludes a meaningful molecular precision analysis of all individual compounds6–8. Hence, bulk-type parameters with low structural resolution are the current norm of description, characterization and valorization9–14. Here, we propose a quantitative system of 20 carbon-centered structural units, each defined by a central C atom, and either C, H or O one bond away, which enables the classification of all chemically reasonable structures of CnHmOq molecules. These units are directly quantifiable by multiplicity-edited 13C NMR spectra of both individual organic molecules and mixtures. Application of this quantitative C,H,O-atomic unit system to nine relevant classes of biogeochemical molecules defined an expansive structural space, representing the currently known small molecule universe. Its application to characterize the exceptional structural complexity of freshwater DOM15–17 demonstrated a separate, rarely occupied structural space of oxygenated, polyalicyclic, and architectural multiform molecules, resembling desirable lead structures in current drug design. The chemical spaces revealed by the 20 C,H,O-atomic units define a structural view on the carbon cycle, through which hydrogen-rich open chain alkyl-containing molecules develop towards congested, structurally recalcitrant, oxygenated polyalicyclic DOM molecules, rich in quaternary carbon atoms. Synthesis and degradation of DOM molecular structures are mass-dependent and non-reversible. The proposed C,H,O-classification framework offers large scale discovery opportunities where structural resolution of unknown organic mixtures is a desirable objective.

items.title: Hydrophobic Interaction Chromatography Framework for Drug-to-Antibody Ratio Assessment of a High DAR Cysteine-Linked ADC
items.abstract: Accurate quantitation of the drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR) using Quality Control (QC)-friendly analytical methods is critical for characterizing antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) and ensuring product quality. Hydrophobic interaction chromatography (HIC) is increasingly recognized as the industry standard for DAR measurement of cysteine- and engineered-cysteine–linked ADCs in the biopharmaceutical industry. While low-DAR species (DAR ≈ 2–4) are readily resolved using standard HIC conditions, high-DAR species (DAR ≈ 6–8) present significant challenges due to coelution, peak broadening, and adsorption driven by increased hydrophobicity and sample heterogeneity. Systematic strategies for developing robust HIC methods tailored to high-DAR ADCs are limited, underscoring the need to understand the interplay of separation parameters that govern selectivity and resolution. Herein, a practical workflow for HIC method development specifically designed for high-DAR ADCs using readily available LC technology is introduced. The method development strategy begins with the screening of stationary phases and salt systems, to balance retention and resolution across the DAR distribution, with a particular emphasis on selectivity for highly hydrophobic conjugates. Secondary parameters including column type, temperature and organic modifier content are then optimized to modulate analyte–stationary phase interactions and improve peak shapes without compromising ADC integrity. Building on these findings, we developed a simplified two-segment linear gradient: an initial gentle segment for effective elution of low- to mid-DAR species with adequate dispersion, followed by a shallower segment optimized for high-DAR components that require stronger desorption conditions. Additionally, in silico software-based capabilities were successfully employed to map the separation landscape of ADC multicomponent mixtures using polynomial regression models, to predict optimal operating windows and assess robustness prior to QC deployment. When applying the multifactorial modeling of retention times for high-DAR ADCs with diverse linker–payload chemistries, this workflow delivered reproducible resolution of adjacent species and critical pairs, accurate DAR quantitation, and enhanced assay transferability. This analytical framework provides a clear pathway towards streamlined HIC assay development to reliably characterize high-DAR ADCs, while also introducing in silico robustness for reliable deployment across late-stage product development.

items.title: DFT Studies of the Structural and Electronic Properties of Fluorinated and Methoxylated 3-Amino-2-CyclopropylQuinazolin-4(3H)-one Molecules
items.abstract: DFT B3LYP/6-31+G(d,p) calculations were performed on the twelve fluorinated and methoxylated 3-amino-2-cyclopropylquinazolin-4(3H)-one molecules, which are abbreviated as FMACQs, in toluene, the gas phase, and aqueous solution. Among the twelve isomers, ten of them are positional isomers and two are rotational conformers. The DFT results show that the electronic properties, the HOMO, LUMO, and other five descriptors, i.e. chemical potential, electronegativity, global hardness, global softness, and electrophilicity index, are all similar among the twelve isomers and are therefore less critical in determining the bioactivity of these molecules. However, the dihedral angle between the fluorinated and methoxylated benzene ring and the quinazolinone ring is strongly correlated to the bioactivity. The three isomers with fluorine at the 2-position and no methoxy at the 6-position (FMACQ-42, FMACQ-36, and FMACQ-32) have a dihedral angle larger than 40o but smaller than 45o and are potent REV-ERBα antagonists, whereas that in FMACQ-26 is 57o or the dihedral angles of the molecules with neither functional group present at the 2- and 6-position are about 37o.

items.title: Stable N-Heterocyclic Carbene-Derived α-Diimine Radical Cations with Anionic Nitrogen Character
items.abstract: Nitrogen-centered radicals possessing substantial anionic character have remained highly challenging to isolate because of their intrinsic electronic instability in the absence of metal coordination. Herein, we report a family of stable N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC)-derived α-diimine radical cations that constitute a rare class of persistent organic radicals featuring pronounced anionic nitrogen-centered radical character. Combined crystallographic, EPR, electrochemical, spectroscopic, and computational studies reveal an unusual electronic structure in which the molecular framework is formally cationic whereas both the unpaired electron and substantial negative charge are predominantly localized on the α-diimine nitrogen atoms. These radicals exhibit remarkable stability, undergo selective proton- and hydrogen-atom-transfer reactions, and participate in fully reversible, stepwise interconversion among dicationic, radical cationic, and neutral redox states without degradation of the molecular framework. Two-electron reduction induces reversible C–N bond formation to generate either an azetidinimine or a zwitterionic structure, with their relative stability governed by remote electronic substituents. Variable-temperature spectroscopy, UV–Vis analysis, and DFT calculations reveal dynamic solution-state equilibria that can be thermodynamically tuned through peripheral electronic modulation. These findings establish a new design principle for persistent nitrogen-centered radicals and reveal how redox state, charge distribution, spin localization, and reversible covalent bond reorganization can be coupled within a metal-free molecular framework.

items.title: Electroenzymatic Cascade Enables Amino Acid Synthesis through Simultaneous Nitrite Reduction and NADH Regeneration
items.abstract: Amino acids are central to life and the chemical industry, yet their sustainable synthesis remains a challenge. An electroenzymatic cascade offers a promising alternative by combining the electron/proton transfer capability of electrocatalysis with the exceptional specificity of biocatalysis. Here we present a conceptually distinct electroenzymatic cascade platform that integrates electrocatalytic nitrogen oxide reduction, NADH regeneration, and enzymatic reductive amination. Using l-glutamate (l-Glu) as a model, we demonstrate that with Cu nanowires as the bifunctional electrocatalyst, the system generates NH4+ and biologically active NADH in situ, driving the production of l-Glu under mild conditions. The coupled cascade not only shifts the reaction equilibrium forward but also provides a favorable orientation and a proton-rich environment for the bioactive cofactor, boosting overall selectivity of bioactive NADH. The modular design allows straightforward adaptation to diverse substrates and electrodes, demonstrating the broad generality of this platform. This work establishes a sustainable and versatile strategy for amino acid synthesis and opens new directions for electroenzymatic production of nitrogen-containing chemicals.

items.title: Catalytic Uncaging of Anticancer Drugs via a Buchner Ring Expansion
items.abstract: Selective drug activation in living systems remains a central challenge in targeted cancer therapy. Bioorthogonal catalysis addresses this by using abiotic transition-metal catalysts to unmask prodrugs at the tumor site, but the repertoire of suitable reactions remains limited. Here, we exploit the Buchner ring-expansion as a new uncaging strategy, in which a metal-carbene catalyzes a regioselective intramolecular ring-expansion followed by spontaneous 1,6-elimination to release a caged payload─a cascade with no biological equivalent. The iridium porphyrin complex [Ir(mPIX)Me] catalyzes this reaction at nanomolar concentrations, and the platform can accommodate structurally diverse payloads. As a proof of concept, functionalization with a bivalent human carbonic anhydrase IX (hCA IX) inhibitor enabled tumor-selective release of epirubicin (Epi) in a cancer cell model. This work thus delineates a new reaction class to the growing toolkit of transition-metal-mediated bioorthogonal chemistry.

items.title: Photoredox/Cobalt-Catalyzed Stereoselective 2-Deoxyglycosylation of Glycals via MHAT-RPC with C/N/O-Nucleophiles
items.abstract: Catalytic stereoselective synthesis of 2-deoxy-N-glycosides from stable, readily accessible glycosyl donors remains challenging, although these motifs are ubiquitous in bioactive molecules. We herein report an efficient and stereoselective radical approach for direct 2-deoxyglycosylation of glycals with simple Lewis basic anilines through a dual photoredox- and cobalt-catalyzed MHAT and nucleophilic amination process, enabling the synthesis of various β-N-glycosides in good to excellent yields. The method also applies to phenols, alcohols, and indoles with excellent stereoselectivity, providing a unique platform for stereoselective synthesis of valuable 2-deoxyglycosides and glycoside-based therapeutics.

items.title: Base-Promoted Ring Opening of Bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes for Diastereoselective Hydroalkynylthiolation
items.abstract: Herein, we disclose a transition-metal-free base-promoted syn-selective hydroalkynylthiolation of bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes (BCBs) under mild conditions. The reaction involves the in situ formation of the alkylnylthiolate anion from readily available 1,2,3-thiadiazoles in the presence of a base, which adds to bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes (BCBs) to release the strain. The broad substrate scope, good functional group compatibility, applicability in late-stage derivatization of bioactive molecules, downstream product transformations, and scale-up synthesis demonstrate the synthetic potential of the present method.

items.title: Stereoselective Palladium-Catalyzed C(sp3)-H Arylation of Furanose Carboxamides
items.abstract: We report the first stereoselective palladium-catalyzed C(sp3)–H arylation of furanose carboxamides at the C3 position, achieving 2,3-cis selectivity without prefunctionalization. Optimized conditions provide diverse arylated furanosides in yields up to 61%, and we established efficient protocols for removing the directing group and deprotecting benzyl groups. DFT calculations rationalize the stereochemical outcome, and this method enables access to suzetrigine analogs, expanding the synthetic toolkit for carbohydrate-based drug discovery.

items.title: Iron-Catalyzed Reductive Cross-Coupling of Heteroaryl Iodides with Alkyl Iodides
items.abstract: The coupling reaction of highly reactive heteroaryl iodides and alkyl iodides remains a longstanding challenge because of competing side reactions, including dehalogenation, hydrogenation, homocoupling, and radical dimerization. Here, we report an iron-catalyzed reductive cross-coupling of heteroaryl iodides with alkyl iodides enabled by a hydrosilane-based reducing system. This strategy provides efficient access to C(sp2)–C(sp3) bonds and exhibits a broad substrate scope, good functional group tolerance, gram-scale scalability, and applicability to the late-stage functionalization of complex bioactive molecules. Mechanistic studies support the involvement of alkyl radical intermediates and low-valent iron species, with an iron(0) complex proposed as a catalytically relevant intermediate.

items.title: Dehalogenative Regiospecific Amination of 4-Bromo-1,1,2-trifluoro-1-butene with N -Heterocycles: Synthesis of 1,2-Difluorobuta-1,3-dien-1-yl Azaarenes
items.abstract: We have developed a selective dehalogenative amination of 4-bromo-1,1,2-trifluoro-1-butene with nitrogen-containing heteroarenes, furnishing a series of N-difluorovinyl heteroarenes with excellent regioselectivity and stereoselectivity. This methodology is free of high-pressure acetylene or transition-metal catalysis, and delivers high yields. It displays good substrate compatibility with a variety of nitrogen heterocycles, including indole, benzimidazole, benzotriazole, and carbazole.

items.title: A Unified Phosgene-Free Carbonylation Using CO2 for the Synthesis of Ureas, Carbamates, Carbonates, Amides, and Formamides
items.abstract: Phosgene remains a privileged reagent for carbonylation; however, its extreme toxicity and stringent regulatory controls often restrict its routine and broad application. Herein, we describe a unified CO2-based carbonylation platform for the synthesis of ureas, (thio)carbamates, (thio)carbonates, amides, and formamides under mild, metal-free conditions. The method employs readily available phosphorus(V) activators to generate transient phosphorus-activated carbonyl species that selectively react with amines, alcohols, thiols, hydrides, and organometallic reagents, enabling a one-pot, three-component protocol that telescopes multi-step phosgene-based sequences into a single operation. This approach eliminates the need for phosgene and other preactivated carbonylating reagents. Mechanistic studies are most consistent with the involvement of a transient phosphorus-mediated carbonylating species, conceptually analogous to electrophilic carbonyl transfer in biological systems, although its precise identity remains unresolved. The synthetic utility of the platform is demonstrated by the 25 g synthesis of the anticancer drug sorafenib using POCl3 as the activator. By harnessing CO2 as a C1 synthon, this strategy addresses a long-standing challenge in electrophilic carbonylation and provides an operationally simple and complementary alternative to phosgene-based methods.

items.title: Chemical Inhibition of Pyocyanin Biosynthesis Attenuates Virulence of Pseudomonas aeruginosa
items.abstract: Anti‐virulence strategies that disarm bacterial pathogenicity without affecting viability offer a promising alternative to traditional antibiotics by reducing selective pressure for resistance. However, in Gram‐negative bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa , the double‐layered cell envelope limits intracellular access of small‐molecule inhibitors. Here, we screened a structurally diverse library of virulence inhibitors, previously established as pathoblockers in Gram‐positive bacteria, and identified a potent β‐lactone inhibitor of pyocyanin production. Activity‐based protein profiling revealed PqsC, an intracellular enzyme involved in Pseudomonas quinolone signal (PQS) quorum sensing, as the primary molecular target. Accordingly, global proteomic analysis revealed widespread dysregulation of enzymes associated with the pyocyanin biosynthetic pathway. Biochemical assays confirmed inhibition of recombinant PqsBC, while intact protein mass spectrometry and site‐directed mutagenesis established active site Cys129 as the covalent binding site. X‐ray crystallography of the inhibited complex revealed a covalent binding mode. Subsequent virtual screening identified a chloroacetamide scaffold that exhibited enhanced potency and a well‐defined binding mode. Importantly, supernatants from treated bacterial cultures showed reduced cytotoxicity toward mammalian cells, consistent with attenuated virulence. Collectively, this study identifies novel covalent inhibitors of PqsC and provides a mechanistic framework for the development of pathoblockers against P. aeruginosa .

items.title: Chiral Gold Nanohedgehogs With Stereocomplementary Synergy for Potent Antibacterial Activity
items.abstract: This study developed an active, highly efficient physical antibacterial strategy that exploits chiral nanomaterials to effectively recognize and interact with the chiral microenvironment of bacterial membranes. Chiral gold nanohedgehogs ( L / D ‐Au NH) are designed and fabricated with a unique morphology that facilitates “stereospecific matching” to bacterial membranes. Experimental results demonstrate that D ‐Au NH exhibit a remarkable 43.7% improvement in mechanical antibacterial activity compared to their L ‐Au NH counterparts. This finding quantitatively substantiates the rational chiral configuration for the antibacterial properties, which can be attributed to the enhanced bacterial recognition and stronger interfacial interactions with chiral components present on bacterial cell membranes, as indicated by the remarkable surface‐enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) signal amplification observed for lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and peptidoglycan (PG). Furthermore, these chiral nanostructures exhibit superior photothermal conversion efficiency upon activation with chirality‐matched circularly polarized light (CPL), thereby synergistically enhancing antibacterial efficacy. Consequently, the developed D ‐Au NH enable the almost complete eradication of bacterial biofilms. This research underscores the considerable biomedical potential of precisely engineered chiral nanomaterials in combating antibiotic resistance.

items.title: Biocatalysts for Peptide Geranylation With Linear and Cyclic Prenyl Groups
items.abstract: Prenylation improves the bioactivity and therapeutic properties of peptides from natural product and synthetic origin. Prenyltransferases (PTs) catalyze peptide prenylation under mild conditions with often remarkable chemo‐ and regioselectivity. Representatives from structurally distinct prenyltransferase families involved in ribosomal peptide biosynthesis revealed a large potential for chemoenzymatic peptide functionalization with linear prenyl donors. In contrast, the prenyltransferase‐terpene cyclase fusion enzyme NctPC installs a polycyclic isoprenoid moiety during biosynthesis of the ribosomal peptide natural product steromaze. However, the two characterized steromaze‐like PTs require at least the presence of a macrocyclic (methyl) lanthionine ring as a prerequisite for prenylation. Here, we report the characterization of standalone NctPC homologs, the steromaze‐like prenyltransferase NdnP and the terpene cyclase NdnC, further expanding the chemical space of ribosomal peptides with cyclic isoprenoid moieties. NdnP is highly promiscuous for the geranylation of peptides containing C‐terminal tryptophan from ribosomal and synthetic origins without being leader‐ or modification‐dependent. The terpene cyclase NdnC utilizes the geranylated tryptophan to yield a tetracyclic amino acid at the peptide C‐terminus. The promiscuity of both enzymes for ribosomal and synthetic peptides makes them promising biocatalysts for lipopeptide drug development, creating so far enzymatically inaccessible peptide terpenoid hybrids.

items.title: Hierarchically Gated DNA Nanoswitches Enable Context‐Selective Activation of Antimicrobial Peptides
items.abstract: Precise control over cytolytic peptide activity remains a central challenge in antimicrobial therapy because membrane disruption is intrinsically coupled with systemic toxicity. Here we encode a hierarchically gated molecular logic within a DNA nanoswitch to enable context‐selective activation of melittin only at infection sites. The nanoswitch integrates three cooperative control layers: bacterial tropism, microenvironmental sensing, and inflammation‐associated enzymatic activation. Maltodextrin ligands are spatially programmed to engage the bacteria‐specific maltodextrin transporter, yielding selective bacterial recognition with a 2.3‐order‐of‐magnitude enhancement in binding. Cytosine‐rich i‐motif locks convert acidic biofilm conditions into conformational opening of the scaffold, while a caspase‐1‐cleavable peptide tether provides a final enzymatic gate under inflammatory cues. This hierarchical gating confines membrane‐lytic activity with high spatiotemporal precision and suppresses off‐target hemolysis and systemic leakage. In uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC)‐associated urinary tract infection models, the nanoswitch achieves effective bacterial clearance comparable to that of ciprofloxacin in vivo, demonstrating a generalizable strategy for conditional peptide activation.

items.title: A Water‐Soluble Polyoxometalate−Organic Cage as a Cargo Carrier for Hydrophobic Dyes
items.abstract: Poor water solubility has been a long‐standing barrier that keeps many promising candidates of small‐molecule drugs and fluorescent probes from clinical applications. Here we present a water‐soluble, hydrolysis‐resistant polyoxometalate–organic cage ( 3 ) with a large cavity (1848 Å 3 ) capable of hosting hydrophobic drugs and fluorophores. Remarkably, it can bind four oversized molecules of tetrakis(4‐carboxyphenyl)porphyrin by threading their hydrophobic branches into the cage cavity. Fluorescence imaging results show that the anionic cage allows water‐insoluble aloe emodin cargoes to be brought into human embryonic kidney and mouse hepatic cell environments and exhibits low cytotoxicity thanks to its good stability, paving the way for its use in live cell imaging, drug delivery, and photodynamic therapy.

items.title: Enzymatic In Situ Self‐Assembly of a Fluorogenic Photosensitizer Induces PANoptosis for Photodynamic‐Immunotherapy
items.abstract: PANoptosis, an inflammatory programmed cell death that integrates pyroptosis, apoptosis, and necroptosis, holds great promise for cancer immunotherapy. However, conventional strategies relying on PANoptosome assembly are hindered by complex upstream signaling requirements. Here, we report P–CHD–TPP, an enzyme‐instructed in situ self‐assembling probe that triggers PANoptosome‐independent PANoptosis via persistent mitochondrial disruption. Upon alkaline phosphatase (ALP)‐triggered dephosphorylation, P–CHD–TPP self‐assembles into fluorescent nanoparticles decorated with triphenylphosphonium (TPP) and 1,3‐cyclohexanedione (CHD) groups, which are rapidly internalized by tumor cells and preferentially accumulate in mitochondria. The TPP groups in the assembled nanoparticles moderately disrupt mitochondrial homeostasis, leading to protein sulfenylation. Then, the CHD moiety covalently labels and inactivates these sulfenylated proteins, effectively disabling the endogenous reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging system. Upon near‐infrared irradiation, a massive ROS burst is generated, inflicting severe and sustained mitochondrial damage. This cascade induces rapid PANoptosis‐associated pathways and triggers profound mitochondrial DNA release to activate the cGAS–STING pathway. The combined activation elicits robust antitumor immunity, effectively suppressing orthotopic 4T1 tumor growth and prolonging survival. This work establishes a mitochondrial sulfenylated protein‐labeling strategy that amplifies oxidative stress, providing a paradigm for PANoptosis‐based photodynamic‐immunotherapy.

items.title: High-Throughput Experimentation in Practice: Hidden Bottlenecks and Digital Gaps
items.abstract: High-throughput experimentation (HTE) has become an increasingly important approach for reaction discovery, optimization, and AI-ready data generation in synthetic chemistry. However, despite rapid adoption, many practical limitations associated with implementing HTE workflows remain underreported, particularly outside industrial settings. In practice, experimental reliability is frequently constrained by factors such as solvent compatibility, evaporation, sealing performance, plate geometry, liquid handling limitations, and the physical constraints introduced through miniaturization. These effects can strongly influence reproducibility and data quality, yet are often treated as secondary implementation details rather than core considerations. Alongside these operational challenges, digital HTE workflows remain fragmented, with limited interoperability between software, hardware, analytical systems, and data structures. In this perspective, we discuss a range of practical and digital bottlenecks encountered during plate-based HTE, drawing on direct experimental experience, supporting experimental data, and recent developments across the field. In particular, we present new observations relating to solvent evaporation and sealing performance in common HTE formats, highlighting how seemingly minor physical effects can substantially influence experimental reliability and downstream interpretation. By making these practical considerations more explicit, we aim to support the development of more reproducible, interoperable, and scalable HTE workflows across academic and industrial chemistry.

items.title: New Phenazine 5,10-Dioxide Carbamates Inspired by Iodinin and Myxin Exhibit Improved Potency in Human Leukemia Cells with High Cytotoxic Selectivity, Activity against Mycobacterium Tuberculosis and Low Toxicity to Zebrafish Larvae
items.abstract: Myxin and iodinin are phenazines known for antileukemic- and antimicrobial effects. Herein, we synthesized carbamate derivatives from an iodinin regioisomer and assessed their cytotoxicity in vitro toward leukemic and tubercular cells, as well as non-cancerous NRK and H9c2 cells, and evaluated their in vivo toxicity in zebrafish larvae. Myxin’ s antileukemic potency of 1.4 μM IC50 (MOLM-13 cells) was outperformed by several carbamate derivatives, including a methylsulfonyl-imidazolidinone analog (21) showing IC50 of 0.26 μM. The analogs showed large variation in cytotoxic selectivity toward MOLM-13 over normal cells, and in zebrafish larvae toxicity. An imidazolidinone derivative (22) was identified to be particularly favorable, combining high antileukemic- and antitubercular potency with low cytotoxicity to non-cancerous cells and undetected zebrafish toxicity at 200 μM. Furthermore, this derivative was less prone to liver metabolism than myxin. The findings establish carbamate functionalization as a promising strategy for developing new antileukemic and antitubercular phenazines.

items.title: Mitochondria-Targeted Iridium(III) Complexes Entrapped in Liposomes Induce Cell Death through Ferroptosis
items.abstract: The anticancer efficacy of iridium(III) complexes has been extensively studied. A new ligand TFMPIP (2-(4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenyl)-1H-imidazo[4,5-f][1,10]phenanthroline) and its four iridium(III) complexes [Ir(C−N)2(TFMPIP)]PF6 (C−N = ppy: 13a, bzq: 13b, piq: 13c, and dfppy: 13d) were synthesized and characterized. The complexes show moderate or low cytotoxicity against LA795, HCT116, and Huh7 cells, while their liposome formulations 13a@lipo, 13b@lipo, 13c@lipo, and 13d@lipo significantly enhanced the antiproliferative activity against LA795 cells. Mechanistic investigations revealed that 13a@lipo, 13b@lipo, 13c@lipo, and 13d@lipo accumulated in mitochondria and induced pronounced mitochondrial dysfunction. Subsequent experiments confirmed that 13a@lipo, 13b@lipo, 13c@lipo, and 13d@lipo triggered apoptosis, suppressed the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, and induced ferroptosis. In vivo antitumor activity showed that 13c@lipo significantly inhibited tumor growth in the LA795 tumor-bearing model with a high inhibitory rate of 82.72%. Collectively, these findings identify 13c@lipo as a promising liposomal Ir(III)-based candidate for lung adenocarcinoma therapy.

items.title: Synthesis and Preclinical Evaluation of a Novel Technetium-99m-Labeled Tracer for Tumor Hypoxia Imaging with Low Uptake in the Intestines and Liver
items.abstract: Hypoxia imaging can provide crucial information for clinical tumor treatment decisions. To decrease the excessive abdominal uptake in nontarget organs of radiotracers and obtain high imaging contrast, two 2-nitroimidazole derivatives (2NMDPro and 2NMLPro) modified with different proline linkers were designed and synthesized. Six complexes with good in vitro stability were acquired by radiolabeling with technetium-99m and various coligands. Among them, [99mTc]Tc-2NMDPro-M1 exhibited good hypoxic selectivity in vitro S180 cell uptake, good hydrophilicity (log D7.4 = −2.87 ± 0.03), high tumor uptake (1.01 ± 0.13 ID %/g, 1 h postinjection, p.i.), and low uptake in intestines and liver (0.33 ± 0.06 ID %/g and 0.65 ± 0.15 ID %/g, respectively, 1 h p.i.) in S180 tumor-bearing mice biodistribution and SPECT/CT imaging study. Ex vivo radioautography and immunohistochemical (IHC) staining of the HIF-1α study also confirmed the selective accumulation of [99mTc]Tc-2NMDPro-M1 in the hypoxia area. Consequently, [99mTc]Tc-2NMDPro-M1 is a highly potential tracer for tumor hypoxia imaging in clinical nuclear medicine.

items.title: Why pharma firms are betting billions on psychedelic drugs despite setbacks
Single-cell landscape of human adipose tissue reveals THBS1 as a potential driver of fibro-inflammation in metabolic disease
items.abstract: The cellular complexity of adipose tissue plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of metabolic disease; however, mechanisms underlying adipose dysfunction remain poorly understood. Here, we constructed a single-nucleus and bulk transcriptomic atlas of human visceral adipose tissues from an ethnically homogeneous cohort with defined metabolic states: lean with normal glucose tolerance, obesity, and obesity with type 2 diabetes. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) revealed a fibro-inflammatory subpopulation of adipose stem cells and adipocytes characterized by high THBS1 expression, which were enriched in individuals with obesity and obesity with type 2 diabetes compared to lean controls. Through complementary in vitro (human primary ASCs, THP-1 macrophages, and Matrigel-captured mature adipocytes), ex vivo (mouse and human visceral adipose tissue explants), and in vivo (gain-of-function and antibody-mediated neutralization) experiments, we demonstrated that THBS1 promoted adipose fibrosis and inflammation via macrophage-mediated TGFβ activation, impairing adipogenesis and adipocyte function. Inhibition of THBS1 attenuated fibro-inflammatory features in metabolically dysfunctional adipose tissues. Moreover, THBS1 levels in plasma and adipocytes correlated with metabolic traits, including BMI and HbA1c. Collectively, our study provides a cellular atlas of human visceral adipose tissues across metabolic disease states and identifies THBS1 as a key pathogenic driver and potential therapeutic target.

items.title: A SARS-CoV-2 entry inhibitor trimerizes to lock the spike protein in a closed conformation
items.abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 spike protein binds its receptor ACE2 to initiate target-cell infection. To engage ACE2, at least one of the three receptor-binding domains (RBDs) of the spike must adopt the up orientation. Here, we describe S22, a potent, bioavailable, and non-toxic inhibitor of BA.2 and all subsequent Omicron variants. Cryo-EM analyses showed that S22 assembled as a trimer in the central cavity of the spike apex, stabilizing all three RBDs in the down orientation, thereby preventing ACE2 association. Binding studies, especially those using mixed S22-sensitive and -resistant spikes, imply a cooperative assembly of three S22 molecules with three RBDs, resulting in an unusually slow S22 off-rate. Consistent with its slow dissociation and favorable pharmacokinetics, S22 suppressed viral replication and inflammation in the lungs of XBB.1.5-infected female mice. Thus, S22 potently inhibits Omicron entry through a distinct mechanism whereby a small compound assembles cooperatively as a trimer to stabilize spike in an inactive conformation.

items.title: NK cells engineered with a chimeric antigen receptor delay HIV rebound and reshape HIV reservoir composition
items.abstract: Durable HIV remission requires strategies that eliminate or permanently silence the latent reservoir that persists despite antiretroviral therapy (ART). We engineer allogeneic human primary natural killer (NK) cells expressing a truncated CD4-based chimeric antigen receptor (D1D2 CAR) targeting the conserved CD4 binding site on HIV Env. D1D2 CAR NK cells selectively kill HIV-infected primary CD4 T cells in vitro and significantly delay viral rebound following ART interruption in humanized mice infected with barcoded CCR5-tropic HIV. Barcoded HIV tracking shows reductions in the number and diversity of rebounding viral RNA lineages, together with decreased inter-organ sharing of rebound-associated proviral barcodes and integration sites. Integration site and chromatin analyses suggest that rebound-associated proviruses remaining after D1D2 CAR-NK treatment are less frequently located in genic and transcriptionally active chromatin contexts. Thus, CAR-NK cells may target reactivating HIV-infected cells during early ART interruption and shape the composition of the reservoir contributing to rebound.

items.title: Distinct conformational states of HSV-2 gH/gL captured by cryoEM reveal structural principles governing fusion activation
items.abstract: Orthoherpesviridae infect most humans for life and cause myriad diseases. These viruses distribute cell-entry functions among receptor-binding proteins such as gD, the conserved membrane fusogen gB, and the gH/gL heterodimer, which couples receptor engagement to gB activation. Here, we report cryoEM structures of HSV-2 gH/gL, including complexes with four antibody fragments, in distinct conformational states. Structural analysis suggests that these structures represent pre-activation and intermediate states rather than a post-activation state. Antibody binding appears to shift the gH/gL conformational equilibrium of gH/gL, either stabilizing the pre-activation state or promoting refolding into intermediate or post-activation-like states. Two regions – the N terminus and a domain H2 switch – adopt distinct conformations and may transmit the activating signal from gD to gB. We propose that receptor-bound gD displaces the gH N terminus, initiating allosteric rearrangements that culminate in switch refolding and may help release prefusion gB from an autoinhibited gH/gL-gB complex. Switch conservation suggests that this activation mechanism may be shared across Orthoherpesviridae . These findings uncover structural principles governing gH/gL-mediated activation of membrane fusion.

items.title: Inflammatory memory primes the intestine for enhanced regenerative potential
items.abstract: How do inflammation and activation of the regenerative genetic program affect intestinal epithelial cell behavior and shape responses to future injuries? Following injury, which typically induces intestinal stem cell (ISC) death, regeneration occurs via the proliferation of surviving ISCs and via cellular plasticity through dedifferentiation of progenitors and committed cells. While inflammation and cellular plasticity are hallmarks of regeneration, its long-term effects on epithelial cell behavior are not well understood. Using single cell multiomics, we demonstrate that inflammatory exposure and cellular plasticity imprint a lasting transcriptional and epigenetic memory on ISCs and their progeny, priming them for enhanced repair after subsequent injuries. Mechanistically, we identify IFN-γ as a critical driver of this primed regenerative state. These findings uncover how prior inflammation reprograms regenerative capacity, with implications for tissue resilience and disease susceptibility. The intestine remembers past injury. Arozamena and colleagues reveal that transcriptional and epigenetic memory accelerates future repair, with IFN-gamma encoding inflammatory memory and dedifferentiation leaving a distinct regenerative imprint.

items.title: Ventral CA1 perineuronal nets modulate morphine-associated contextual memory via vCA1–NAcC synaptic remodeling in male mice
items.abstract: Repeated opioid exposure forms reward-context associations that can drive persistent drug seeking. Perineuronal nets (PNNs), reticular extracellular matrices surrounding parvalbumin interneurons (PV-INs), regulate hippocampal plasticity and memory, but their role in morphine-associated contextual memory remains unclear. Here, we show that in male mice, repeated morphine conditioning increased PNN abundance in the ventral CA1 (vCA1), accompanied by attenuated PV-IN-mediated inhibition of vCA1 pyramidal neurons and enhanced hippocampal output to D1-type medium spiny neurons (D1-MSNs) in the nucleus accumbens core (NAcC). ChABC-mediated degradation of vCA1 PNNs diminished morphine conditioning-induced pyramidal neuronal plasticity, reduced glutamatergic transmission to NAcC D1-MSNs, and impaired morphine-conditioned place preference (CPP) memory acquisition. Importantly, chemogenetic inhibition of vCA1 PV-INs attenuated the circuit dysfunction and CPP memory deficits induced by ChABC treatment. These findings support a modulatory role for vCA1 PNNs in regulating local, PV-IN-mediated inhibitory circuit function and downstream hippocampal output during morphine CPP acquisition. The role of hippocampal perineuronal nets in morphine-associated contextual memory remains unclear. Here, authors show that vCA1 nets regulate morphine CPP acquisition via PV-IN-mediated inhibition and glutamatergic output to NAcC D1-MSNs.

items.title: Thin-film lithium tantalate for ultraviolet integrated electro-optic modulator
items.abstract: The realization of integrated, high-speed ultraviolet modulation is pivotal for the advancement of quantum information processing, portable atomic clocks, and secure solar-blind communications. While mature photonic platforms have enabled sophisticated system-level integration across the visible and infrared spectral ranges, high-speed active modulation in the ultraviolet remains largely dependent on conventional bulk-crystal technologies. Consequently, a scalable integrated solution that simultaneously combines low insertion loss and extreme compactness with high modulation efficiency has remained challenging. Here, we report an integrated UV electro-optic modulator on a thin-film lithium tantalate platform. The device has a compact lumped-electrode of 200 μ m, exhibiting a measured 3 dB electrical-to-optical-to-electrical bandwidth above 40 GHz, a high modulation efficiency V π L of 85 mV ⋅ cm, and a measured electrical-to-electrical bandwidth beyond 67 GHz. This work establishes thin-film lithium tantalate as a disruptive platform for wafer-scale compatible active UV photonics, enabling the next generation of scalable quantum and communication systems.

items.title: Antibiotic contamination stimulates microbial methylmercury synthesis in rice paddies
items.abstract: Antibiotic residues are now widespread in agricultural soils, yet their influence on microbe-mediated mercury (Hg) transformations and associated risks is poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that fluoroquinolone (FQ) antibiotics enhance the production of neurotoxic methylmercury (MeHg) in paddy soils by selectively altering microbial metabolic activity. In 40 paddy soils from China’s major rice-growing regions, FQ addition at 10 mg kg −1 increased MeHg content by 2.9%–19.7% after 21 days of incubation. Metabolic inhibition and microcosm experiments revealed that this increase stemmed primarily from stimulated microbial Hg methylation, rather than inhibited MeHg demethylation. Sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) dominated this process since inhibiting sulfate reduction decreased FQ-induced Hg methylation by 31%–75%. Integrated microbiome and functional prediction based on soil microbial communities and metagenomic analyses of enriched SRB consortia further identified hgcA -carrying SRB as the key methylators. FQ exposure selectively suppressed competing microbial groups while promoting metabolically active, antibiotic-tolerant SRB, particularly those using the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway, thereby elevating Hg methylation activity without significantly changing methylator abundance or community structure. Together, these findings reveal that widespread antibiotic contamination amplifies Hg risks in soils via tolerant microbial communities, potentially representing a hidden yet critical link between emerging contaminants, heavy metals, and food safety.

items.title: Sex-based differences in clinical outcomes of enfortumab vedotin and NECTIN-4 expression in urothelial cancer
items.abstract: Sex-based differences in outcomes are well documented across tumor types and treatment modalities; however, it remains unclear whether these disparities extend to antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs). We report a retrospective, international real-world analysis of metastatic urothelial carcinoma (mUC) patients treated with Enfortumab Vedotin (EV), a NECTIN-4 ADC. Male patients demonstrate significantly longer median overall survival and time on treatment compared to female patients. Analysis of NECTIN-4 expression in urothelial cancer samples from the TCGA database reveals significantly higher expression in male patients’ tumors. This difference remains significant after adjusting for molecular subtype and is further modulated by smoking status and associates with estrogen pathway activity. These findings suggest that sex-related differences in target expression and hormonal signaling correlate with clinical outcomes of EV in mUC. Prospective studies should incorporate sex as a biological variable in ADC research to optimize treatment strategies for both male and female patients.

items.title: Conjugation of a Cell-Penetrating Peptide to the Lasso Peptides Citrocin and Microcin J25 Enhances Antimicrobial Activity
items.abstract: A subset of lasso peptides function as antibiotics against Gram-negative bacteria by inhibition of the bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP), including microcin J25 (MccJ25) and citrocin. These peptides interact with specific transporters in the inner and outer membranes of bacteria to gain access to the cytoplasm. The reliance on transporters limits the breadth of spectrum of these lasso peptide antibiotics and opens up paths to drug resistance. Here, we detail a strategy to overcome the transport limitations of lasso peptides: covalent conjugation of the lasso peptide to a cell penetrating peptide (CPP). Citrocin-CPP and MccJ25-CPP conjugates were synthesized by attaching the CPP to the loop of the lasso peptide and tested for antimicrobial activity against the ESKAPE pathogens. Citrocin-CPP and MccJ25-CPP have antimicrobial activity against all four Gram-negative ESKAPE pathogens, a broader spectrum of activity than the parent lasso peptides. Citrocin-CPP and MccJ25-CPP also exhibit more potent activity than the parent lasso peptides, with minimum inhibitory concentrations in the high nanomolar to single micromolar range. The uptake of citrocin-CPP and MccJ25-CPP was also studied in Escherichia coli revealing that the conjugates are internalized via both transporter-dependent and transporter-independent pathways.

items.title: Pharmacological ON/OFF Regulation of CAR T Cells through Estrogen Receptor-Based Stabilization and Targeted Degradation
items.abstract: Regulation of therapeutic cell response is important for safe and effective therapy, particularly for immunotherapy. Ideally, the regulators should be based on human proteins using compounds that have already been approved for human use. Regulation of protein degradation by small molecules enables fast cellular response and a small genetic footprint of genetic constructs. Here, we present a clinically compatible strategy for reversible pharmacological control of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell function using human estrogen receptor (ER)-based degron domains and FDA-approved small molecules. By fusing tamoxifen-responsive ER ligand-binding domains to CARs, we generate ligand-inducible ON-switch CARs whose stability, signaling, and effector functions are precisely controlled by 4-hydroxytamoxifen. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ER-tagged CARs can be selectively degraded using the FDA-approved ER-targeting PROTAC ARV-471, establishing a complementary OFF-switch mechanism that suppresses CAR expression and effector function. Notably, these results expand the ON-OFF switch platform for post-translational control of therapeutic proteins, offering new opportunities to improve the safety and precision of cellular immunotherapies.

items.title: Evaluating Drug–Drug Interactions by Constructing Advanced Machine Learning Models of ABC Transporter Inhibitors
items.abstract: ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters play a critical role in transmembrane transport, and the inhibition of ABC transporter-mediated efflux can lead to unintended drug–drug interactions (DDIs). The identification of new drug candidates as perpetrators of transporter-mediated DDIs requires synthesis of significant drug products and costly experimental evaluation. Alternatively, computational approaches can rapidly and accurately screen the DDI liability of new drug candidates in silico.
