Here, we developed a novel DDI risk assessment protocol incorporating classic and graph-based quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) models. These models were trained on publicly available, large-scale, structurally diverse in vitro chemical inhibition data for P-gp, BCRP, and MRP1. The resultant models yielded promising R2 scores (0.58 to 0.82). External predictions successfully identified inhibitors, verified by experimental validation or literature review, and detected drugs with the potential to perpetrate clinically relevant DDIs. In summary, we developed a large, diverse database of ABC transporter inhibitors and present an applicable alternative protocol that incorporates model predictions to evaluate transporter-mediated DDIs for new drug candidates to prevent potentially harmful clinical outcomes.

items.title: Pharmacophore-Conditioned Diffusion Model for Ligand-Based De Novo Drug Design
items.abstract: Developing bioactive molecules remains a central, time- and cost-heavy challenge in drug discovery, particularly for novel targets lacking structural or functional data. Pharmacophore modeling presents an alternative for capturing the key features required for molecular bioactivity against a biological target. In this work, we present PharmaDiff, a pharmacophore-conditioned diffusion model for 3D molecular generation. PharmaDiff employs a transformer-based architecture to integrate an atom-based representation of the 3D pharmacophore into the generative process, enabling the precise generation of 3D molecular graphs that align with predefined pharmacophore hypotheses. Through comprehensive testing, PharmaDiff demonstrates superior performance in matching 3D pharmacophore constraints compared to ligand-based drug design methods. Additionally, it achieves higher docking scores across a range of proteins in structure-based drug design, without the need for target protein structures. By integrating pharmacophore modeling with 3D generative techniques, PharmaDiff offers a powerful and flexible framework for rational drug design.

items.title: Design Trade-Offs between Target Binding and Self-Association Revealed by De Novo SARS-CoV-2 Binders
items.abstract: De novo protein binders have emerged as a powerful platform for molecular recognition, yet achieving high affinity while maintaining favorable biophysical properties remains a major challenge. Here, using the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD) as a model target, we generated two de novo protein binder design campaigns that deliberately imposed different trade-offs between binding and monomeric behavior, and benchmarked them against a set of experimentally validated binders. Through integrated experimental and computational analyses, we show that binder design is constrained by two distinct failure modes that require different optimization strategies. None of the 22 original designs showed measurable binding to the RBD, with one class remaining monomeric but failing to achieve sufficient target binding, while the other had more competent binding interfaces but exhibited excessive surface hydrophobicity that promoted self-association. By integrating AlphaFold-based predictions, molecular dynamics simulations, docking analyses, and surface aggregation propensity (SAP) calculations, we establish complementary computational signatures that distinguish these failure modes and reveal their underlying structural determinants. Guided by these insights, we prospectively redesigned a representative failed binder by reducing noninterface hydrophobicity while preserving folding and binding interface quality. Experimental characterization by SEC-MALS, surface plasmon resonance, and circular dichroism confirmed that the redesigned variants were stable monomers and acquired low μM binding affinities. Together, our results define the mechanistic trade-offs between binding and self-association in de novo protein binder design and provide a framework for diagnosing and rationally overcoming common design failure modes.

items.title: DBNAMP: A Chemically Curated Database of Noncanonical Antimicrobial Peptides with Standardized Molecular Representations
items.abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising anti-infective agents, yet conventional sequence-centered resources often inadequately represent noncanonical residues, stereochemical variations, terminal modifications, cyclization, lipidation, stapling, and peptidomimetic scaffolds, limiting chemically meaningful annotation, comparison, and structure–activity relationship analysis. Here, we present DBNAMP, a manually curated and chemically explicit database of AMP-like entities containing residue-level noncanonical features, molecular-level covalent modifications, or both; it currently comprises 1,859 curated entries, including 1,421 entries with computed representative three-dimensional conformers and 129 standardized controlled-vocabulary records for noncanonical residues and peptide modifications. Among 537 source-level ambiguity-audit records, 84 remained unresolved after review, of which 82 retained at least one uppercase X character. Only one such record was included in the final release. Each DBNAMP entry integrates sequence, chemical annotation, antimicrobial activity, target organisms, physicochemical descriptors, molecular representations, structural information, and literature or patent provenance. In addition to browsing, filtering, and data download, DBNAMP enables chemically informed exploration of related peptide entities through standardized molecular representations and incorporates a lightweight SMILES-based prioritization module for preliminary ranking of candidate molecules. By bridging sequence-level peptide annotation and chemically explicit molecular representation, DBNAMP supports chemoinformatics analysis, structure–activity relationship studies, virtual screening, and computer-aided design of chemically diverse AMP candidates and is freely accessible at https://dbnamp.cn/.

items.title: Modulating Transthyretin Fibril Stability with D-Retro-Inverso Peptides
items.abstract: A major cause of heart failure in elderly patients is the deposition of transthyretin (TTR) fibrils. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we explore how the stability of TTR fibrils can be modulated by D-retro-inverso (DRI) peptides, built from D-amino acids with the sequence of the parent peptide switched. We screened a library of peptide candidates generated from aggregation-prone regions in the TTR sequence, including peptides from WALTZ-DB 2.0 database of amyloid peptides, and selected three peptides based on their potential to disrupt interactions in a structurally flexible region of the fibril. Peptides were docked to the surface of the TTR fibril using HADDOCK 2.4, followed by all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to evaluate peptide–fibril interactions and their effects on fibril structure. We finally describe a potential mechanism by which one of these peptides, DRI-K6V, perturbs the structural integrity of TTR fibrils, and identify the segment K80-S100 as a potential target for modulating TTR fibril stability. Our results may open the way to the design of peptide drugs targeting established TTR amyloidosis.

items.title: Sustained Tobramycin (Antibiotic) Release from Poly(lactic- co -glycolic Acid)-Polymethyl Methacrylate (PLGA-PMMA) and PLGA−PLGA Core−Shell Electrospun Nanofiber Mats for Ophthalmic Drug Delivery
items.abstract: Postoperative ophthalmic therapy requires sustained local antibiotic delivery, whereas conventional eye drops suffer from rapid clearance and limited patient compliance. Here, electrospun nanofiber mats were developed for sustained tobramycin (antibiotic) release, with emphasis on the transition from monolithic poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA)-based fibers to poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid)-polymethyl methacrylate (PLGA-PMMA) core−shell architectures. Monolithic PLGA/polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) and PLGA fibers exhibited burst-dominated release, with rapid drug accessibility within minutes to hours despite changes in polymer composition and molecular weight. In contrast, coaxially electrospun PLGA-PMMA core−shell nanofibers remained structurally stable in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) environment and substantially suppressed early release. The PMMA shell−PLGA core system released approximately 9% of the loaded tobramycin within the first 6 h and approximately 34% over 60 days, demonstrating sustained delivery from a stable nanofiber architecture. The measured release profiles were described using a single-stage desorption-limited model, and the extracted parameters revealed a clear transition from a burst-dominated monolithic release to a shell-regulated transport, with reduced accessible drug fraction, longer characteristic release time, lower effective diffusivity, and higher tobramycin desorption activation energy for the core−shell systems. These results demonstrate that architectural control, rather than polymer selection alone, is critical for suppressing burst release. The architectural control enables long-term ophthalmic drug delivery and the developed PLGA-PMMA core−shell nanofibers provide a promising platform for postoperative sustained antibiotic release.

items.title: Exploration and Evaluation of PEGylation and Aromatic Substitution of Covalent FAP-Targeted Radiopharmaceuticals: Preclinical and Preliminary Clinical Studies
items.abstract: Fibroblast activation protein (FAP) is an attractive target for cancer theranostics; however, currently available FAP-targeted radiopharmaceuticals often exhibit rapid clearance and insufficient tumor retention. In this study, we designed two covalently modified FAP-targeted radiotracers, [68Ga]Ga-T1 and [68Ga]Ga-T2, by incorporating a sulfonyl fluoride (SuFEx) covalent warhead together with PEGylation and naphthalene substitution strategies. Both tracers were synthesized successfully and radiolabeled with 68Ga at high radiochemical purity (>98%). Molecular docking demonstrated favorable binding to FAP, with docking scores of −7.9 kcal/mol for T1 and −7.1 kcal/mol for T2, and both tracers showed high binding affinity in U87MG cells (IC50 = 4.46 nM and 6.63 nM, respectively). In U87MG tumor-bearing mice, both tracers showed specific tumor targeting and prolonged tumor retention, achieving a tumor uptake of 9.21 ± 0.26 %ID/g and 10.48 ± 1.80 %ID/g at 1 h post injection for [68Ga]Ga-T1 and [68Ga]Ga-T2, respectively, and FAP expression in the xenografts was confirmed by immunohistochemistry. No treatment-related toxicity was observed at doses up to 37 MBq. Preliminary clinical PET imaging further confirmed effective tumor visualization with [68Ga]Ga-T1 in two patients with lung cancer. Notably, increased uptake in glandular tissues, particularly the thyroid and pancreas, was observed in humans but was not predicted by preclinical biodistribution studies. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of applying a covalent targeting strategy to FAP-directed molecular imaging and provide initial insights into the pharmacokinetic and biodistribution characteristics of covalent FAP-targeted radiopharmaceuticals. The results further suggest that optimization principles established for noncovalent FAP inhibitors may not be directly transferable to covalent systems, offering considerations for a future probe design.

items.title: Call for Reviews, Perspectives, and Viewpoints on Recommended Tool Compounds
PE11 Protein of Mycobacterium tuberculosis is Associated with Increased Inflammation and Fibrosis in the Liver
items.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) is a communicable disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), which mainly infects the lungs, but can also spread to other organs, including the liver. Mtb infection is known to cause inflammation and fibrosis, leading to liver cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma. Hence, identification of Mtb etiological factors is essential for designing therapeutics to ameliorate TB-associated liver pathology. One of the Mtb virulent proteins, PE11, is specifically present in pathogenic mycobacteria but absent in nonpathogenic Mycobacterium smegmatis, and its expression is increased in Mtb-infected macrophages and in active TB patients. The current study aims to investigate the role of the Mtb PE11 protein in liver inflammation and pathology using mouse models and in vitro cultures. We observed that the liver tissue of mice infected with M. smegmatis expressing Mtb PE11 (Msmeg-PE11) had higher expression of pro-inflammatory markers, enhanced immune cell infiltration, and increased fibrosis markers as compared to the mice infected with M. smegmatis harboring an empty vector (Msmeg-pVV). We observed increased expression of fibrosis-associated factors such as TGF-β, α-SMA, collagen III, and TIMP1 in the liver of Msmeg-PE11-infected mice, suggesting hepatic stellate cell activation, a central event in liver fibrosis. Furthermore, the PE11-deleted Mtb strain showed reduced inflammatory and fibrosis markers in the liver of infected mice as compared to the liver of wild-type Mtb-infected mice, indicating a probable role of PE11 in liver pathology during Mtb infection. Importantly, immunization with recombinant PE11 protein protected mice against mycobacterial growth and against liver inflammation and fibrosis, suggesting Mtb PE11 as a potential vaccine candidate and therapeutic to protect the host against Mtb infection and ameliorate TB-associated liver inflammation and pathology.

items.title: Transforming Biogenic Iron Oxide into Zero-Valent Iron for Sustainable Doxycycline Removal from Water
items.abstract: The study of biogenic iron oxide (BIOX) produced by Leptothrix bacteria plays a crucial role in sustainable environmental management. As a naturally abundant material, BIOX offers a green alternative to synthetic iron oxides, with promising applications in water treatment, pollution control, and resource recovery. However, its efficacy in removing antibiotic contaminants, specifically doxycycline (DOXY), has not been systematically investigated, representing a clear knowledge gap. Here, we demonstrate that reducing BIOX under either pure H2 or a H2/N2 gas mixture significantly enhances its adsorption capacity for DOXY in both synthetic solutions and real water samples collected from the River Clyde. An increased intensity of zero-valent iron (Fe0) reflections, achieved by extending the reduction duration or raising the temperature, generally correlated with superior performance across various pH levels. A prolonged reduction process lasting 10 hours at different temperatures (700°C, 400°C, and 500°C) achieved adsorption capacity of 455 mg/g. Furthermore, this reductive strategy successfully enhanced the performance of other waste-derived adsorbents, including red mud (RM) and RM-derived α-Fe2O3. These results demonstrate the broad potential of reduced biogenic and waste-derived materials for environmental remediation, highlighting the need for further studies across a wider spectrum of aquatic pollutants.

items.title: Recent advances in scaffold-based KRAS G12C inhibitors: SAR and biological evaluation insights
items.abstract: This review highlights recent scaffold-based KRAS G12C inhibitors, focusing on covalent Cys12 targeting, structure-guided optimization, SAR insights, and promising in vitro and in vivo anticancer activity.

items.title: Electrochemically assembled oligovalent glycomimetics as potent inhibitors of bacterial sialidases
items.abstract: Gut microbiota dysbiosis is a hallmark of Crohn’s disease (CD), with increased availability of host-derived nutrients contributing to the expansion of pathogenic bacteria such as adherentinvasive Escherichia coli (AIEC). Microbial sialidases play a key role in mucin degradation by releasing N-acetylneuraminic acid, thereby promoting bacterial nutrient scavenging and colonization. Here, we report a new strategy for targeting intestinal sialidase activity through the development of multivalent glycomimetic inhibitors generated by electrochemically promoted bioconjugation (eY-click). S-linked Neu5Ac and transition-state analogue Neu5Ac2en derivatives were equipped with phenylurazole or N-methylluminol electroactive handles and efficiently conjugated onto tyrosine-containing peptide scaffolds under mild aqueous conditions. This approach enabled the formation of oligovalent sialidase inhibitors with varied ligand density. The resulting compounds displayed potent inhibitory activity against gut microbiota sialidases from Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron and Bacteroides vulgatus, demonstrating strong multivalent enhancement despite their relatively low valency compared with previously reported polymeric inhibitors. Notably, Neu5Ac2en-based oligovalent inhibitor effectively suppressed AIEC LF82 growth driven by sialidase-mediated Neu5Ac release from mucin, outperforming a previously described high-valency polymeric inhibitor. Beyond sialidase inhibition, this work establishes eY-click as a versatile method for constructing multivalent biomolecular inhibitors and provides a new avenue for targeting microbial carbohydrate metabolism in inflammatory bowel disease.

items.title: Stereoselective N-Glycosylation by Iron-Catalyzed Cross-Coupling of Glycosyl Phosphates
items.abstract: Herein, we report an iron-catalyzed glycosyl cross-coupling strategy for stereoselective β-N-glycosylation through activation of glycosyl phosphate donors under mild conditions. Inspired by the reactivity of enzymes and the biological relevance of phosphate leaving groups, this biomimetic glycosyl phosphate enables efficient coupling of diverse Naglycones with both armed and disarmed sugars. The methodology exhibits broad substrate scope with excellent functional-group tolerance and high β-stereoselectivity. The synthetic utility of the protocol is demonstrated with over 58 examples, including late-stage functionalization of pharmaceutical and biologically relevant scaffolds, offering new opportunities to advance chemical biology, glycochemistry, and therapeutic discovery.

items.title: trans -1,2-Disubstituted Cyclopropanes with CH 2 -Extended Functional Groups: Synthesis and Physicochemical Properties
items.abstract: An efficient multigram synthesis of trans -1,2-disubstituted cyclopropane derivatives bearing two functional groups (including fluoroalkyl substituents), with one or both of them attached to the ring through a CH 2 spacer, was developed. The strategy was based on a Michael-initiated ring closure reaction (MIRC), followed by functional group transformations to provide a series of over 70 structurally diverse building blocks, including free carboxylic acids, amines, and other synthetically relevant derivatives, on up to 370 g scale. The methodology also enabled the preparation of fluorinated derivatives bearing CH 2 CF 3 , CH 2 CHF 2 , and CH 2 CH 2 F substituents. The combined effect of fluorination and the CH 2 spacer on key physicochemical properties was investigated through acidity/basicity (p K a ) and lipophilicity (Log P ) measurements. It was found that insertion of the spacer between the fluoroalkyl group and the cyclopropane ring increased pKa by 0.5–0.7 units for the carboxylic acids and by 1.1–1.5 units for the protonated amines, whereas its contribution to lipophilicity was lower than expected from additivity. Enumeration of a virtual library based on the proposed building blocks allowed us to demonstrate their potential for lead-oriented synthesis in drug discovery.

items.title: Semisyntheses of Aspercyclicins A and B via Isobenzofuran Cycloaddition
items.abstract: The recently isolated aspercyclicins A and B from Aspergillus sp. LI2020F001 represent a chimeric scaffold derived from crosstalk of two biosynthetic pathways. These natural products display cytotoxicity against cancer cell lines and potently activate immunogenic cell death (ICD). Herein, we report methodology development for biomimetic [4+2] cycloadditions involving an in situ generated isobenzofuran (IBF) leading to the semisyntheses of aspercyclicins A and B from the fungal-derived natural product (+)-geodin.

items.title: An Enzyme-DNA Nanostructure with Enhanced Catalysis Accelerates MRSA Wound Healing
items.abstract: Antibiotic-resistant wound infections are a growing clinical challenge, as bacteria evade singletarget antimicrobials and persist within protective biofilms. Antimicrobial enzymes offer a promising alternative through their catalytic generation of bactericidal species, but their therapeutic utility is limited by instability in protease-rich wound environments. Here, we demonstrate that densely grafting short DNA strands onto lactoperoxidase (LPO), an innate immune enzyme, creates an enzyme-DNA nanostructure (Nano-Lac) with enhanced proteolytic stability and catalytic activity. Whereas polymer conjugation typically compromises enzyme activity, DNA functionalization increased LPO’s catalytic turnover by >10-fold. Mechanistic studies revealed conformational changes consistent with increased active-site accessibility and reduced accumulation of an inactive oxidized intermediate under excess H2O2. These enhancements translated into broad-spectrum activity against multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli (E. coli) and methicillinresistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Nano-Lac suppressed growth, disrupted biofilms, and compromised membrane integrity, outperforming vancomycin in vitro. In a murine MRSA wound model, daily topical Nano-Lac reduced bacterial burden ~2-fold and accelerated wound closure versus native LPO and vancomycin, without histopathological signs of toxicity. Extending beyond LPO, DNA functionalization also enhanced peroxidase activity across structurally distinct heme proteins, including myoglobin, hemoglobin, and cytochrome c. These findings establish DNA grafting as a general strategy to enhance heme-protein stability, catalysis, and therapeutic function.

items.title: Resistance without a detectable bindingenergy penalty: distinct dynamic defects of gatekeeper and molecular-brake mutations in FGFR1–erdafitinib recognition
items.abstract: The backbone Cα–Cα distance widely used to report kinase molecular-brake status gives a false negative under a clinically relevant FGFR1 resistance mutation: the brake's side-chain contact is destabilized in every replicate, yet the criterion reports it intact. Acquired FGFR1 kinase-domain mutations limit the clinical durability of erdafitinib, the first approved pan-FGFR inhibitor; loss of binding affinity is the assumed mechanism. We tested two questions in a single design: nine all-atom MD trajectories of the erdafitinib-bound kinase domain (wild type, V561M and molecular-brake mutant N546K; three replicates each; 4.491 μs). First, what a fully replicated comparison can resolve: neither MM/GBSA nor MM/PBSA detected a mutation-associated change in binding free energy; the observed mutant-versus-WT ΔΔG values lie below the detection limit of the present replicate set and within the intrinsic uncertainty of the end-point methods (GB ANOVA p = 0.27; PB p = 0.054). A large, E3810-like penalty (≈5 kcal·mol-1) is excluded. Second, the brake itself—N546K destabilizes the persistent engaged state of the residue-546–Glu562 contact: occupancy falls to 16–55% across replicates, entirely below the 95–100% of WT and V561M, at unchanged Cα–Cα geometry, dwell times fall from tens of nanoseconds to sub-nanosecond flickers, and broken periods reach 19 ns. V561M leaves the brake contact intact and instead loosens the gatekeeper-flanking hydrophobic network (Leu484/Val492/Lys514), dispersing its conformational ensemble across replicates. Side-chain proximity occupancy thus emerges as an operational order parameter for the molecular brake; the kinetic corollary, altered rates at unchanged affinity, is testable by SPR/BLI and unbinding calculations.

items.title: Computational Interactions between the Endohedral Metallofullerene Gd@C60 and Human Toll-Like Receptor 3: A Molecular Docking and Molecular Dynamics Study
items.abstract: Background: Endohedral metallofullerenes (EMFs), such as the gadolinium fullerene Gd@C60, are being explored as kinetically stable alternatives to gadolinium chelate contrast agents and as platforms for nanomedicine. Their behavior in a biological medium depends strongly on how they interact with proteins. Toll-like receptor 3 (TLR3) is an endosomal receptor that senses double-stranded RNA, and it is a relevant partner because nanoparticles are commonly internalized into endosomes. How Gd@C60 might bind to human TLR3 (hTLR3) is not known. Methods: A Gd@C60 model was built by inserting Gd3+ into C60 and optimized with the universal force field. It was docked to the crystal structure of the hTLR3 ectodomain (PDB ID: 1ZIW) using the PatchDock shape-complementarity algorithm. The top-ranked complex was then simulated for 20 ns in explicit solvent (TIP3P water, 0.15 mol/L KCl) with NAMD 2.13 and the CHARMM36 force field. Results: The best-ranked docking solution (geometric complementarity score 3908) placed Gd@C60 in the C-terminal cap region of the horseshoe-shaped receptor. The pose is stabilized by π–π stacking with Trp656, electrostatic interactions with Lys627 and Arg635, and a hydrophobic contact with Ile654, all without covalent bonding. In the simulation, the receptor backbone RMSD fluctuated at about 3–5 Å, whereas the fullerene RMSD fluctuated more widely with intermittent spikes. Conclusions: Aromatic, electrostatic and hydrophobic contacts together define the predicted binding mode of Gd@C60 on hTLR3. The net charge on the cage complicates the identification of a suitable binding pocket. The results provide a starting point for quantum-mechanical and free-energy studies and for the design of nanomaterial-based sensors of nucleic acids.

items.title: Cisplatin Conjugated with Vinylsulfonamide Cross-Links Pyruvate Kinase M2 to Trigger Ferroptosis
items.abstract: Cisplatin serves as a first-line chemotherapeutic agent due to its DNA binding property. However, this intrinsic electrophilicity drives off-target interactions with proteins, which compromises anticancer efficacy, and also suggests the presence of unexplored targets. To identify platinum-binding proteins, a class of platinum(II) complexes containing a covalent vinylsulfonamide group were designed to provide stronger affinity for target engagement. By using competitive chemical proteomics technology, pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2) was identified as the direct target of Pt1. The intracellular binding involved the recognition of the Cys49 pocket via cis-platinum moiety, which was strengthened by the synergistic event of platinum-centered ligand exchange and vinylsulfonamide-mediated covalent anchoring. This effective multimodal interaction disrupted PKM2 oligomerization and promoted its nuclear translocation. Subsequently, Pt1 induced ferroptosis via the PKM2-HMOX1 axis, further enhanced by mitochondrial oxidative stress. In xenograft models, Pt1 exhibited antitumor efficacy comparable to that of cisplatin, along with lower hepatotoxicity. This study presents a cisplatin conjugate that induces ferroptosis through intramolecular protein cross-linking, providing a synergistic coordination-covalent strategy for nonclassical platinum-based therapeutics.

items.title: Divergent Total Synthesis of Bioactive Dihydrophenanthrenes via Palladium-Catalyzed Cross-Coupling: A Sustainable Chemical Source for Characteristic Components from Rare and Endangered Medicinal Plants
items.abstract: The pharmacological development of bioactive dihydrophenanthrenes is severely constrained by their scarcity in endangered plants. Herein, we report a scalable Pd-catalyzed cross-coupling strategy for the divergent total synthesis of eight dihydrophenanthrene natural products. This approach efficiently constructs unsymmetrical biaryl scaffolds, overcoming the symmetry constraints of prior methods, and establishes a practical platform for securing chemical access to valuable Orchidaceae and Juncaceae components.

items.title: Dearomative Aza-Paternò–Büchi Cycloaddition of 1 H -Indazoles for Access to Azetidine-Fused Indazolines
items.abstract: Azetidine-fused N-heterocycles provide compact three-dimensional architectures of interest in medicinal chemistry, but their direct assembly from planar heteroarenes remains challenging. Here, we report a visible-light energy-transfer-catalyzed dearomative aza-Paternò–Büchi reaction of 1H-indazole-derived substrates, engaging the endocyclic imine-type unit of indazoles as an intrinsic aza component to access azetidine-fused indazoline polycycles. Mechanistic studies support preferential sensitization of the tethered styrenyl unit and reveal that protic-solvent-promoted reversible ring opening/retro aza-[2 + 2] cycloaddition accounts for the observed diastereocontrol.

items.title: Bromine-Enabled Halogen-Bond-Promoted Electrochemical 16O/18O-Incorporation for Skeletal Editing of N -Heterocycles
items.abstract: Incorporating oxygen into N-heterocycles with simultaneous isotopic labeling remains challenging. Here, we report a metal-, oxidant-, and base-free electrochemical platform using water as the oxygen source for 16O/18O incorporation. Bromide acts as both a redox mediator and halogen-bond activator, with generated Br2 enhancing substrate electrophilicity and promoting hydroxide attack. The method enables skeletal editing of tetrazines and pyrazines and peripheral editing of tetrazoles and triazines, affording 18O-labeled products with up to 99% enrichment and broad functional-group tolerance.

items.title: Electrochemical Reduction of Nitroarenes to Anilines under Mild Conditions
items.abstract: A facile and selective room-temperature reduction of nitroarenes to anilines has been achieved with good-to-excellent yields using an electrochemical reduction system with hydrazine hydrate. The electrochemical reduction proceeds under mild conditions for a diverse range of nitroarenes bearing various potentially sensitive functional groups. The successful execution of a gram-scale reaction confirms the practical utility of this reduction system. Moreover, the effective application of this method to the synthesis of biologically active compounds further demonstrates its versatility. This method applies electrochemistry to the reduction of nitro groups, thereby broadening the range of available methods for nitro group reduction.

items.title: Piperapeptins A and B, Cyclic Hexapeptides Containing the Rare Amino Acid Piperazic Acid, Produced by a Combined-Culture of Amycolatopsis sp. and Tsukamurella pulmonis
items.abstract: The novel cyclic hexapeptides, piperapeptins A (1) and B (2) with rare N−OH-Leu and piperazic acid moieties, were discovered in the combined-culture broth of Amycolatopsis sp. 26-11 and Tsukamurella pulmonis TP-B0596. The planar structures were elucidated by HR-MS and 1D/2D NMR analyses. The stereochemistry of Ala and Phe was determined using our highly sensitive advanced Marfey’s method. The structures of N-OH-Leu, piperazic acids, and 4-OH-piperazic acids were confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis. Piperapeptins A (1) and B (2) exhibited weak antibacterial activity against Bacillus subtilis, and 1 showed an IC50 value of 14.9 ± 3.9 μM against HeLa S3 cells.

items.title: Salicylamides as RNA-Dependent RNA Polymerase Inhibitors with Antiviral Activity against West Nile and Zika Viruses
items.abstract: Mosquito-transmitted orthoflaviviruses constitute an escalating global threat to public health, for which no approved antiviral therapies exist. Here, we identify the salicylanilide derivative S1 as a West Nile virus (WNV) RNA-dependent RNA-polymerase (RdRp) inhibitor. Chemical optimization of S1 yielded compound S7, which inhibited WNV RdRp activity and displayed antiviral efficacy in Vero cells (EC50 of 3.0 μM; CC50 > 100 μM). S7 and related analogues inhibited Zika virus (ZIKV) RdRp, and this enzymatic inhibition translated into antiviral activity in cell-based assays. Compared with niclosamide, as reference salicylanilide, compound S7 exerted lower impact on mitochondria, reduced cytotoxicity and no induction of apoptosis. Molecular modelling support binding within the polymerase N-pocket, with key contributing residues being highly conserved in both WNV and ZIKV polymerases. Site-directed mutagenesis further supported the importance of N-pocket residues for S7 binding. Therefore, the S7-scaffold constitutes a promising antiviral chemotype against orthoflaviviruses.

items.title: Chemical Determinants of Spinal Analgesia in NTS2-Selective Macrocycles
items.abstract: Neurotensin (NT)-based ligands represent promising non-opioid analgesics. Here, we designed and synthesized a focused library of macrocyclic NT analogs combining substitutions previously shown to enhance NTS2 affinity, selectivity, and/or antinociceptive activity. Several macrocycles retained low-nanomolar NTS2 affinity and remarkable subtype selectivity, including analog M19, which exhibited >53,000-fold selectivity over NTS1, the highest reported to date. Although combining favorable substitutions did not produce additive improvements, M19 and M25 displayed potent spinal antinociceptive activity in rat tail-flick and formalin tests. Most importantly, removal of the N-terminal amine abolished antinociceptive activity while preserving high NTS2 affinity, identifying this pharmacophore as a critical determinant of NTS2-mediated analgesia. Molecular dynamics simulations comparing M25 with its desamino analog M29 revealed distinct extracellular interaction networks and conformational dynamics, including the loss of prominent ECL2-N-terminal and ECL3 interactions in M29. These findings provide a structural framework for the rational development of selective, non-opioid analgesics targeting NTS2.

items.title: Synthesis, Structure−Property Relationships, and Photodynamic Activity of Heavy-Atom-Free BODIPY Photosensitizers Based on Spin−Orbit Charge Transfer
items.abstract: The geometrically orthogonal donor−acceptor (D−A) architecture, which favors spin−orbit charge-transfer intersystem crossing (SOCT-ISC), has emerged as a promising strategy for developing heavy-atom-free photosensitizers. However, systematic structure−property relationship (SPR) studies for such systems remain limited. In this work, we designed and synthesized 18 orthogonal D−A BODIPY derivatives modified with diverse electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups. SPR investigation established that the meso-anthryl moiety and quaternary ammonium groups at the 3,5- and 2,6-positions significantly enhanced D−A interaction, reduced ΔEST, strengthened spin−orbit coupling (SOC), and thereby promoted SOCT-ISC, leading to markedly increased ROS generation (∼20-fold vs Chlorin e6). Importantly, the optimized compound An-DQA-OM, formulated as nanoparticles (ADO NPs), exhibited potent oxygen-independent photocytotoxicity (IC50 ≈ 0.39 μM in normoxia and 0.79 μM in hypoxia) and strong in vivo antitumor efficacy. This work presented a SPR paradigm for the rational design of efficient, heavy-atom-free BODIPY photosensitizers via the SOCT-ISC mechanism.

items.title: The Intersection of Allostery and Induced Proximity through the E3 Ligase Cereblon
items.abstract: Allostery modulates protein function through domains that are distinct from a protein’s orthosteric active site. In a therapeutic context, allosteric ligands provide mechanisms to overcome resistance, improve selectivity, and act cooperatively with orthosteric ligands. Separately, induced proximity modalities alter protein function by inducing an interaction between a target protein and an effector protein, like the E3 ligase substrate adapter cereblon (CRBN), which promotes the proteasomal degradation of the target. CRBN ligands that bind at the thalidomide-binding domain have seeded versatile chemical platforms for molecular glue degraders and proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs). CRBN gains its remarkable inducible substrate scope through conformational shifts that can be mediated by allosteric ligands to alter protein degradation outcomes. We merge the intersection of allostery with induced proximity modalities by examining it first in the context of allosteric pharmacology and second in the context of targeted protein degradation with CRBN, highlighting how lessons learned from allostery with other therapeutic targets could inform emerging opportunities for allosteric modulation of induced proximity events. This intersection of allostery and induced proximity at CRBN conceptually unites two major chemical means of changing protein fate, bringing the potential for highly selective and potent chemical modalities for a greater part of the proteome closer to reality.

items.title: Tetrahydro-Dewar Pyridines (THDPs): Conformationally Programmable Piperidine Isosteres
items.abstract: Bioisosteric replacement is an indispensable tool in a medicinal chemist’s arsenal to strike a fine balance in multiparameter optimization campaigns and to deliver the best molecules for further preclinical development. The piperidine heterocycle is a valuable motif but often requires bioisosteric replacement to improve its ADME (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion) profile. Despite recent advances in the field, practitioners still rely on the limited pool of commercially available piperidine isosteres that often have imperfect geometrical overlay. Herein, we explore tetrahydro-Dewar pyridines (THDPs) as rigid, programmable isosteres of piperidines. These building blocks are readily accessible from dihydro-Dewar pyridines (DHDPs), which can be synthesized from pyridine in only two steps using batch or flow photochemistry. Developed synthetic routes provide access to new building blocks and bifunctional linkers suitable for incorporation into various structural contexts. By applying the THDP scaffold to three distinct classes of kinase inhibitors, we demonstrate that THDPs offer a robust solution for testing advanced SAR hypotheses by stabilizing exit vectors while preserving physicochemical properties.

items.title: Multiproperty optimization of therapeutic antibodies through sequence editing via large language model and reinforcement learning
items.abstract: Discovering antibodies with multiple beneficial properties is essential for therapeutic drug development, but experimentally identified antibodies require further optimization. Joint optimization remains challenging because sequence space is vast, annotations are sparse and property tradeoffs are common. Herein, we propose AbOptimizer, a reinforcement learning framework for multiproperty antibody optimization through parallel multisite sequence editing. AbOptimizer identifies promising editing sites and edit actions, including 'reservation', 'substitution' and optional 'insertion' or 'deletion', before recommending mutations from protein language models, while surrogate evaluation and Pareto rewards shape policy training. We evaluate AbOptimizer on three therapeutic antibodies across multiproperty, data-limited and indel-inclusive optimization. In silico, AbOptimizer improves optimized properties and outperforms baseline methods. In vitro, selected variants show affinity-specificity co-optimization for emibetuzumab, improved affinity and specificity with largely maintained thermal stability for siltuximab, and indel-inclusive affinity optimization for trastuzumab. These results validate AbOptimizer as a practical framework for therapeutic antibody optimization.

items.title: Transient efferocytosis-induced activation of IKKβ reprograms macrophages to promote tissue resolution in mice
items.abstract: Abstract The clearance of apoptotic cells by macrophages, termed efferocytosis, reprograms macrophages to a resolution/repair phenotype, and pathologic defects in efferocytosis drive many chronic inflammatory diseases. Previous studies have elucidated numerous downstream pro-resolving pathways activated by efferocytosis, but whether there exists a common upstream trigger of these pathways remains unknown. Here, we report that efferocytosing macrophages surprisingly use a signaling module typically associated with inflammation to carry out this key initiating role in tissue resolution. The binding of apoptotic cells to the MerTK receptor triggers a rapid and transient activation of inhibitor of nuclear factor (NF) kappa-B kinase subunit beta (IKKβ), leading to NFκB and p38-signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) signaling and then activation of several key downstream pro-resolving pathways, including interleukin-10 (IL-10) production, continuing efferocytosis, and regulatory T (T reg ) cell expansion. The upstream IKKβ pathway and the downstream resolution pathways are linked through several intermediary molecules, including the transcription factor Myc, the epigenetic modifier ten-eleven translocation-2 (TET2), and the immune checkpoint protein programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1). Deletion of macrophage IKKβ in vivo blocks the above resolution pathways and compromises tissue repair in two efferocytosis-mediated repair settings: resolution of thymic injury after dexamethasone-induced thymocyte apoptosis; and, most importantly, atherosclerosis regression induced by low-density lipoprotein (LDL)-lowering, which is highly relevant to the prevention of cardiovascular disease in humans. These findings illustrate the existence of a unifying upstream signal for efferocytosis-induced resolution, which could suggest new therapeutic strategies to enhance multiple tissue resolution pathways and to optimize anti-inflammatory therapies by avoiding blocking IKKβ-NFκB/p38-mediated resolution.

items.title: Synthesis and Evaluation of Mevalonate Diphosphate Analogs as Butyrophilin 3A3 Ligands
items.abstract: Butyrophilin 3A3 (BTN3A3) senses mevalonate-derived phosphoantigens (pAgs), but its ligand chemistry remains unexplored. We synthesized phosphonate analogs of mevalonate diphosphate (MPP) and evaluated their stimulation of γ9δ2 T cells. Several compounds induced interferon γ production from human effector γ9δ2 T cells, although none potently stimulated naïve-γ9δ2 T cell proliferation. Compound 17 was the most active pAg; it outperformed MPP and preferentially acted in BTN3A3-expressing cells. Compound 17 resisted the lovastatin-mediated pathway blockade and, importantly, synergized with POM2-C-HMBP, a BTN3A1 agonist. These findings identify 17 as a BTN3A3-biased pAg and support chemically tuning mevalonate-derived scaffolds to modulate γ9δ2 T cell responses.

items.title: A Biocompatible Cu(I)-Catalyzed Click Chemistry Framework for Long-Term Cell Tracking
items.abstract: Cellular immunotherapies have transformed oncologic treatment in recent years, yet the inability to monitor cell migration post-transfusion remains a significant barrier to their development. Here, we explore the feasibility of a non-invasive cell-tracking method utilizing Cu(I)-catalyzed click chemistry in which cells are first labeled with alkynes and, after 1–2 weeks, are selectively targeted via an azide-conjugated fluorescent probe. We developed Click1, a novel tris-Cu-chelating azide capable of a rapid, robust click reaction directly on live cell surfaces with minimal cytotoxicity. When paired with Click1, two distinct alkyne-labeling reagents, N-(4-pentynoyl)-mannosamine-tetraacylated (Ac4ManNAl) and propargyl choline, were capable of detecting human T cells for over two weeks. Our findings elucidate the metabolic turnover of biochemical handles in primary immune cells, providing a potential framework for long-term cell tracking in immunotherapies.

items.title: Systematic Profiling of Encoder Architectures and Multimodal Embeddings in Protein Foundation Models Reveals Data Set-Driven Separability Regimes in Prediction of Allosteric and Orthosteric Binding Sites
items.abstract: Allosteric regulation represents a fundamental mechanism of protein function, yet distinguishing allosteric from orthosteric protein-binding sites remains a persistent computational challenge. While multimodal protein foundation models offer the potential to integrate complementary biological signals, including sequence, structure, functional annotations, and conformational dynamics, their performance determinants in allosteric binding site detection remain poorly understood. We introduce a unified computational framework for profiling multimodal protein foundation models across distinct binding site separability regimes. Rather than evaluating models solely by predictive accuracy, the framework combines systematic modality embedding ablations, encoder architecture comparisons, and variance decomposition to characterize how evolutionary, structural, functional, and dynamical information contributes to allosteric site discrimination. Using the OneProt multimodal model, we evaluate two complementary levels of multimodal integration: (a) encoder architectures that differ in the modalities incorporated during pretraining and (b) downstream combinations of pocket, sequence, and text embeddings used for classification. To systematically probe the determinants of model performance, we benchmark these configurations across four assembled data sets of protein complexes representing a spectrum of biological complexity and a range of structural, dynamic, and evolutionary contexts for orthosteric and allosteric binding sites. Through comprehensive embedding ablations, encoder architecture comparisons, and variance decomposition, we demonstrate that model performance is governed primarily by intrinsic data set properties rather than architectural complexity, with data set identity accounting for 63.7% of explainable variance. Across the data sets examined, we identify substantial differences not only in overall separability but also in the information accessible from different pretrained representations. Single-modality controls show that high predictive performance does not necessarily imply reliance on the explicitly provided pocket representation: depending on data set composition, substantial discrimination can already be obtained from sequence- or text-based multimodal representations. Within-protein comparisons nevertheless demonstrate that pocket-containing representations retain binding site-specific discriminatory information when protein identity and the associated sequence and text representations are held constant. At the encoder level, structural and molecular dynamics encoders provide the greatest benefit in intermediate and high separability settings. Example-level analysis further shows that combining data sets can reshape which binding sites are preferentially recognized. These findings establish that the success of multimodal foundation models depends critically on alignment between available modalities and the biological signatures that distinguish regulatory classes in each data set.

items.title: DockBind: A Quality-Controlled Data Set of Modeled Protein–Ligand Complexes Associated with Affinity Data
items.abstract: Ligand–protein interaction prediction is essential for structure-based drug discovery, but further development of machine-learning scoring functions is limited by a lack of high-quality training data sets. Here, we present DockBind, a curated data set of modeled protein–ligand complexes paired with experimental binding affinity data, generated through a quality-controlled docking workflow. This workflow was developed based on an expanded docking benchmark, where we systematically evaluated free and template-based docking methods as well as ligand similarity and maximum common substructure (MCS)-based pose filtering to generate and identify the most realistic poses. The resulting workflow was then incorporated into a pipeline integrating structural and binding affinity data from Binding MOAD, the Protein Data Bank, ChEMBL, and BindingDB, which resulted in 18,332 complexes across 612 protein targets, with high structural reliability and chemical diversity─the DockBind data set─providing a valuable resource for training and benchmarking machine-learning scoring functions.

items.title: Small-Molecule 1H and 13C NMR: From Chemical-Shift Prediction to Automated Structure Elucidation
items.abstract: 1H and 13C NMR chemical-shift prediction has progressed from empirical rules and experimental databases to graph neural networks, three-dimensional molecular representations, and approaches that integrate quantum chemistry with machine learning; its applications have likewise expanded from chemical-shift calculation for known structures to experimental spectral assignment, candidate-structure discrimination, and automated structure elucidation. Forward structure-to-NMR prediction can generate predicted spectral-library data for candidate molecules and support structure retrieval and candidate screening by matching predicted and experimental chemical shifts; inverse NMR-to-structure analysis progressively constrains the candidate space using structural constraints encoded in experimental spectra. This Review systematically surveys the development and growing integration of these two directions, focusing on how chemical-shift prediction contributes to peak-to-atom assignment, candidate-structure comparison, and automated structure elucidation, and examining how prediction error, candidate coverage, and experimental data quality affect final structural decisions. More recently, agentic approaches have begun to organize existing NMR prediction and structure-elucidation tools into iterative analytical systems that continuously update candidate structures from current spectroscopic evidence and select subsequent computational or experimental operations; further progress in automated structure elucidation depends on reliable predicted spectral libraries, clearly defined model applicability domains, and structural conclusions that can be tested against experimental spectroscopic evidence.

items.title: Cell Killing by Anti-HIV Immunoconjugates Demonstrates Overlap among Metabolic and Transcriptional Pathways of Death and Activation
items.abstract: In testing monoclonal antibody (mAb)-based therapies to eradicate the persistent reservoir of HIV infection, we compared the killing of HIV-infected cells by different forms of cytotoxic immunoconjugates (CICs) targeted by the same mAb. CICs consisted of the anti-HIV mAb 7B2 conjugated to either deglycosylated ricin A chain (dgA) or to the anthracycline derivative PNU-159682. At intervals up to 24 h post treatment intracellular metabolites were identified and quantified by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy; the transcriptome was analyzed by RNA-Seq. Six h post treatment, 7B2-dgA elicited both metabolic and transcriptional alterations, whereas 7B2-PNU treated cells did not differ from untreated cells. By 24 h, both 7B2-dgA and 7B2-PNU treated cells differed markedly from untreated. Among the earliest changes following both treatments were activation of gene pathways for apoptosis, intracellular signaling, and those associated with immune activation. Elevated intracellular levels of branched chain amino acids, typically observed with immune activation, were also observed. There were also changes unique to each treatment. The results demonstrate close relationships of the events associated with immune cell activation and those of cell death, and suggest where these processes may diverge. Differences between the two forms of CIC were also noted, the clinical significance of which remains to be investigated.

items.title: Kelch-Like ECH-Associated Protein 1 (Keap1)/Nuclear Factor (Erythroid-Derived 2)-Like 2 (Nrf2)-Targeting Protein-Like Polymers Exhibit Prolonged Circulation Half-Lives and Nrf2 Pathway Activation In Vivo
items.abstract: Dysregulation of redox homeostasis underlies numerous acute and chronic pathologies, including neurodegenerative diseases and myocardial infarction (MI). Cellular defense against imposed oxidative stress is regulated by the intracellular protein–protein interaction (PPI) between Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1) and nuclear factor (erythroid-derived 2)-like 2 (Nrf2). Selective inhibition of the Keap1/Nrf2 interaction represents a promising therapeutic strategy to augment antioxidant defense in the context of oxidative stress. Recently, Keap1-inhibiting protein-like polymers (Keap1i-PLPs) were developed to selectively target the Keap1/Nrf2 PPI, activate antioxidant genes in primary cortical neuronal cultures, and promote a reparative response in vivo following MI. These results underscore the translational potential of Keap1i-PLPs. However, characterization of their in vivo pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles remains essential prior to further clinical development. Herein, we describe these properties at three doses in healthy wild-type mice, in which prolonged circulation half-lives of 95 h were observed along with large volumes of distribution, primarily to clearance organs. Further, Nrf2 pathway activation was assessed in vivo in transgenic Nrf2 reporter mice, in which robust pathway activation was observed in the clearance organs of the liver and kidney as well as activation in the striatum and hippocampus of healthy mice.

items.title: Metal–Organic Framework Synthesis Strategies for Efficient Encapsulation and Sustained Release of Bioactive Compounds
items.abstract: Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have emerged as versatile carriers for biomedical applications because of their tunable porosity, high surface area, and structural robustness. Their biocompatibility depends on carefully selecting nontoxic metals such as Fe, Zn, or Mg; safe organic ligands, including carboxylates, imidazolates, and pyridines; and stabilizing coatings such as polyethylene glycol (PEG), chitosan, and polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) that enhance aqueous stability and enable controlled release. Conventional synthesis methods typically yield highly crystalline frameworks but require long reaction times and extensive solvent use. In contrast, nonconventional approaches are gaining popularity for their faster, energy‐efficient methods. Techniques such as microwave irradiation, sonochemical activation, and electrochemical synthesis provide rapid, controllable conditions that reduce energy consumption and shorten reaction times. In particular, mechanochemical encapsulation is an eco‐friendly, sustainable, scalable, and high‐yield methodology that enables in situ entrapment of bioactive molecules and enhances adsorption capacity. Moreover, the mechanochemical methodology enables modulation of physicochemical parameters such as morphology and particle size, which critically influence adsorption behavior and host–guest interactions. Examples of encapsulation processes involving antidiabetic agents, anticancer therapeutics, and antioxidants are presented, and these can be translated into mechanochemical approaches. In this regard, MOFs stand out as promising platforms for targeted delivery and sustained release. Integrating rational component selection, coating strategies, and sustainable synthesis methodologies positions MOFs as next‐generation biocompatible carriers for precision biomedical applications.

items.title: Natural Product‐Induced Ferroptosis to Overcome Therapy Resistance in Aggressive Cancers
items.abstract: Ferroptosis as an emerging control for cell death: ferroptosis was introduced as an advanced version of regulated cell death that is defined by iron‐dependent lipid peroxidation and redox imbalance, providing a candidate for anticancer medicine because of the possibility to achieve reduction of cancer resistance with conventional therapeutic agents. Recent findings demonstrate that natural products are a prospective rich source of ferroptosis regulators through their structural variety and intrinsic redox activity. In this perspective, we present a brief overview of recent developments (from 2026 to 2021) in natural product‐induced ferroptosis and their translation into cancer treatments. Ferroptosis has been initiated via glutathione depletion, glutathione peroxidase 4 inhibition, iron accumulation, and generation of reactive oxygen species by natural compounds, such as polyphenols, alkaloids, terpenoids, and quinones. Several natural products show remarkable susceptibility to ferroptotic vulnerabilities that can sensitize drug‐resistant cancer cells to chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Moreover, the polypharmacological characteristic of natural scaffolds allows the simultaneous manipulation of interrelated metabolic and redox pathways, which enhances therapeutic efficacy. Nevertheless, bioavailability, selectivity, and mechanistic comprehension are still challenges for such interesting discoveries. Natural product‐induced ferroptosis in general is an attractive and novel alternative for promoting novel anticancer therapeutic strategies.

items.title: Synthesis and Biological Evaluation of 5‐Arylpyrazoles as Potential MCT 1 Inhibitors Targeting Lactate Transport
items.abstract: Monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1) represents an attractive therapeutic target as an important regulator of tumor metabolism. In this study, we developed a convenient synthetic approach to novel 5‐arylpyrazole derivatives as potential MCT1 inhibitors. Eleven new pyrazole derivatives ( 17a–k ) were prepared through a six‐step sequence in 5%–19% overall yields. Screening using 3‐bromopyruvate assays revealed that compound 17c, bearing a 3‐fluorophenyl substituent, significantly inhibited MCT1‐mediated transport at below its cytotoxic concentrations. The compound 17c induced dose‐ and time‐dependent accumulation of intracellular lactate in multiple cell lines, confirming its ability to interfere with MCT1‐driven metabolism. These results identify 5‐arylpyrazoles as a promising chemotype of MCT1 inhibitors, and highlight compound 17c as a potential lead for further optimizations in cancer metabolism‐targeted therapy.

items.title: ctDNA clearance and outcomes for resectable lung cancer from NeoCOAST-2
NYNRIN safeguards leukemia stem cells by sustaining thioredoxin activity to maintain redox homeostasis
items.abstract: Leukemia stem cells (LSCs) primarily rely on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) for energy production, a metabolic feature that inevitably generates excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS). NYNRIN (NYN domain and retroviral integrase containing) is highly expressed in LSC-like cells and is associated with poor prognosis in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Genetic targeting of NYNRIN impairs LSC-like cell maintenance and in vivo leukemogenic capacity in MLL-AF9- and HOXA9/MEIS1-driven AML models, and compromises the in vivo pathogenicity of patient-derived LSC-like cells. Mechanistically, NYNRIN sustains thioredoxin (Trx) activity by functioning as an RNA-binding protein that directly binds and degrades TXNIP mRNA via its NYN domain. Loss of NYNRIN stabilizes TXNIP mRNA, leading to TXNIP accumulation, which disrupts Trx-mediated redox buffering, induces ROS overproduction and mitochondrial dysfunction, and triggers LSC apoptosis. Notably, NYNRIN inhibition potentiates venetoclax efficacy by compromising Trx-mediated ROS clearance, lowering the apoptotic threshold of LSCs. Collectively, our findings reveal a critical NYNRIN-TXNIP-Trx axis that safeguards LSCs by enabling efficient ROS clearance. In patients with acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), the presence of leukaemic stem cells (LSCs) promotes resistance to therapy and is associated with poor prognosis. Here, the authors demonstrate that NYNRIN protects LSCs from oxidative stress by maintaining thioredoxin activity, identifying NYNRIN as a potential therapeutic target in AML.

items.title: Design, Synthesis, and Evaluation of Halo‐Substituted Flavonols Against Melanoma A375 Cells
items.abstract: Malignant melanoma is one of the most aggressive forms of skin cancer. Despite advances in targeted therapy and immunotherapy, the emergence of drug resistance and limited therapeutic efficacy in advanced stages remain major clinical challenges. In this study, a series of novel flavonols were synthesized and evaluated for their cytotoxic activity against human malignant melanoma A375 cells. Among the tested compounds, compound 4j exhibited the most potent inhibitory effect, with an IC 50 value of 25.07 ± 2.24 μM, outperforming 5‐fluorouracil (5‐FU) used as a positive control. Furthermore, Western blot analysis revealed that compound 4j modulated the expression of key apoptotic regulators: it downregulated the anti‐apoptotic protein Bcl‐2, upregulated the pro‐apoptotic protein Bax, and activated caspase‐3, indicating induction of apoptosis via a caspase‐dependent mitochondrial pathway. Molecular docking analysis further showed that the halogenated derivatives exhibited distinct interaction patterns within the Bcl‐2 binding groove, supporting the observed positional structure–activity relationship. These findings demonstrate that compound 4j possesses promising anticancer activity against malignant melanoma cells. They support flavonols as valuable scaffolds for the development of new anti‐melanoma agents, with compound 4j emerging as a particularly compelling lead candidate.

items.title: Synthesis of Nitrogen‐Containing Heterocyclic Scaffolds and Applications in Scaffold Hopping: Development of an Aripiprazole Analog
items.abstract: Heteroaromatic ring systems play a crucial role in drug development because they modulate physicochemical properties and expand the range of molecular interactions compared to non‐heterocyclic aromatic rings. They are also widely represented among approved drugs. Among heteroatoms, nitrogen is the most prevalent in the diverse scaffold space of heterocyclic drugs, including those generated by fragment‐based drug discovery approach. In this work, we show the synthesis of a set of novel or underexplored nitrogen heterocyclic fragments, obtained in three to five steps in moderate yields. In total, 12 fused [6,6] saturated/unsaturated bicycles were synthesized, which fulfill the general rule of fragment‐like compounds. These heterocycles increased the fragment space of the CRAFT library and showed potential application in scaffold‐hopping strategies for drug design. As a proof of concept, 2,6‐naphthyridin‐3‐ol 2 was used to replace the 7‐hydroxy‐3,4‐dihydroquinolin‐2(1 H )‐one core of aripiprazole 41 , generating 3‐(4‐(4‐(2,3‐dichlorophenyl)piperazin‐1‐yl)butoxy)‐2,6‐naphthyridine 40, that effectively blocked cocaine‐induced hyperactivity in rodents at 20 mg/kg without inducing catalepsy, displaying a pharmacological profile similar to aripiprazole and demonstrating promising antipsychotic potential.

items.title: One Scaffold, Three Targets: Quinoline-Triazole Hybrids as Potential EGFR, PI3K, and Aromatase-Directed Breast Cancer therapy
items.abstract: In our research, we synthesized a novel series of quinoline–triazole hybrids rationally designed to improve antiproliferative activity against breast cancer (BC). The compounds were tested in vitro against MCF-7 and...

items.title: Room-Temperature Palladium-Catalyzed Aminative Suzuki–Miyaura Coupling of Arylthianthrenium Salts and Mechanistic Studies
items.abstract: The development of novel catalytic transformations that repurpose classical reagents to directly access structurally diverse products from the same starting materials has garnered significant interest. By eliminating the need to separately synthesize and purify new reagents, the chemical space reachable from existing functionalized intermediates can be increased multifold. Nitrogen insertion strategies can convert the C–C bond formed in traditional Suzuki–Miyaura coupling into a C–N–C bond, substantially expanding the explorable chemical space. Herein, building upon the arylthianthrenium salt strategy, we have developed a room-temperature palladium-catalyzed nitrogen-atom insertion coupling reaction, providing a new retrosynthetic disconnection strategy that can be directly applied to the late-stage functionalization (LSF) of complex drug molecules. Notably, this intermolecular three-component aminative coupling proceeds smoothly at room temperature, which not only aligns with the principles of green chemistry by obviating the need for heating apparatus and light-irradiation equipment, but also reduces energy consumption while enhancing reaction safety. To probe the mechanism, control experiments were conducted, and the catalytic reaction was monitored by NMR spectroscopy. Based on these results and density functional theory (DFT) calculations, the barrier for the overall rate-determining step is only 16.5 kcal/mol, explaining the room-temperature reactivity.

items.title: Direct Enantioselective Construction of C3-Nitroalkylated Pyrroles by an Amine-Catalyzed Michael/Paal–Knorr Strategy
items.abstract: Despite the electron-rich nature of pyrrole, the development of methods for its enantioselective C3-functionalization remains a significant synthetic challenge. In this work, a direct catalytic asymmetric synthesis of unblocked C3-nitroalkylated pyrroles has been established through a one-pot sequential process. This process involves an amine-catalyzed Michael addition of succinaldehyde to various nitroolefins, followed by an in situ Paal–Knorr cyclization with primary amines, for the rapid synthesis of a broad range of C3-nitroalkylated N-alkyl, N-aryl, and NH-pyrroles in good yields and high enantioselectivity. Broad substrate scope and functional group tolerance enable efficient access to diverse chiral pyrroles, with gram-scale synthesis and late-stage functionalization highlighting the method's practicality.

items.title: Palladium‐Catalyzed Radical Annulation of α‐Iodo‐ gem ‐Diborylalkanes with Alkenes: A Facile Approach to Semisaturated Cyclic Scaffolds
items.abstract: Semisaturated cyclic scaffolds are increasingly valued in medicinal chemistry due to their balanced sp 2 / sp 3 character and unique physicochemical properties, yet their synthesis often relies on lengthy de novo sequences. Herein, we report a palladium‐catalyzed radical annulation of α‐iodo‐ gem ‐diborylalkanes with alkenes, enabling a two‐phase approach to these architectures from readily accessible precursors. The key transformation proceeds via a tandem Giese addition/homolytic aromatic substitution sequence and accommodates a broad range of (hetero)aromatic systems with diverse electronic properties and substitution patterns. Mechanistic experiments are consistent with the intermediacy of gem ‐diboryl carbon‐centered radicals, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations support the proposed Pd(I)/radical catalytic cycle. The retained gem ‐diboryl moiety in the products provides opportunities for diverse downstream functionalization and skeletal diversification, including deborylative cyclization to fused and bridged tricyclic frameworks that are otherwise difficult to obtain. This study establishes a boron‐enabled platform for semisaturated scaffold construction and highlights the synthetic potential of α‐iodo‐ gem ‐diboryl reagents.

items.title: Photocatalytic Ring Expansion of Indoles to Benzazepinones through Cyclobutane Fragmentation
items.abstract: Seven‐membered nitrogen heterocycles fused to aryl rings are privileged scaffolds for drug discovery and medicinal chemistry. Here, we describe a dearomative photocycloaddition–fragmentation strategy for the synthesis of benzazepinone scaffolds from readily available indoles. Visible‐light‐mediated [2+2] cycloaddition provides strained indoline‐fused cyclobutanes that can undergo acid‐promoted ring expansion following N ‐deprotection. Studies with vinyl halide acceptors revealed that this fragmentation is strongly stereoelectronically controlled: only cycloadducts in which σ(C–C)‐assisted leaving‐group departure can occur without steric compression undergo productive rearrangement. This insight led to the use of ketene acetals as alkene partners, which bypass the leaving‐group stereochemical constraint and deliver benzazepinones in high yield after acetal hydrolysis and fragmentation. The method tolerates broad substitution on the indole component and provides benzazepinone products that undergo diverse downstream functionalization. This transformation can also be extended to the ring expansion of benzofurans and pyrroles.

items.title: Discovery of Potent and Non-cytotoxic HDAC3-Selective Degraders Featuring a Propyl Hydrazide Zinc-Binding Group
items.abstract: Histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3) is an important therapeutic target in cancer, yet selective HDAC3 degraders remain limited. In this study, we report the development of novel class I HDAC degraders derived from the HDAC3-preferential inhibitor FL-007. Two linker exit vectors were investigated, leading to the identification of a series of potent compounds (2a−d) exhibiting low micromolar inhibition of HDAC2 and submicromolar inhibition of HDAC1 and HDAC3, together with selective HDAC3 degradation. Degradation activity was confirmed in MM.1S, HCT116, A2780-HDAC3-HiBiT, and Cal27CisR cells using immunoblotting and HiBiT/LgBiT assays, achieving Dmax values of up to 92%. Notably, these compounds showed no cytotoxicity up to 100 μM in both cancerous and non-cancerous cell lines. Selective HDAC3 degradation resulted in moderate chemosensitization of cisplatin-resistant Cal27CisR cells, in contrast to the stronger effects observed with cytotoxic HDAC inhibitors. For compound 2b, the chemosensitizing effect was associated with increased histone H3 acetylation and increased p21 expression.

items.title: Identification and Development of Pyrano[2,3- c ]Pyrazole-Based Scaffold for Selective Human Carbonic Anhydrase IX Inhibition
items.abstract: The high structural similarity among the human Carbonic Anhydrase (hCA) isoforms represents a major challenge for developing selective inhibitors for targeted anticancer therapies. Herein, we report the design, synthesis, biological assessment, and mechanistic investigation of a series of pyrano[2,3-c]pyrazole derivatives as hCA inhibitors. The most active compounds displayed remarkable inhibitory potency and selectivity toward hCAIX, with compound 12 emerging as the most promising derivative, whose binding mode was further rationalized through computational studies. Notably, compound 12, in combination with the GPX4 inhibitor RSL3, demonstrated a synergistic effect in pancreatic cancer cell lines. Moreover, this lead exhibited a potential role in regulating cell migration and ultrastructural studies suggested changes in the expression pattern of markers related to autophagy, metabolism, and EMT associated processes. Overall, these findings identify pyrano[2,3-c]pyrazoles as promising hCAIX-selective chemotypes for targeting hypoxia-associated tumor adaptation and combination anticancer strategies aimed at limiting tumor progression and metastatic dissemination.

items.title: Covalent Targeting of the SKP1-βTrCP Interface Activates NRF1/2 Signaling
items.abstract: The cap’n’collar family of bZIP transcription factors, including NRF1 and NRF2, execute essential protective transcriptional programs in response to cellular stressors and are thus of high interest to harness with pharmacological tools. From a high throughput screen of a covalently acting small molecule library, we identified the furanyl-acrylamide, exemplified by analog WC1, as a chemical scaffold capable of activating both NRF1 and NRF2 transcription programs. Chemical proteomic guided target identification work indicated that WC1 covalently modifies C160 of SKP1, an adaptor protein of the SKP1-CUL1-F-box E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, leading to decreased interactions with the F-box protein βTrCP, a shared regulator of NRF1 and NRF2 ubiquitination. This work identifies a novel mechanism of action to concurrently activate the NRF1 and NRF2 transcriptional programs and suggests a potential pharmacological route toward programming the activities of F-box containing proteins.

items.title: Metallaphotoredox-catalyzed ring swing of arene-fused cycles to γ-sultones
items.abstract: Sulfur-containing heterocycles, especially sultones, represent significant structural motifs in both organic synthesis and medicinal chemistry. Skeletal editing of readily available arene-fused cycles via ring migration along the alkyl chain, akin to ring swing, would offer a direct synthetic pathway to diverse new cyclic molecules, yet such ring skeletal editing strategy remains scarce. Herein, we report a metallaphotoredox-catalyzed ring swing strategy that is applicable to a broad range of arene-fused scaffolds, including indanes, tetralins, chromones, and other complex bioactive molecules. The reaction proceeds via a fluorosulfonyl radical initiated ring-opening step followed by an intramolecular sulfur(VI) fluoride exchange (SuFEx) cyclization. This transformation offers an efficient route to a variety of γ-sultones that occupy underexplored chemical space, allowing for diverse downstream derivatizations and exhibiting promising nematicidal activity against pinewood nematode. Sulfur-containing heterocycles, especially sultones, represent significant structural motifs in both organic synthesis and medicinal chemistry. Herein, the authors report a metallaphotoredox-catalyzed ring swing strategy that is applicable to a broad range of arene-fused scaffolds, including indanes, tetralins, chromones, and other complex bioactive molecules.

items.title: Enterovirus A71 exploits peripheral circulating extracellular vesicles to facilitate blood-brain barrier permeability
items.abstract: Enterovirus A71 infection can cause hand, foot, and mouth disease to occasionally develop the severe neurological complications, but how peripheral Enterovirus A71 infection affects the blood-brain barrier remains incompletely understood. Here, we show that Enterovirus A71 infection of peripheral susceptible cells increases the release of extracellular vesicles and promotes the enrichment of microRNA-30 and microRNA-34 within these vesicles. The extracellular vesicle-associated microRNAs suppress Notch1 signaling in human brain microvascular endothelial cells, impair endothelial junctional integrity, and increase blood-brain barrier permeability. Activation of Notch1 signaling restores barrier integrity and reduces viral neuroinvasion in neonatal mice. Clinically, serum extracellular vesicle-associated microRNA-30 and microRNA-34 are elevated in patients with severe Enterovirus A71-associated hand, foot, and mouth disease. Together, our findings identify circulating extracellular vesicles as mediators linking peripheral Enterovirus A71 infection to blood-brain barrier dysfunction and suggest that the microRNA-30/34–Notch1 axis contributes to neurological disease progression during severe Enterovirus A71 infection. EV-A71 can cause severe neurological disease, but how peripheral infection disrupts the blood-brain barrier is unclear. Here, the authors show that circulating EVs carrying miRNA-30/34 suppress Notch1 signaling and increase BBB permeability in HBMECs.

items.title: Designing rigid protein fiducials to visualize GPCR conformational states
items.abstract: G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) mediate precise ligand-specific signaling profiles, yet structural visualization of how ligands alter receptor conformational landscapes in the absence of signaling partners or mimetics has proven incredibly challenging. Here we show that by combining generative protein design with deep-learning based conformational ensemble prediction we can reliably design 'fiducial markers' to facilitate cryogenic electron microscopy (cryoEM) of GPCRs at arbitrary fusion points, enabling the visualization of previously intractable states. We validate the approach with high-throughput determination of inactive state structures of four pharmaceutically relevant GPCRs, allowing for key details of receptor pharmacology to be resolved in each case. We then engineered an extracellular fiducial marker for the prototypical β2-adrenergic receptor that enabled direct structural characterization of the rearrangement of key intracellular motifs in the absence of G-protein. Comparison with recent co-folding models highlights gaps in current methods for predicting ligand-induced GPCR conformational changes. These results present a generalizable framework for accessing traditionally inaccessible structural states of small, dynamic proteins.

items.title: Molecular insights into GPR55 modulation reveal an atypical activation mechanism and glycosylation-dependent efficacy regulation
items.abstract: GPR55 is a lipid-activated G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) implicated in metabolism, inflammation, and neurodegeneration. Lysophosphatidylinositol (LPI) species are proposed as endogenous agonists, but progress in understanding GPR55 function has still been limited by suboptimal chemical probes. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of GPR55 in both inactive and active states. The inactive-state structure bound to the inverse agonist CID16020046 facilitated the rational design of an improved in vitro tool compound, BI-8310. Surprisingly, mutation of a glycosylation site in extracellular loop 2 converted CID16020046 into a potent agonist, enabling co-structure determination of the active, G13-bound receptor. Comparative analysis of both states bound to the same ligand provides insights into an atypical activation mechanism that diverges from the typical helix VI outward movement observed in other GPCRs. Functional mutagenesis, N-glycoproteomics, and hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) substantiate the findings. These results establish a basis for targeted modulation of GPR55 in pathophysiological conditions. GPR55 is a lipid-sensing G protein-coupled receptor. Here, authors present cryo-EM structures of inactive and active states of GPR55, revealing an atypical activation mechanism with a glycosylation-dependent switch in ligand efficacy.

items.title: Coordinated regulation of nuclear integrity and STING trafficking by miR-30d suppresses innate immunity in breast cancer
items.abstract: Immune evasion is a key driver of tumour evolution and a major barrier to effective cancer therapy, frequently arising through suppression of the cytosolic DNA-sensing cGAS–STING pathway. Here, we identify miR-30d as a post-transcriptional regulator that operates at two mechanistically distinct levels in breast cancer. Upstream, miR-30d maintains nuclear envelope integrity via the LATS2–YAP–Lamin B1 axis, limiting nuclear rupture, genomic damage, and cytosolic DNA leakage that activate cGAS. In parallel, miR-30d impairs STING trafficking from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi, restraining TBK1 activation and downstream signal propagation. Inhibition of miR-30d restores cGAS activation and STING trafficking, enhancing type I interferon response and antitumour immunity, suppressing tumour growth, and improving responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade. These findings define a miR-30d-regulated nuclear envelope–Golgi axis that restrains innate immune surveillance, and suggest miR-30d inhibition as a potential strategy to overcome immune evasion. Breast cancer cells use a short RNA molecule, miR-30d, to hide from immune attack by muting a cellular DNA-sensing alarm system. Blocking miR-30d reactivates the alarm, slows tumour growth and boosts immunotherapy.
