Using a machine learning approach, we semi-automatically quantified BAT activity in approximately 8,700 patients and demonstrated that higher BAT activity, especially in the axillary depot, is associated with lower odds of cardiometabolic diseases and healthier white fat distribution. People with BAT also exhibited more favourable glycaemic parameters, lipid profiles, inflammatory markers and echocardiographic indices. Analysis of medication usage demonstrated that angiotensin receptor blocker use was positively associated with BAT presence. As proof of concept, we showed that the angiotensin receptor blocker losartan increased brown adipocyte activity and whole-body energy expenditure. Altogether, our studies harnessing artificial intelligence and big data identify new clinical phenotypes linked to BAT and serve as a platform for drug repurposing to activate this tissue in humans. Artificial intelligence-enabled quantification and analyses of brown adipose tissue (BAT) activity uncover links between BAT and a healthier metabolic profile along with lower rates of psychiatric disease, and can identify pharmacologic agents that could be repurposed to activate this tissue in humans.

items.title: De novo design of cysteine proteases
Computational design of metalloproteases
Engineered TYK2 dependence enables myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonism
items.abstract: Interleukin-10 (IL-10) is a central anti-inflammatory cytokine that suppresses immune responses in myeloid cells but can also activate T cells, limiting its therapeutic use in chronic inflammatory diseases owing to narrow efficacy windows and dose-limiting toxicities 1–5 . Here we show that myeloid and T cells differ in their dependence on JAK-family kinase pairing for IL-10 signalling and function. We took advantage of this differential kinase dependence to engineer a tetravalent nanobody-based myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonist (msIL-10R agonist) that fully recapitulates IL-10’s potent suppression of monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells while avoiding stimulation of T cells. Cryo-electron microscopy structural analysis reveals a distinct receptor cross-linking geometry of the msIL-10R agonist compared with native IL-10 family cytokines. This tetravalent architecture renders signalling strictly TYK2-dependent and highly sensitive to IL-10Rα and IL-10Rβ receptor abundance, thereby conferring selective activity in myeloid cells. This msIL-10R agonist reduces inflammation in humanized mouse models of lipopolysaccharide challenge, delayed-type hypersensitivity and colitis. A humanized version exhibits IgG-like pharmacokinetics, sustained receptor occupancy and durable myeloid suppression up to 30 days without T cell activation or haematological toxicities in non-human primates. These findings establish a geometry-based strategy for achieving cell-type-selective cytokine signalling and identify the msIL-10R agonist as a therapeutic candidate for myeloid-driven inflammatory diseases, including inflammatory bowel diseases.

items.title: Integrated multi-omics identifies distinct immune signatures with diagnostic and therapeutic implications in immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced myocarditis
items.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis (ICI-myocarditis) is a rare but frequently fatal immune-related adverse event. A comprehensive understanding of the cellular and molecular determinants driving ICI-myocarditis is essential for improving diagnostic precision and developing targeted interventions. We delineate the immune landscape of ICI-myocarditis via scRNA-seq, flow cytometry, Olink proteomics, and multiplex cytokine profiling. We demonstrate that high levels of baseline ISG15⁺CD8⁺ T cells are linked to the proinflammatory features of monocytes and in vitro experiments confirm the existence of circulating ISG15⁺CD8⁺ T cells with a high potential to induce cardiomyocyte apoptosis, supporting their pathogenic potential for cardiomyocyte cytotoxicity. Notably, intercellular crosstalk between these subsets is possibly mediated via the CCL2-CCR2 axis, and its blockade attenuated ICI-induced cardiac injury in vivo. Based on the inflammatory signature in ICI-myocarditis, we develop an 8-protein custom panel with promising performance in distinguishing ICI-myocarditis from other ICIs-treated controls. JAK-STAT pathway activation promotes inflammatory programs in both ISG15⁺CD8⁺ T cells and monocytes. Furthermore, JAK-STAT inhibition ameliorates cardiac dysfunction and inflammatory infiltration while enhancing the response to anti-PD-1 therapy in mouse models. In summary, this study implicates immune-pathogenic features of ICI-myocarditis and provides a possible basis for future therapies.

items.title: Enhancing ω-transaminase catalysis of bulky substrates guided by binding mechanism
items.abstract: Chiral amines are indispensable building blocks in pharmaceutical synthesis. (R)-3-([1,1′-biphenyl]-4-yl)-2-aminopropan-1-ol (ABP), a key chiral amine intermediate of the drug Entresto, has remained difficult to access via enzymatic asymmetric synthesis due to the inability of ω-transaminases to accommodate its bulky ketone precursor. Here, we engineer an ω-transaminase from Bacillus megaterium by integrating Funnel metadynamics, PathDetect-SOM, and path collective variables to reconstruct the free energy surface of substrate binding, pinpointing high-energy barrier regions of the binding process and the trade-off between tunnel accessibility and productive binding. Dynamic cross-correlation network analysis further identifies distal regulatory sites governing these bottleneck regions. Iterative experimental optimization yields the 13M variant, exhibiting catalytic activity 106 times that of the wild type with >99% enantiomeric excess, enabling the efficient enzymatic asymmetric synthesis of ABP. This integrated computational-experimental framework for resolving the tunnel-pocket binding trade-off offers a generalizable strategy for engineering ω-transaminases toward bulky substrates in green pharmaceutical synthesis. This study combines enhanced sampling with experiments to reveal how bulky substrates enter and bind to ω-transaminases. Distal-site engineering balanced tunnel access and binding stability, yielding 106-fold activity and >99% selectivity.

items.title: Lesion penetration predicts tuberculosis treatment shortening through a validated translational tool to de-risk development
items.abstract: Anti-tuberculosis (TB) drugs must reach the disease site to be effective, but complex TB pathology limits drug distribution and efficacy, as bacteria in the necrotic center of lung cavities are difficult to access and kill. Our study generates the most comprehensive database of site-of-disease distribution for 24 drugs and drug candidates in a rabbit model of cavitary TB. We validate a lung lesion penetration model with clinical data and develop an integrated approach that combines microenvironment-specific pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Next, we simulate site-of-disease coverage of shortened regimens tested in major Phase 3 trials over the past decade, allowing direct comparisons with trial outcomes. We propose that regimens including at least two drugs achieving bactericidal concentrations in pulmonary cavities are more likely to meet primary clinical endpoints in patients with cavitary disease. Our translational platform constitutes a validated tool to support drug evaluation, smart regimen design, and de-risking of late-stage trials.

items.title: Whole-genome sequencing reveals inter-household networks of gut-colonising ESBL-producing Escherichia coli in two rural Malawian districts
items.abstract: Infection with extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli (ESBL-Ec) is a global health concern that disproportionately affects sub-Saharan Africa. Gut mucosal colonisation is thought to precede invasive infection. Understanding ESBL-Ec colonisation and transmission across communities is therefore essential. Here, we investigate the genomic epidemiology and spatial structure of 159 gut-colonising ESBL-Ec isolates from the faeces of 211 people in two rural Malawian villages using longitudinal sampling (2023–24), whole-genome sequencing and household mapping. Colonisation prevalence rose from 34.1% (95% CI: 27.8–41.0) to 54.2% (95% CI: 46.0–62.3) over one year. Isolates belonged to 33 sequence types (STs), most commonly ST38 and ST131, harbouring 46 distinct antimicrobial resistance gene types. Fifteen strains were identified in ≥3 households that were typically separated by short geographic distances ( < 400 m). Of 190 pairwise comparisons between same-strain isolates from different households sampled concurrently within villages, 88.9% differed by ≤10 single nucleotide polymorphisms, consistent with multi-household involvement in community transmission networks. Lineage-specific ST38 and ST131 network analyses linked rural isolates to urban Malawian isolates collected within the last decade. Our findings provide a transferable framework for inferring ESBL-Ec flow in community settings and highlight the need for One Health surveillance and improved sanitation infrastructure to limit transmission.

items.title: Rapid Renin Angiotensin Aldosterone System inhibitor optimisation in patients with chronic kidney disease and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction using potassium binder: a randomised, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial
items.abstract: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone inhibitors (RAASi) improve outcomes in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), but their use is often limited by hyperkalaemia in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. This double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial evaluated whether sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) enables RAASi up-titration in HFrEF patients with CKD stages 3–5 and serum potassium of 5.0–5.5 mmol/L over 14 weeks. The primary binary outcome was defined as achieving the target dose of RAAS inhibition therapy without reaching hyperkalaemia (serum potassium ≥5.6 mmol/L) over 14 weeks or otherwise. Participants ( n = 112) were randomised 1:1 to receive sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) or placebo. The per-protocol (PP) analyses included 43 out of 53 (81%) in the SZC arm and 53 out of 59 participants (90%) in the placebo arm; the intention-to-treat (ITT) analyses included all 112. At the end of the trial, 24 of 43 participants (56%) in the SZC group achieved the target RAASi dose without developing hyperkalaemia compared with 15 of 53 patients (28%) in the placebo group (PP analysis, p = 0.006, ITT analysis, p = 0.007,). Participants in the SZC group were 3 times more likely to reach the target dose without reaching potassium 5.6 mmol/L (OR = 3.16; 95% CI 1.35–7.39; p = 0.008) than in the placebo group (ITT analysis). No significant differences in adverse events between the two groups were observed. SZC appears to safely support rapid RAASi optimisation in HFrEF patients with CKD. This trial was funded by AstraZeneca via Externally Sponsored Scientific Research grant ESR-19-20174. Trial Registration: Clinicaltrials.gov NCT05004363 and EudraCT number 2020-002946-18.

items.title: Fever enhances host bacterial defence while limiting mitochondrial damage
items.abstract: Infection triggers the fever response, but the response’s effect on antimicrobial peptide (AMP) function remains unknown. We discovered that human AMP LL-37 antibacterial activity is temperature-dependent and were curious as to why. Its temperature dependence is not an accident, as AMPs from other animals with different body temperatures have distinct temperature sensitivities. We find that AMP temperature sensitivities are tuned to animals’ body temperatures, and that for animals able to raise their body temperature, this is used to increase the AMP’s antibacterial efficacy. This effect reflects a balance between optimizing antibacterial killing while minimizing mitochondrial damage. In contrast, cold-blooded animals that are unable to raise their body temperature use a different strategy to avoid mitochondrial damage. Together, this study suggests that fever is beneficial for antimicrobial defense by raising AMP activity towards bacteria while reducing mitochondrial damage when pathogens are absent.

items.title: 11 million days of longitudinal Fitbit data reveal novel future health insights
items.abstract: Wearable devices offer a scalable, objective measurement of physical activity, but most studies reduce these data to a single metric over 7-days. Here, we compare wearable-derived phenotyping approaches to understand their impact on activity-disease associations, analyzing 11 million days of Fitbit data from 29,303 All of Us Research Program participants. We derive four daily activity metrics (step count, peak 1-min cadence, peak 30-min cadence, and heart rate per step) across five time-windows (1-day, 1-week, 1-month, 6-months, 1-year), then run phenome-wide analyses across > 700 incident and >1,400 prevalent disease outcomes. Though all phenotypes are highly correlated, longer measurement windows yield stronger, more stable associations: 1-year step count was associated with 389 prevalent and 61 incident outcomes (versus 271 and 33 for 1-day step count) after Bonferroni-correction, including novel links to chronic pain syndrome and SARS-CoV-2. Differences between prevalent and incident associations suggest that activity metrics may act as both early markers of disease and risk factors. These findings highlight how large-scale, longitudinal wearable data can advance understanding of health and disease.

items.title: Discovery of Small Peptides as Dual Inhibitors of IL-4 and IL-13 Signaling
items.abstract: Interleukin-4 (IL-4) and interleukin-13 (IL-13) signaling are central drivers of type 2 inflammation. While monoclonal antibodies targeting this pathway are clinically effective, their use is limited by high production cost, poor tissue penetration, increased risk of adverse effects, and parenteral administration requirement. Peptides offer advantages including structural tunability, favorable safety profiles, and improved tissue accessibility. Here, we employed an alternating phage display biopanning strategy to identify small peptides capable of dual modulation of IL-4 and IL-13 signaling. Sequential selection against IL-4 receptor α (IL-4Rα) and IL-13Rα1 enriched ligands with intrinsic dual-targeting capability. Lead peptide FMI-15 inhibited IL-4/IL-4Rα and IL-13/IL-13Rα1 interactions with IC50 values of 7.98 and 3.13 μM, respectively. In HEK-Blue reporter assays, FMI-15 suppressed IL-4- and IL-13-induced signaling with EC50 values of 25.1 and 31.6 μM, respectively. The peptide exhibited minimal cytotoxicity and moderate serum stability (t1/2 = 28.9 min). These findings establish alternating phage display as an effective strategy for identifying dual-targeting peptide modulators of cytokine signaling.

items.title: Novel Compounds as Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists for Treating Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and Obesity
items.abstract: Provided herein are novel compounds as GLP-1R agonists, pharmaceutical compositions, use of such compounds in treating type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity, and processes for preparing such compounds.

items.title: A Nontoxin Aminopyrimidine Probe for Near State-Independent NaV1.7 Inhibition
items.abstract: The voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.7 is among the most compelling genetically validated pain targets; however, advanced small-molecule inhibitors, including voltage-sensing domain IV (VSD4)-directed series, have not yet achieved robust clinical efficacy, potentially reflecting pharmacological limitations such as pronounced state dependence. Here, we report a nontoxin aminopyrimidine series that serves as a differentiated pharmacological probe for near state-independent NaV1.7 inhibition. Using a high-throughput automated patch clamp screening cascade designed to deprioritize established local anesthetic pore binders, we identified hit 1 and optimized it to compound 6, which combines balanced resting- and inactivated-state potency (IC50 = 1.00 and 0.45 μM, respectively). It displays a 29-fold selectivity margin over NaV1.5 and a tetrodotoxin (TTX)-like isoform profile that includes comparable activity on NaV1.7 and NaV1.1. Structure–activity studies identified the aminopyrimidine core and methylene-linked aniline motif as key determinants of this profile, while NaV mutant profiling supports a functional fingerprint consistent with pore-proximal modulation distinct from VSD4-directed inhibition.

items.title: Evaluation of Physics-Based Pose Prediction and the Role of Receptor Flexibility in a Community Antiviral Blind Challenge
items.abstract: Prediction of protein–ligand binding modes is a key step in computer-aided drug design, since incorrect pose prediction inevitably limits the achievable accuracy of downstream physics-based affinity predictions. The ASAP-Polaris-OpenADMET antiviral competition was launched in 2025 as a means to prospectively test computational methods across a range of measurements that guide early prioritization during a drug discovery campaign including pose prediction. Here, we describe our two open-source, physics-based entries to the pose prediction challenge, which are based on templated molecular growth with hybrid machine learning/molecular mechanics interatomic potentials. We show that our approach was among the top-performing physics-based methods, and with a retrospective change to the workflow to make greater use of the training data as templates, we obtain a success rate of 74% across SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV main protease target protein structures. Finally, we investigate the importance of receptor side-chain flexibility on retrospective performance. We find that building poses against an ensemble of feasible side-chain conformers is useful in generating improved binding poses but that the tested scoring functions are unable to successfully pick out native structures from the generated ensemble.

items.title: PDI-Spot: A Robust Representation Learning Framework for Identifying Energetic Hotspots in Protein–DNA Complexes
items.abstract: The binding affinity of protein–DNA complexes is concentrated within a subset of interface residues, called “hotspots”, which are critical for maintaining stable interactions. Therefore, identifying these energetic anchors is essential for elaborating on how mutations disrupt transcriptional regulation and for identifying druggable regions within disease-associated interfaces. In this study, we introduce our novel prediction model, PDI-Spot, that leverages representation learning to capture the complex features of protein–DNA interfaces. Unlike traditional methods that rely on limited, handcrafted descriptors, PDI-Spot extracts high-dimensional, structure- and sequence-driven representations to achieve better predictive performance. We trained the PDI-Spot model on a curated protein–DNA complex data set and rigorously validated its performance on an independent test set to ensure generalizability across different structural families. Following the extraction of residue-level embeddings, an optimal feature set was identified through a combined approach of minimum redundancy maximum relevance and multilayer perceptron architectures. By training a neural network on the optimal feature set, we developed a robust predictive framework for hotspot identification. On an independent test set, PDI-Spot achieved an AUROC of 0.809, an F1-score of 0.667, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.625. We also verified via permutation tests that PDI-Spot captures biologically meaningful patterns beyond random chance. PDI-Spot consistently demonstrates competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, providing a reliable model for mapping the energetic landscapes of protein–DNA interfaces. The source code and pretrained models are publicly available at https://github.com/ebsrn0/pdi-spot.git.

items.title: Integrating Gaussian Accelerated Molecular Dynamics, β-Variational Autoencoders, and Markov State Models Reveals the Activation Landscape of FGFR3 Kinase
items.abstract: Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) kinase plays a crucial role in cellular differentiation, proliferation, and skeletal development. Activation of the kinase domain through phosphorylation regulates the downstream signaling cascades, and its dysregulation leads to human dwarfism, skeletal dysplasia, and multiple cancers. However, the mechanistic basis of FGFR3 regulation by phosphorylation and ligand binding remains unclear. Here, we introduce an integrated GaMD-βVAE-MSM pipeline, a hybrid physics-ML framework for studying kinase activation. Gaussian-accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) enhances simulations by reducing the energy barrier. The variational autoencoder with tunable regularization was used for nonlinear dimension reduction and identifying slow collective variables. The Markov state model (MSM) was used for identifying metastable states spanning active-inactive conformations. Our results show that phosphorylation drives pronounced domain rearrangement and activation-loop dynamics. The coordinated movement of the molecular brake and regulatory spine governs the kinase activation. Ligand interaction stabilizes the active phosphorylated state with a free energy of −19 kcal/mol. Protein structure network analysis uncovers the long-range allosteric pathways. The potential regulatory sites involving αCβ4, β34, and β45 loops can be further exploited for allosteric intervention. Overall, this study highlights that phosphorylation and ligand binding dual regulate FGFR3 kinase through allosteric communication networks. The integrated GaMD−βVAE–MSM pipeline provides mechanistic insights into FGFR3 activation and may help the rational design of next-generation FGFR3-targeted therapeutics resistant to gatekeeper mutants.

items.title: Characterization of Carboxymaltose Structure and Interactions with the Iron Core in Ferric Carboxymaltose (Injectafer) Using NMR Spectroscopy
items.abstract: Ferric carboxymaltose (FCM), marketed as Injectafer, is an intravenous iron formulation used to treat iron deficiency. It is composed of polynuclear Fe(III)-oxyhydroxide/oxide cores surrounded by carboxymaltose. Although it has been on the market for over 10 years, the structure of carboxymaltose and its interaction with the iron core are not fully understood. This study used nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) to investigate both the structure of carboxymaltose and how it interacts with the iron core in Injectafer. Carboxymaltose was isolated from Injectafer and compared with other carboxymaltose samples made from maltodextrin with various dextrose equivalents (DEs). The results showed that carboxymaltose from Injectafer resembles most closely a lab-synthesized carboxymaltose with a DE of 4−7. Carboxymaltotriose was also synthesized to help with assigning the peaks in the NMR spectra of carboxymaltose. NMR was also used to study Injectafer in its as-is and diluted form. Compared to the spectra of diluted samples, peaks of the as-is sample were broadened and downfield-shifted in the 13C NMR spectra of Injectafer, due to the presence of iron and possibly due to interactions of carboxymaltose with the iron core. 1H NMR spectra of significantly diluted Injectafer showed 1H NMR peaks adjacent to the carboxy group only at dilutions of 400× or more, whereas the other peaks were observed at 100×. This suggests that the carboxy group interacts with the iron core and that it separates from the core at higher dilutions. Competitive binding studies using both low- and high-molecular-weight carboxymaltose, along with trimethylsilyl propionate (TSP), were used to characterize the binding affinity of carboxy groups to the iron core, as well as the maximum amount of carboxy groups that can bind to the surface of the iron core in Injectafer.

items.title: In Vitro−In Silico Screening for Assessing Variability in Food Effects for Different Solid Forms of a Free Base Drug
items.abstract: Understanding and predicting food effects for weakly basic, poorly soluble drugs remain a major challenge in oral drug development. Posaconazole (PSZ), a highly lipophilic antifungal agent, exhibits pronounced fasted-fed variability when administered as the free base. In this work, we developed an integrated in vitro-in silico screening strategy to evaluate the impact of physiological variability on the dissolution and predicted absorption of PSZ and its 4-aminobenzoic acid cocrystal form, PSZ-4ABA. Using a two-stage dissolution framework, key gastrointestinal parameters, including pH, bile salt concentration, buffer capacity, gastric residence time, and gastric-to-intestinal volume ratio, were systematically varied within physiologically relevant ranges to assess their influence on drug solubility, supersaturation, and precipitation risk. PSZ-4ABA consistently demonstrated higher apparent solubility and reduced sensitivity to physiological fluctuations compared to the free base, particularly under fasted conditions, where PSZ exhibited greater precipitation risk. Normalized AUC values derived from dissolution profiles revealed that the cocrystal form substantially attenuates variability across fed and fasted states. Physiologically based biopharmaceutics modeling (PBBM), built by incorporating the solubility-pH profile of the free form and cocrystal, further supported these findings. Overall, this study highlights the utility of combining biorelevant dissolution testing with PBBM to identify solid forms with reduced food-effect liability and to anticipate variability arising from gastrointestinal physiology.

items.title: Preclinical Study of the 89Zr/177Lu-Labeled Engineered VHH-based Antibody for CLDN18.2-Targeted Radiotheranostics
items.abstract: Claudin 18.2 (CLDN18.2) is a tight junction protein aberrantly expressed in gastric and pancreatic cancer. In this study, we developed the novel nanobody 18.2−50H and VHH-Fc fusion antibody 18.2−50C radiolabeled with 89Zr/177Lu for CLDN18.2-targeted radiotheranostics. Zolbetuximab (IMAB362), 18.2−50H, and 18.2−50C were conjugated with DFO and labeled with 89Zr, respectively. Radiochemical purity and in vitro stability were determined by radio-TLC. CLDN18.2-targeting specificity was evaluated using HEK-293T and HEK-293T/CLDN18.2 cells. PET/CT imaging and biodistribution studies were performed in mouse models and cynomolgus monkeys. Subsequently, 177Lu-DOTA-18.2-50C was prepared and assessed for tumor targeting in gastric cancer PDX models. 89Zr-DFO-IMAB362, 89Zr-DFO-18.2-50H, and 89Zr-DFO-18.2-50C were prepared with satisfactory radiochemical yield, specific activity, and stability. Tumors were clearly visible as early as 1 h post-injection of 89Zr-DFO-18.2-50H, with an uptake value of 9.07 ± 2.36 %ID/g and a tumor-to-muscle ratio of 27.35 ± 3.72. Fc-fused 89Zr-DFO-18.2-50C exhibited improved retention and higher tumor uptake than 89Zr-DFO-18.2-50H and 89Zr-DFO-IMAB362, with % ID/g increasing continuously from 5.07 ± 0.29 at 1 h to 32.95 ± 1.57 at 168 h. Notably, the introduction of the Fc chain also markedly increased the radiation exposure in the liver and spleen. Consistently, PET imaging in cynomolgus showed that 89Zr-DFO-18.2-50C is mainly concentrated in the liver, but no apparent abnormality was observed. Furthermore, 177Lu-DOTA-18.2-50C presented remarkable tumor selectivity with prolonged retention (16.92 ± 1.94 % ID/g at 5 d post-injection) in PDX models. Nanobody 89Zr-DFO-18.2-50H demonstrated a superior tumor-to-background ratio, positioning it as a promising tracer for detecting CLDN18.2-overexpressing lesions. 89Zr/177Lu-labeled VHH-Fc antibody 18.2−50C exhibited sustained higher tumor uptake than commercially available IMAB362 and provides a novel potential candidate for CLDN18.2-targeted radionuclide therapy.

items.title: Mechanochemical Engineering of High-Dose Inhalable Antibiotic Powders for Lower Respiratory Tract Infections
items.abstract: Lower respiratory tract infections require high local antibiotic concentrations in the lung, yet current dry powder inhaler (DPI) technologies are poorly suited to delivering high drug payloads while maintaining particle stability, dispersibility, and antimicrobial function. Here, we report a novel solvent-minimized mechanochemical strategy for the design of high-dose inhalable antibiotic powders based on ciprofloxacin−maleic acid (CIP−MA) salt formation. CIP−MA was prepared by oscillatory ball milling and co-processed with l-leucine (L-Leu), polyvinylpyrrolidone 10,000 (PVP), or D-mannitol (D-Man) using a design of experiment approach to tune the milling frequency, processing time, and excipient loading. The process generated crystalline, thermally stable powders with respirable particle sizes, controllable morphology, and reduced hygroscopicity compared with raw ciprofloxacin. Excipient selection provided distinct formulation functions. L-Leu improved dispersibility and achieved the highest proportion of particles with geometric diameter below 5 μm (89%) and fine particle fraction < 5 μm (∼37%) measured using a next-generation impactor at a 200 mg dose in the OrbitalTM high-dose DPI. However, PVP and D-Man favored improved device emptying and altered dissolution behavior. All CIP−MA formulations retained antimicrobial potency, with minimum inhibitory concentrations comparable to raw ciprofloxacin and approximately 95% reduction in viable Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilm. Importantly, the formulations showed accelerated dissolution under pulmonary-relevant flow-through conditions, releasing 70−80% of ciprofloxacin within 30 min, compared with the slower dissolution of raw ciprofloxacin. These findings establish oscillatory ball milling as a lower solvent use, tunable solid-state approach that integrates salt formation, preservation of crystallininty, particle engineering, high-dose aerosol delivery, and biological performance for next-generation inhalable antibiotic formulations.

items.title: Enhancing TB Therapy with Precision: Immunomodulatory Nanoparticles Co-Delivering Rifampicin and Vitamin D3 for Macrophage-Targeted Treatment
items.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a leading cause of death worldwide, with over 6.2 million cases and nearly 2 million deaths annually. Despite available chemotherapies, significant challenges persist, including prolonged treatment, poor compliance, and the rise of multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains. This study developed a biocompatible, multifunctional drug-delivery system using 1,3-β-glucan-functionalized chitosan-polycaprolactone nanoparticles (1,3-β-Glu-CS-PCL) for co-delivery of Rifampicin (RIF) and Vitamin D3 (VITD3) to alveolar macrophages. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation was enhanced by Glu-CS-PCL-RIF (1.5- to 1.8-fold) and Glu-CS-PCL-VITD3 (1.7-fold higher than non-functionalized nanoparticles). Glu-CS-PCL-VITD3 also stimulated TNF-α secretion (1.8-fold increase), indicating a shift in the immune response towards macrophage activation. Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) studies showed superior bactericidal activity of Glu-CS-PCL-RIF against a drug-susceptible laboratory strain and clinically resistant isolates of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), with a MIC of 0.00149 μg/mL, 2-fold lower than that of standard RIF. The combination of RIF and VITD3 demonstrated significant potency against drug-resistant TB with an effective dose 4x lower than standard treatment. Intracellular killing studies in THP-1 macrophages revealed that CS-PCL-RIF significantly reduced Mtb CFU counts (while containing approximately 15 times less RIF than the standard 50 μg/mL treatment). Glu-CS-PCL-VITD3 showed a notable reduction in CFUs compared to non-functionalized counterparts, illustrating the impact of 1,3-β-glucan functionalization. In conclusion, these multifunctional nanoparticles demonstrate strong potential for targeted anti-TB therapy by combining immunomodulation with enhanced antibacterial efficacy for future clinical applications.

items.title: The Ergogenic Effect of Caffeine in Rodents: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis, with a Narrative Synthesis of Adenosine A2A Receptor Mechanisms
items.abstract: Caffeine is a widely consumed ergogenic aid and a nonselective antagonist of adenosine receptors, including the facilitatory A2A subtype (A2AR), yet the magnitude of its performance-enhancing effect in rodents has not been formally quantified. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of rodent studies administering caffeine before exercise, with risk of bias assessed using the SYRCLE tool (PROSPERO CRD420250653223). Fourteen studies met the eligibility criteria. Six studies of a single systemic dose preceding an aerobic task, comprising 71 animals were pooled using a restricted maximum likelihood random-effects model with a Hartung–Knapp interval, yielding a large ergogenic estimate with wide uncertainty (Hedges’ g = +1.31; 95% CI + 0.29 to +2.32; I2 = 71%). Prespecified rules, applied independently of the observed effects, precluded pooling of the two anaerobic studies, which measured different performance constructs, and of the three chronic-exposure studies, whose dosing regimens and exercise modalities were not comparable; these are reported descriptively, as are the intracerebral administration experiments. Risk of bias was frequently unclear or high in the randomization and blinding domains. Receptor-level evidence is reported separately as a narrative synthesis, because the search was not constructed to retrieve mechanistic studies: the ergogenic response was abolished in global and forebrain A2AR-knockout mice and reproduced by the selective antagonist SCH 58261, whereas A2AR agonism with NECA was ergolytic and reversed by caffeine, and deletion of CD73, which depletes the extracellular adenosine pool preferentially supplying A2AR, recapitulated the ergogenic phenotype. The rodent evidence provides preclinical support for A2AR involvement in exercise-induced fatigue on an evidence base too small and too heterogeneous to support therapeutic or performance translation.

items.title: Inhibitors of PIM‐1 Signaling Pathways as Anticancer Agents: Pharmacological and Structural Viewpoints
items.abstract: Pim‐1, a carcinogenic threonine and serine kinase, inhibits apoptosis and advances the cell cycle. It is overexpressed in several human cancers. The proviral integration site of Moloney murine leukemia virus 1 is Pim‐1. Previous studies have shown that the Pim‐1 30‐UTR regulates the stability of Pim‐1 mRNA. Threonine and serine are identified as the proto‐oncogene Pim‐1 kinase. Pim‐1 mediates numerous biological processes, including apoptosis, cell division, proliferation, and cancer. Pim‐1‐mediated anticancer activity has been reported in several analogs of thiazole/ bis ‐thiazole, tetrazine, thiophenes, quinoline, pyrazolopyrimidine, 3‐cyanopyridine, thiazolidine‐2,4‐dione, thieno[2,3‐ b ]pyridine, triazolo[4,3‐ b ]pyridazine, pyrazolo[1,5‐ a ]pyrimidines, and pyrazolo[3,4‐ b ]pyridine derivatives. Additionally, flavonoids and amino alcohol compounds that constitute Pim‐1‐mediated cancer therapy have also been identified thus far. Many compounds with Pim‐1‐mediated cytotoxicity have been discovered up to this point, and scientists are currently concentrating on bringing novel compounds with anticancer potential to the market.

items.title: Design and synthesis of 5,11- and 5,12-disubstituted benzophenanthridinone analogues as DNA topoisomerase IB (TOP1) inhibitors and their anticancer activity
Dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) mono-esters and amides: synthesis and application in treating metal induced drug resistance in lung cancer
items.abstract: This study outlines the synthesis of dimercaptosuccinic mono-esters and amides from commercially available sources for tackling metal induced resistance to chemotherapy. Squarespace AI 7.1 was used to increase the resolution of the cell image/metal elements in this Table of Contents graphic.

items.title: Gas-Conditioned Message Passing Graph Neural Network for Permeability Prediction in Polymeric Membranes
items.abstract: Designing polymeric membranes for diverse gas-separation applications remains a critical challenge. Machine learning (ML) models can significantly accelerate this effort by capturing complex relationships between polymer-gas pairs and enabling permeability prediction over an extended chemical space of gases and polymers. In this work, we present a novel ML framework, the gas-conditioned message passing neural network (GC-MPNN), that jointly combines gas descriptors and polymer chemistry in a fused neural network model. Polymers are represented at the monomer level and encoded as molecular graphs, where node and edge information is propagated through message-passing layers. Six gas species (He, H2, N2, O2, CH4, and CO2) are represented using multiple descriptor sets spanning thermodynamic, kinetic, and electrostatic properties, along with one-hot encodings and combined feature sets that include kinetic plus thermodynamic descriptors and the full physicochemical descriptor set. For each descriptor combination, model hyperparameters are optimized using Bayesian optimization within a leave-one-gas-out (LOGO) validation framework. Test performance is then evaluated on the gas species excluded entirely from the corresponding training fold (out-of-training set) and compared across descriptor sets. For most gas species, the model achieves strong predictive performance (R2 ∼ 0.86–0.96), while CO2 remains more challenging in terms of absolute prediction accuracy (R2 ∼ 0.44). Active learning sampling further improves model performance by adding a few labeled samples from the test gas species into the training set. Among the three strategies tested, deep ensemble-based sampling and random sampling show strong improvement, with R2 reaching approximately ∼ 0.95 for all gas species, while evidential regression shows less consistent improvement. The model is further evaluated on a smaller polymer-gas dataset containing hydrocarbon species (C2H4, C2H6, C3H6, C3H8, and n-C4H10) using the GC-MPNN trained only on the six base gases, achieving moderate to strong Pearson correlations (r ∼ 0.77–0.89) for these out-of-training gases. Overall, this work presents a machine learning model that can learn transferable polymer-gas relationships from known gas species and extend them to previously unseen gases.

items.title: Reaction-Level Machine Learning for Condition Optimization in Suzuki–Miyaura Cross-Coupling
items.abstract: Selecting the ligand, base and solvent for a Suzuki–Miyaura coupling remains largely empirical, and highthroughput experimentation (HTE) screens are usually mined only for one reaction’s best condition. This study tests whether condition–yield relationships learned from some reactions transfer to reactions a model has never seen. Using a published HTE dataset of 5,760 reactions (15 quinoline couplings × 384 ligandbase–solvent combinations), models were trained in MATLAB on categorical condition descriptors with whole reactions held out: a global strategy trained on 12 reactions and was tested on 3; a focused strategy trained on 3 reactions sharing a boronic acid and was tested on a fourth. Selected models were compared with a majority-class predictor and a no-learning condition-average ranker, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Ranking transferred: high-yield (≥62%) precision–recall AUC was 0.21–0.34 where only 6–8% of conditions were high-yield and 0.92–0.96 where most were, above the base rate on every held-out reaction. However, the condition-average ranker matched the trained models within overlapping confidence intervals on all four held-out reactions, so what transfers is mainly the persistence of good-on-average conditions. At a fixed 62% cut-off, a RUSBoosted ensemble flagged 58–96% of high-yield conditions against 6–27% for the untuned average. Accuracy misled: naive Bayes scored 94.8% where always predicting low yield scores 94.3%. Exact yields did not transfer (external R2 at or below zero on most reactions), and focusing the training set left ranking unchanged (PR-AUC 0.943 vs 0.942). Reaction-level splits, minority-class metrics and a condition-average baseline should be standard when evaluating models on HTE data.

items.title: Synthesis and focused structure-activity investigation of the BB3 receptor antagonist, Bantag-1
items.abstract: The bombesin family G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), BB3, is an orphan GPCR linked to obesity and cancer. Limited selective chemical tools are available and only one high-affinity selective antagonist, Bantag-1, has been reported. Commercial supply of Bantag-1 has been sporadic, so we sought to develop an in-house synthesis pipeline of Bantag-1 to enable further BB3 research. Herein, we report the successful synthesis and pharmacological characterisation of Bantag-1 and a very focused structure-activity investigation. Pharmacological characterisation confirms the antagonistic properties of the synthesised peptide and provides insight into the possible contribution of the chosen counterion to storage stability. In GCaMP-based Ca2+ assays, the active synthesised peptide exhibited competitive antagonism of BAG-1-mediated BB3 signalling with a mean pA2 of 8.97, and a non-competitive antagonist profile against MK5046. Targeted structure-activity investigations further identified the C-terminal quaternary amine of Bantag-1 as a crucial moiety for antagonist activity, which is supported by our AI-based structural modelling and conventional docking of Bantag-1 with BB3. Together, we provide a practical synthetic route to the BB3 antagonist Bantag-1, establish key determinants of its activity and stability, and offer a structural framework for the rational design of next-generation BB3 chemical probes.

items.title: Engineered Phenylalanine Ammonia Lyases Enable Biocatalytic Synthesis of a Non-Canonical Phenylalanine Derivative at Scale.
items.abstract: Phenylalanine ammonia lyases (PALs) are an enzyme class of high synthetic utility as they catalyze the synthesis of chiral non-canonical phenylalanine amino acids from readily available cinnamic acids using simple ammonia as the amine donor. However, the applications of PAL in chemical manufacturing have been rare due to the challenges in identifying PALs active under industrially relevant conditions. Herein, we report our efforts towards engineering a PAL enzyme from Planctomyces brasiliensis (PbPAL) for the synthesis of L-3-cyanophenylalanine as an intermediate in the synthesis of Enlicitide, the clinically approved macrocyclic peptide to lower cholesterol levels. Protein engineering identified several key mutations that resulted in an evolved PbPAL variant with >100-fold improved activity and enhanced recombinant expression in E. coli. The computational studies suggest the final variant has increased substrate accessibility to the active site, which enabled high conversion (up to 97%) to L-3-cyanophenylalanine with excellent enantioselectivity at low enzyme loading (3 w/w%), demonstrated at up to 250-gram scale. In addition, the final variant represents a broad substrate scope against a variety of heterocyclic cinnamic acids with high enantioselectivity. This work showcases how protein engineering can enable the biocatalytic synthesis of non-canonical amino acids at scale.

items.title: Multivalent Avidity in C-type Lectins: How Glycan Surface Density and Presentation Define Superselective Recognition by DC-SIGN
items.abstract: Multivalent lectin–glycan interactions (MLGIs) are fundamental to many biological processes. While individual carbohydrate recognition domains (CRDs) determine glycan specificity, their clustering enhances binding affinity and selectivity through multivalency. However, the number of CRDs engaged during binding can vary, and individual CRDs may exhibit weak, non‑specific interactions with off‑target glycans. How these factors collectively shape MLGI behaviour remains unclear. Here, we address this question using a vitally important tetravalent, mannose‑specific C-type lectin DC‑SIGN (4M) and its engineered variants – a heterotetramer containing two mannose‑specific and two galactose‑specific CRDs (2M2G), and a fully galactose‑specific tetramer (4G) – and model surfaces presenting mannose at tuneable densities and defined organisation. We find that DC-SIGN 4M binding increases superlinearly with the increasing mannose density, although such ‘superselective’ recognition is attenuated at high mannose densities (≥50%). Interestingly, DC-SIGN 4M binds more strongly to mannose surfaces diluted by a low-affinity, non-specific galactose over a non-binding hydroxyl-terminated spacer. Whilst both 4M and 4G show weak cross‑binding to surfaces presenting non‑cognate glycans, 4M displays only ~2.7‑fold stronger binding to 100% mannose surface than 2M2G despite its higher mannose-specific valency. Confronting the experimental data with a mathematical model, we quantify the gradually decreasing contributions of the first, second, third and fourth CRD binding to the overall binding avidity, and how these are shaped by the balance of intrinsic CRD-glycan affinity, steric constraints imposed by the glycan surface and conformational constraints imposed by DC-SIGN 4M’s molecular organisation. Together, these results demonstrate that by modulating CRD number and glycan engagement, multivalent lectins can fine‑tune their binding avidity and selectivity for glycan surfaces of varying density and heterogeneity, thus affording them diverse functions and the ability to discriminate heterogeneous glycan environments on cell and pathogen surfaces.

items.title: Photocatalytic Divergent Skeletal Remodeling through Strain Release: Modular Access to Carbocycles and Heterocycles
items.abstract: Deconstructive skeletal remodeling of three-dimensional architectures offered a unique strategy to access structurally distinct carbocyclic and heterocyclic frameworks. A common, highly strained central σ-bond enabled two divergent skeletal-reorganization pathways, providing direct access to 1,3-disubstituted naphthalenes and pyrroles. A subtle change in reaction environment dictates divergent product formation during this photocatalytic double-strain-release skeletal-remodeling process. Under rigorously anhydrous conditions, skeletal reorganization furnishes carbocycles, whereas the addition of water redirects the reaction pathway toward heterocycle formation. The method accommodates a wide range of functional groups and substitution patterns. Mechanistic studies show that both pathways proceed through a common electron-transfer manifold and shared reactive intermediate. A delicate change in reaction conditions then leads to distinct aza-diene intermediates, driving divergent, regioselective outcomes.

items.title: Structure-Independent Genetic Algorithm-Based Molecular Optimization Using Pocket-Aware Molecular Representations
items.abstract: De novo molecular design typically depends on target structures or ligand poses, limiting its applicability when structural information is unavailable. Here, we introduce the pocket-aware molecular representation-guided genetic algorithm (PAMR-GA), a target-structure-independent molecular optimization framework that learns pocket-aware representations from structure–activity relationship (SAR) data using only molecular structures represented as SMILES strings and experimental pIC50 values. By encoding latent spatial constraints inferred from SAR without requiring target structures, the learned representations guide genetic algorithm-based molecular optimization through a Gaussian process surrogate model. Benchmarking on BACE-1 demonstrated that PAMR-GA achieved comparable predictive performance, docking scores, and drug-likeness profiles to existing optimization approaches while generating molecules with substantially greater structural novelty and higher Murcko scaffold diversity. Evaluation on four additional targets, including a kinase, serine proteases, and an NADbinding enzyme, further showed consistent improvements in molecular novelty. These results highlight PAMR-GA as a complementary approach for incorporating SAR-derived spatial constraints into de novo molecular design without requiring target structures. 1 Scientific Contribution PAMR-GA enables structure-independent molecular design by learning binding constraints implicitly from 2D structure–activity relationship data, without requiring protein structures or ligand poses. By introducing a pocket-aware molecular representation that integrates solvent-accessible surface area and partial-charge features, PAMR-GA bridges molecular topology with 3D binding compatibility. Our results demonstrate that constrained generation, rather than improved activity prediction alone, drives structural novelty. Evaluation across five diverse targets from four protein classes highlights the generalizability of PAMR-GA as a broadly applicable framework for target-aware molecular design.

items.title: Directing Generation of Polynuclear Plutonium Species with Reduction and Protonation
items.abstract: Formation of multinuclear complexes is a defining feature of plutonium chemistry, but such reactivity tends to be uncontrolled under most conditions, hindering selective transformation of compounds containing this challenging element.Here, the chemistry leading to formation of two multinuclear complexes of plutonium coordinated by a chelating, dianionic ligand (denoted L N M ) has been studied.The complexes are generated on-demand via reduction and proton-assisted condensation of a mononuclear plutonyl(VI) complex.One complex contains two plutonium(IV) centers bridged by a central µ 2 -oxo and each capped with κ 2 -acetate ligands.The other complex contains the same [Pu IV2 O] core but is instead capped by anionic [Pu V O 2 L N M ] -fragments, thus constituting a linear tetrameric motif of the form [PuOL N M (µ 2 -O)PuL N M ] 2 (µ 2 -O).The capping interactions can be viewed through the lens of Sullivan-type "cation-cation" interactions between the Lewis-basic oxo moieties of the [Pu V O 2 L N M ] -species and Lewis-acidic Pu IV centers.Although such cation-cation interactions are generally favored by pentavalent actinyls, direct binding of [Pu V O 2 ] to [Pu IV ] has not been observed in prior work; this motif has been characterized here with Raman spectroscopy and Xray diffraction analysis.Electroanalytical, spectroscopic, and H/D kinetic isotope effect (KIE) data support a mechanism leading to the polynuclear species that involves sequential reduction, proton transfer, and condensation.As [AnO oxo -H] species are likely intermediates in the observed reactivity, experimentally measured reduction potentials and computationally predicted pK a values have been used to compute [AnO oxo -H] bond dissociation free energies (BDFEs) across the U, Np, Pu series.The results, considered in the broader context of proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) chemistry, suggest that actinyl-derived hydroxide complexes could be potent H-atom donors and thus could be used to direct new types of reactivity.

items.title: Editing-site selection for constrained QED improvement through frozen GenMol remasking
items.abstract: Shallow network, boosted decision-tree and graph-attention models were trained on a remaskingsite selection task utilizing the GenMol generator and a subset of bioactive molecules (30,000 training and 5,000 validation) from the ChEMBL 37 dataset. Models learned to optimize fragment selection policies by maximizing the fraction of successful remasked candidates, with success contingent on an increase in the RDKit quantitative estimate of drug-likeness (QED) under several chemical constraints. All three models show a marked increase in generation of at least one successful derivative out of 16 remasking runs on a held-out test set comprising 5,000 bioactive molecules: 66.0%–66.9%, 67.0%–67.4% and 66.3%–66.7% for the shallow network, boosted decision-tree and graph models, compared to 54.8%–55.6% for a fixed policy selecting the largest fragment (one-sided bootstrap 𝑝 < 10−4 for all models). A trivial baseline, selecting fragments randomly, displays 47.3% success. The fraction of valid candidates produced by all policies is about 99%. Analysis of learned policies showed consistent trends among the three models. Selection is biased toward larger pendants. Additionally, pendant selection shows several trends conditioned on the pendant-side, but not core-side, attachment atom. Larger carbon-and oxygen-attached fragments are selected more often (two-sided binomial 𝑝 < 10−10 in every model); a reversed tendency, albeit not statistically significant (𝑝 ≈ 0.02–0.30), is observed for nitrogen attachments. Controlling for fragment size, learned policies show preference for pendant-side nitrogen over oxygen and carbon, and for both chlorine and bromine over fluorine and carbon. Only LightGBM displays a statistically significant (two-sided exact binomial 𝑝 < 0.01) preference for sp2 over sp3 hybridization of pendant-side carbon atoms. At equal size, carbonyl-attached pendants are preferred to hydrocarbons.

items.title: Cu-Catalyzed Enantioconvergent Synthesis of N-Alkyl Amides from Racemic Alcohols
items.abstract: Enantioconvergent amidation of racemic alcohols offers a powerful retrosynthetic disconnection to convert abundant, readily accessible alcohol feedstocks into chiral N-alkyl amides, while streamlining access to valuable enantioenriched primary amines. However, a mechanistic framework that can integrate efficient C(sp3)–O bond cleavage with enantioselective amidation has remained understudied. Herein, we report the enantioconvergent deoxygenative amidation of racemic alcohols through a Cu-catalyzed radical relay. β-Scission of oxidant-derived electrophilic alkoxy radicals was leveraged as a radical-umpolung event, producing nucleophilic methyl radicals that effectively activate alcohol substrate-derived xanthates. Computation-guided optimization revealed that increasing xanthate electrophilicity facilitates methyl-radical addition and improves reaction efficiency. The transformation accommodates a variety of alcohols and amides with high enantioselectivity, and the reaction conditions are compatible with medicinally relevant functional groups, heterocycles, and pharmaceutical frameworks. Synthetic applications of this protocol streamline access to enantioenriched β-amino alcohols and biologically active primary amines, circumventing the need for enantioenriched alcohol precursors. Mechanistic studies revealed that polarity matching favors the capture of electron-deficient carbon-centered radicals by electron-rich CuII–amidates. Under catalytic conditions, however, the greater acidity of electron-deficient amides facilitates transmetalation, accelerating the formation of CuII–amidate and enhancing coupling efficiency.

items.title: Molecular Property Prediction with Well-Calibrated Uncertainties via Graph Neural Networks and Conformal Quantile Regression
items.abstract: Accurate predictive uncertainty quantification (pUQ) is critical for assessing chemical property predictions. Incorrect quantification could lead to costly synthesis and characterization of drug candidates destined to fail, or result in misguided environmental regulations. This work integrates Conformal Quantile Regression (CQR) with graph neural networks to achieve accurate molecular property prediction and well-calibrated predictive uncertainty quantification. By combining conformal prediction with quantile regression, CQR provides model-agnostic, distribution-free prediction intervals with valid coverage for finite samples. We benchmark it against established pUQ approaches, including ensembling, Monte Carlo dropout sampling, mean-variance estimation, and evidential regression. Our experiments on datasets spanning quantum mechanics, physical chemistry, and pharmacokinetics show that CQR generally provides strong calibration while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy and uncertainty-ranking performance. It also effectively captures heteroskedastic noise across the data, which is a key requirement for robust pUQ. Furthermore, we demonstrate its efficacy with an uncertainty-guided retrospective virtual screening experiment for antibiotic discovery, achieving hit rates above 90%. These results establish CQR as a promising, scalable tool for pUQ in molecular property prediction, supporting informed decision-making in applications such as active learning and compound screening for drug discovery and materials design.

items.title: Rapid mechanochemical dinitrogen fixation for single-atom skeletal editing
items.abstract: Direct utilization of dinitrogen (N2) in organic synthesis remains an unmet challenge in sustainable chemistry, particularly under mild conditions. Conventional transition-metal-mediated N2 functionalization typically requires elaborately designed catalysts under harsh conditions, limiting operational practicality. Here, we report a mechanochemical strategy that achieves rapid, lithium-mediated N2 reduction at ambient pressure and temperature in under two minutes, delivering polymorphic mixtures of α- and β-lithium nitride. The resulting metal nitride serves as a versatile platform for single nitrogen-atom transfer: applied to skeletal conversion reactions, it enables direct O-to-N transmutation of furans and aromatic oxonium salts into the corresponding pyrroles and pyridine derivatives, establishing a formal incorporation of N2 into N-heterocycles. The photophysical consequences of the single-atom edit on excited-state properties of the molecular chromophores were evaluated.

items.title: Computational design and prioritization of database-absent small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist candidates from public bioactivity data
items.abstract: Public bioactivity data were used to construct a reproducible workflow for the computational prioritization of small-molecule glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonist candidates. Exact IC50, EC50, and Ki measurements were standardized, converted to pActivity, and deduplicated after structural exclusion of peptide-like records. The resulting dataset comprised 337 compounds and 155 Murcko scaffolds. Morgan fingerprints and physicochemical descriptors were evaluated using ridge regression, random forest, and XGBoost with scaffold-based validation. Random forest provided the lowest mean five-fold cross-validation root-mean-square error (RMSE; 0.497 pActivity units). Its scaffold-disjoint holdout performance was R2 = 0.236, RMSE = 0.760, and mean absolute error = 0.499. Local modifications of orforglipron generated 1,701 valid, unique analogs. Composite prioritization incorporated predicted activity, quantitative estimate of druglikeness, synthetic accessibility, and database absence. All 146 queried structures were absent from ChEMBL and PubChem under the implemented identity criteria. Of these, 46 passed an exploratory physicochemical filter, and 20 were shortlisted. No generated candidate passed the stricter drug-likeness filter. The leading candidate, GLP1R-01162, had predicted pActivity 7.677 and composite score 0.5400. These results defined an auditable set of computational hypotheses; they did not establish agonism, experimental potency, synthetic feasibility, or global novelty. Functional testing and independent novelty assessment remained necessary.

items.title: BRACE: Bayesian Residual-covariance Adaptive Calibration for Multi-Endpoint ADMET Prediction
items.abstract: Deciding which ADMET assays to run on a compound requires a calibrated probability that it will pass each assay not yet measured, given those already run. A multi-task predictor supplies these via the cross-assay covariance of its prediction errors (residuals), but this covariance is usually estimated once, from historical data. It therefore misses correlations specific to a program’s chemical series (scaffolds) and knows nothing about assays unique to the program. With only hundreds to thousands of program compounds, we adapt this covariance rather than retrain the predictor. BRACE merges historical and program residuals by expectation–maximization into one covariance covering every assay, then corrects it per scaffold series with an Inverse-Wishart hierarchical model; an optional copula handles non-Gaussian data. A closed-form identity makes its posterior-mean covariance equal the Ledoit–Wolf shrinkage estimator exactly, so its prior strength comes from the data, without cross-validation. On a semi-synthetic 36-assay benchmark built from the residual covariance of about 780,000 real ADMET compounds, BRACE cuts the pass-probability mean absolute error by up to 76% versus the QComp multi-task baseline. Its always-on merging step matches or beats QComp in all 29 settings of a robustness sweep; the optional per-scaffold step helps when series-specific structure exists and hurts when it does not, and we map when to use it (chosen with hindsight here; an automatic rule is future work). On a real temporal split, the per-scaffold steps raise AUC-ROC from 0.789 to 0.860 and MCC from 0.37 to 0.53, and lower Brier from 0.187 to 0.152. However, about 96% of that gain comes from recalibrating each series’ mean and variance, which simple untuned shrinkage also achieves; BRACE’s distinctive cross-assay term adds about 4% here and matters mainly under strong cross-assay structure.

items.title: ARGUS: A Four-Signal Joint Model for H5N1 Neuraminidase Inhibitor Resistance Prediction
items.abstract: Oseltamivir and zanamivir are the primary antivirals against H5N1 influenza, yet resistance profiles at the structural level remain incompletely characterized. Phenotypic screening requires one to two weeks in biosafety level 3 containment; during an active spillover event, this timescale is incompatible with clinical decisions. We present ARGUS (Affinity-and Representation-Guided Unified Scoring), a learned joint model combining four independent structural signals into a unified resistance risk framework: molecular docking affinity, protein language model evolutionary likelihood, perturbation response scanning, and all-atom pocket volume analysis. This work comprises two major components: (1) a comprehensive dual-drug saturation mutagenesis of the H5N1 neuraminidase binding pocket (1,102 mutations, 551 per drug) revealing a striking 166:1 asymmetry between oseltamivir-specific and zanamivir-specific resistance mutations, reflecting zanamivir’s substrate-mimicking pharmacophore; and (2) a novel four-signal learned joint model validated against 37 published fold-resistance measurements spanning H5N1, H1N1pdm09, H3N2, and H7N9 backgrounds (oseltamivir fold-resistance was the fitting target). The four-signal model achieves leave-one-out Spearman ρ = 0.628 (p = 0.000032), with a 95% bootstrap interval of [0.428, 0.845] for the in-sample correlation and a permutation p < 0.001. The earlier two-signal linear blend reached ρ = 0.659 (p = 0.0142) on only n=8 mutations, so the two figures are not directly comparable. The learned weights make docking the dominant signal (96.3% of the total weight) with ESM-2 LLR at 3.7%, which fits the view that protein language models alone conflate evolutionary constraint with drug-resistance specificity. Applied to the 2024 US H5N1 B3.13 outbreak, all 21 outbreak mutations are pocket-distal for both drugs, predicting maintained efficacy of both antivirals. ARGUS provides immediate structural assessment of any novel neuraminidase mutation without experimental work, and the full saturation landscape and trained models are released as a public resource on Zenodo.

items.title: Bioinspired Quantum-Guided Engineering of Activatable Probes via Intermolecular Electron Transfer for Single-Cell Molecular Diagnosis
items.abstract: Fluorescence imaging holds theoretical sensitivity for single-cell molecular diagnosis, yet practical performance is limited by residual probe-intrinsic fluorescence arising from incomplete control of intramolecular electron transfer within the probe scaffold. Inspired by natural photosynthesis, where spatially organized pigments enable quantum-coherent excitation transport and precise intermolecular electron transfer, we develop a bioinspired quantum chemistry-guided engineering (BQCE) strategy that programs intermolecular electron transfer to construct molecular assembly based background-eliminating activatable molecule probes (BEAMs). Guided by BQCE, the peroxynitrite-responsive hemicyanine-based BEAM1, despite the intrinsically difficult-to-quench nature of this fluorophore scaffold, achieves near-zero background fluorescence, 103.5-fold activation, and an unprecedented detection limit of 1.3 nM. BEAM1 resolves basal ONOO– fluxes at single-cell resolution, enabling single-cell molecular diagnosis that distinguishes malignant from normal cells based solely on endogenous redox signatures. In vivo, BEAM1 enables detection of lymph nodes containing sparsely distributed metastatic cells, with subsequent ex vivo histological analysis identifying metastatic deposits as small as ∼ 35 μm, extending fluorescence imaging into the regime of single-cell level early cancer detection.

items.title: Macrocycle Screening against the C-Terminal Region of CHD4 Uncovers Its Role as an Interaction Hub in the Formation of the Nucleosome Remodeling and Deacetylase Complex
items.abstract: The Nucleosome Remodeling and Deacetylase complex (NuRD) plays a key role in regulating hemoglobin expression in adult erythroid cells. Selectively disrupting this complex potently induces the expression of fetal hemoglobin, a proven therapeutic strategy for treating beta-hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell anemia. In these studies, we have used mRNA display to identify small macrocyclic peptides that inhibit the interaction between two core components of NuRD, the SANT-SLIDE domain of CHD4 and the CR2 domain of GATAD2A. In addition, the screen suggested a second binding site on the CHD4 domain. Based on this observation, we hypothesized and confirmed that CDK2AP1 bound to this region of CHD4, leading us to purify and determine the structure of the ternary complex between CHD4, GATAD2A, and CDK2AP1. The results of our studies show that the SANT-SLIDE domain of CHD4 functions as a critical interaction hub in the formation of NuRD and suggest a strategy to block NuRD function for therapy.

items.title: Redox-Induced Polymeric Micelle-to-Coacervate Transition for Enhanced Endosomal Escape, Prolonged Drug Retention, and Improved Sequential Drug Delivery
items.abstract: Polymeric micelles (PMs) and coacervate microdroplets (CMs) are both promising delivery vehicles, yet each suffers from distinct limitations. The delivery efficiency of PMs is often hindered by factors, such as limited endosome escape and uncontrolled drug release. On the other hand, CMs are prone to coalescence and aging, which hamper long-term storage and systemic injection. Here, by employing an intracellular morphological transition strategy, these drawbacks can be efficiently addressed without compromising their inherent advantages. The system exists as nanosized PMs during storage and circulation. Upon internalization by the tumor cells, the highly reductive intracellular environment induces the detachment of the poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) shell and results in in situ formation of CMs. The formed CMs can effectively escape from endosomes by disrupting the endosomal membrane, facilitating the release of drugs into the cytoplasm. Furthermore, the CMs can serve as drug reservoirs, protecting the cargo from burst release and degradation, thus significantly prolonging the retention time and improving systemic delivery efficacy. Notably, the CMs can also sequester free drugs from the surrounding environment, enhancing sequential therapy by increasing the intratumoral accumulation of the temporally staggered agents. Thus, this micelle-to-coacervate transformable platform illuminates new possibilities for both types of drug-delivery systems.

items.title: Construction of Difluoro-Functionalized Heterocycles via Annulation and Concomitant Fluorine Incorporation
items.abstract: Herein, we report a novel cascade annulation strategy for the expedient synthesis of difluoro-functionalized quinolines and quinoxalines. This protocol is compatible with both 2-aryl and 2-vinyl anilines, enabling the controllable incorporation of various fluorine-containing functionalities, including CF2H, SCF2H, and SeCF2H. For CF2H installation, the annulation of 2-aryl/vinyl anilines with BrCF2CO2Et was developed, in which BrCF2CO2Et serves as a C1 building block and a difluorocarbene precursor. Notably, in the presence of external sulfur or selenium sources, a one-pot reaction with S/Se and BrCF2CO2Et was realized, providing a diverse array of valuable fluoromethylthio(seleno)-functionalized N-heterocycles under metal-free conditions. Furthermore, the direct introduction of the SCF2H moiety into quinoxalines was achieved via difluoromethyl thiolation under the same reaction conditions.

items.title: Bioinspired Total Syntheses of Tricrilactones D and F, Crispatumine I, and 2,3- trans -Crispatumine I
items.abstract: The bioinspired total syntheses of tricrilactones D and F, crispatumine I, and 2,3-trans-crispatumine I are reported. The conserved lactone-fused 9/5/6 spirocyclic core of these products was constructed via a mild bioinspired one-pot three-component cascade of protrilactione A, the purported biosynthetic precursor. Variation of the aldehyde and β-ketolactone components enable access to both homo- and heterocoupled natural products, each in 13 steps (longest linear sequence).

items.title: Practical C(sp3)–F Bond Construction via Metal-Free Heterogeneous Photodecarboxylative Fluorination in Continuous Flow
items.abstract: We report a robust, metal-free heterogeneous photocatalytic protocol for the direct decarboxylative fluorination of aliphatic carboxylic acids utilizing graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4). Operating under visible light, this strategy exhibits good substrate generality, particularly for activated aliphatic carboxylic acids and facilitates the late-stage functionalization of complex pharmaceutical scaffolds. The operationally simple photocatalyst can be recycled over seven consecutive cycles while maintaining high catalytic efficacy. Crucially, a continuous-flow, gram-scale synthesis validates its practical scalability. Mechanistic studies confirm a closed-loop photoredox pathway, establishing a versatile platform for C(sp3)–F bond construction.

items.title: Stereoselective Defluorinative Thiolation of gem -Difluoroalkenes with Thiols via Nucleophilic Substitution
items.abstract: Monofluoroalkenes are valuable mimics of enol and amide bonds, making them important structural motifs in drug discovery. Herein, we report a transition-metal-free, stereoselective defluorinative thiolation of gem-difluoroalkenes with thiols under simple base promotion. This transformation proceeds efficiently through a nucleophilic substitution pathway, affording a broad array of monofluoroalkenyl sulfides in generally good yields with excellent stereoselectivities (Z/E up to 24:1). This protocol features a broad substrate scope and excellent functional group tolerance, representing a convenient approach to stereodefined monofluoroalkenyl sulfides.

items.title: Highly Diastereoselective Synthesis of Trifluoromethylated Spirocyclopropanes from 2-(2′-Ketoalkyl)-1,3-Indandiones and CF3-Imidoyl Sulfoxonium Ylides
items.abstract: A metal-free and highly diastereoselective strategy for the synthesis of trifluoromethylated spirocyclopropanes has been developed using CF3-imidoyl sulfoxonium ylides (TFISYs) and 2-(2′-ketoalkyl)–1,3-indandiones. The transformation proceeds through a base-mediated cascade process to furnish densely functionalized trifluoromethylated spirocyclopropanes in good to excellent yields with excellent diastereoselectivity. The protocol exhibits a broad substrate scope, gram-scale applicability, and synthetic versatility through post-functionalization, providing efficient access to fluorinated spirocyclic architectures of potential medicinal relevance.

items.title: Hybridization‐Mediated Reversible sgRNA Caging Enables Tumor‐Selective Gene Editing for Potentiating Antitumor Immunity via cGAS Demethylation
items.abstract: Spatiotemporal precision remains a critical challenge against the gene editing technology used for disease treatment. We herein developed a tumor cell‐selective CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system by introducing a complementary single‐stranded DNA (ssDNA) containing apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) sites (AP‐ssDNA) along the target region of single‐guided RNA (sgRNA). The engineered hybrid (AP‐ssDNA/sgRNA) could tracelessly release the native sgRNA in tumor cells due to cleavage of AP‐ssDNA by the overexpressed apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (APE1), thus enabling tumor‐selective gene editing. Subsequently, a biodegradable lipid nanoparticle based on dynamic covalent bonding was developed to codeliver Cas9‐encoding mRNA (mCas9) with AP‐ssDNA/sgRNA targeting the SUV39H1 gene, which mediated silence of cyclic GMP‐AMP synthase (cGAS) methylation to activate stimulator of interferon genes (STING) and enhanced antitumor immunity. As thus, when coupled with radiotherapy, the gene editing platform provoked robust antitumor efficacy in B16F10 xenograft tumor‐bearing mice. This study provides a versatile paradigm for conditionally controlled gene editing and highlights the therapeutic potential of cGAS demethylation in reactivating cGAS‐STING pathway for antitumor immunotherapy.

items.title: Hierarchically Molecular Programming of Antiparallel H‑Aggregates for NIR Type I Photochemistry
items.abstract: Developing near‐infrared (NIR) photosensitizers with effective type I reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation remains challenging. H‑aggregates promote triplet formation and charge transfer, but often suffer from substantial absorption blueshifts and excessive thermal deactivation that compromise photosensitization efficacy. Herein, a hierarchically molecular programming strategy is proposed to construct minimal‐blueshift H‐aggregates as robust NIR type I photosensitizers. Primary engineering via π‐bridge extension and acceptor strengthening within a twisted–planar donor–π–acceptor scaffold endows the antiparallel H‐packed TNCF3‐C6‐C2 aggregates with strong NIR absorption (749 nm) and predominant type I ROS generation. Secondary side‐chain programming further regulates the H‐packing and intermolecular electronic interactions to enhance type I ROS generation. Structural, photochemical and theoretical investigations revealed that the branched side chains promote molecular planarization and robust H‑packing, thereby enhancing intersystem crossing and intermolecular charge transfer. The optimized TNCF3‐2C6 with symmetric branched side chain exhibited minimal absorption blueshift (20 nm) upon H‐aggregation, enhanced NIR harvesting ability and a further ∼2‐fold enhancement in ROS generation over the initial TNCF3‐C6‐C2 H‐aggregates, thereby delivering potent tumor inhibition both in vitro and in vivo. Built upon the hierarchical programming of H‐aggregates, this work establishes a supramolecular design paradigm toward modulating excitonic coupling and excited‐state dynamics for high‐performance photo‐functional materials.

items.title: Perturbation of the Electron Transport Chain by Guanidinium‐Based Cationic Polymers Induces Metabolic Collapse in Persister‐Enriched Bacterial Populations
items.abstract: Bacterial persisters are widely regarded as dormant or hypometabolic cells that survive antibiotic treatment with suppressed metabolic activity. Here, we show that this apparent quiescence is accompanied by a heightened vulnerability to electron transport chain (ETC)‐associated perturbation by guanidinium‐based cationic polymers. PO 3 G, a representative polymer, preferentially kills persister‐enriched populations while markedly perturbing respiratory electron transfer. Following this ETC‐associated perturbation, persister‐enriched populations exhibit sustained superoxide‐associated oxidative stress and fail to restore NADH/NAD + homeostasis, leading to progressive loss of viability. Consistent with this ETC dependency, PO 3 G also markedly reduces persister‐enriched population induced by diverse triggers across bacterial species and achieves up to 7‐log reductions in bacterial burden in vivo. These results establish a mechanistic link between cationic polymer‐induced ETC‐associated perturbation and persister elimination, highlighting limited recovery from respiratory and redox perturbation as a vulnerability underlying the preferential killing of persisters.

items.title: A general synthesis of tryptophan-crosslinked macrocyclic peptides enabled by a dual-functional directing group
Optimized and Automated Production of [18F]FFNP for Progesterone Receptor PET Imaging
items.abstract: [18F]FFNP is a promising investigational radiopharmaceutical for PET imaging of progesterone receptor (PR) expression in breast cancer. [18F]FFNP PET imaging enables noninvasive assessment of PR expression and serves as a valuable diagnostic tool for determining the functional endocrine status of ER+ breast tumors to guide endocrine therapy. In this study, we report a robust and fully automated radiosynthesis of [18F]FFNP using a commercially available radiosynthesizer. The ratio of the mesylate precursor to the K2.2.2/K2CO3 complex was found to be critical for optimizing radiochemical yield. The optimized and automated radiosynthesis process was completed within 50 min and successfully passed three consecutive validation runs, producing [18F]FFNP activity in 19.52–23.91% decay-corrected radiochemical yields at the end of synthesis. Approximately 215–265 mCi (7.96–9.81 GBq) of [18F]FFNP activity was obtained with high radiochemical purity (99.65–99.72%) and molar activity (16.83–37.40 Ci/μmol [623–1384 GBq/μmol]) in our cGMP-compliant PET Radiochemistry facility. All drug product specifications passed quality control (QC) testing and met the requirements for clinical investigational use.

items.title: Can GLP-1s heal the brain? Obesity drugs get a makeover for addiction and depression
Disrupting the NAD+/NAM metabolic ratio driven by IL-1β inflammatory response potentiates chemotherapy and chemoimmunotherapy in mice
items.abstract: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) replenishment sensitizes tumors to immunotherapy. However, chemotherapy-induced NAD+ metabolic reprogramming remains poorly understood. Here, we show that chemotherapy induces a macrophage-dependent IL-1β inflammatory response and NAD+ metabolic reprogramming, thereby conferring chemoresistance via CD44. Mechanistically, IL-1β-induced NAD+ salvage cooperates with the clearance of nicotinamide (NAM), the physiological inhibitor of the NAD+-consuming enzymes sirtuins, to drive CD44-mediated chemoresistance by boosting the NAD+/NAM ratio for sirtuin activation. NAM phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT)-mediated NAD+ salvage recycles NAD+ from NAM and further triggers serine biosynthesis, ultimately supporting NAM N-methyltransferase (NNMT)-mediated NAM clearance.
